metadata.title: Derived categories of families of sextic del Pezzo surfaces

extraction_notes.note: The introduction's informal restatements of Theorem 5.2, Propositions 5.13, 5.16, 6.2, 6.6, 6.8, 6.9 and Corollary 5.19 get no nodes (the numbered environments are kept). The outlook paragraphs and the closing discussion of Section 6.1 (Severi-Brauer and Weil-restriction generalizations) are not extracted either.

The classification into Types 0-5 is a cited description list followed by two TikZ tables of curve configurations and toric polygons. The list is one external theorem node; the pictures are not extracted.

Definition or claim: each sentence introduces notation (the derived dual, the relative duality functor, the modules E_i) and also asserts a property (anti-autoequivalence, generation). Typed as definitions because the symbols are used later.

These numbered equations define objects (the bundles frak E_Z, h_d, M_d(X), F_d(X), the functors Phi_d). Kept as equation nodes as the numbered-equation rule requires, with definition-like uses edges from them.

Serre duality for Gorenstein schemes and the Picard lattice lemma are folklore (uncited), and Lemma 2.4 is attributed to Bridgeland. All three are marked external, while their proofs in the paper are origin paper.

Corollary 5.5 is justified only by the clause 'Considering base changes to geometric points of S and using Theorem 4.5, we obtain', which runs straight into the environment with no colon or period. That clause is used as a prose proof node.

The parser marks only the third item of the first itemize in the proof of Lemma 6.1 as an author label. Steps therefore start at that item, which splits the 'either ... or ... or' sentence across two steps.

Two finishing-step warnings are left in place because the symbol is used in another sense. E_i stands for both the exceptional divisors (Section 2) and the standard exceptional modules (Appendix A, used in the proof of Proposition 3.17). S_0 stands for both the open set S minus S_1 (Section 6.3) and the simple module (Appendix A).
The source says 'in case (3)' for the Jordan type labelled (2), and Lemma 5.9 has the typo 'compativle'. Both are copied verbatim.

nodes.name: Non-existence of S-linear decompositions for degree <= 4 (Auel-Bernardara)
nodes.statement: For $d \le 4$, however, the results of~\cite[Theorem~5.1]{auel2015semiorthogonal} show that an $S$-linear semiorthogonal decomposition for a general flat family~${\mathscr{X}} \to S$ whose components are twisted derived categories of finite coverings of~$S$ does not exist.
nodes.statement_short: For del Pezzo families of degree at most 4 there is in general no S-linear decomposition into twisted derived categories of finite covers.

nodes.name: Characteristic of the base field
nodes.statement: Throughout the paper we work over a field ${\mathsf{k}}$, whose characteristic is assumed to be distinct from~2 and~3.

nodes.name: Bounded derived category D(X)
nodes.statement: For a scheme $X$ we denote by ${\mathbf{D}}(X)$ the bounded derived category of coherent sheaves on $X$, and unless something else is specified explicitly, this is what we mean by a derived category.

nodes.name: Twisted derived category D(X, beta)
nodes.statement: For a Brauer class $\beta$ on a scheme $X$ we denote by ${\mathbf{D}}(X,\beta)$ the twisted bounded derived category of coherent sheaves.

nodes.name: Sextic du Val del Pezzo surface
nodes.statement: A {\sf sextic du Val del Pezzo surface} is a normal integral projective surface $X$ over a field ${\mathsf{k}}$ with at worst du Val singularities and ample anticanonical class such that $K_X^2 = 6$.
nodes.definiendum: sextic du Val del Pezzo surface
differentia: with at worst du Val singularities
nodes.label: definition:dp6

nodes.name: du Val surfaces are Gorenstein
nodes.statement: Recall that du Val surface singularities are just canonical singularities or, equivalently, rational double points. In particular, any surface $X$ with du Val singularities is Gorenstein, so $\omega_X$ is a line bundle, $K_X$ is a Cartier divisor, and its square is well-defined.
nodes.statement_short: du Val singularities are rational double points, so such surfaces are Gorenstein and $K_X$ is Cartier.

nodes.name: Minimal resolution $\pi \colon \widetilde{X} \to X$
nodes.statement: Let $\pi \colon {\widetilde{X}} \to X$ be the minimal (in particular crepant) resolution of singularities of $X$.

nodes.name: Weak del Pezzo resolution as a triple blowup of P^2
nodes.statement: It is well-known (see, e.g.~\cite[Section~8.4.2]{dolgachev2012cag}) that the surface ${\widetilde{X}}$ is rational and can be obtained from ${\mathbb{P}}^2$ by a sequence of three blowups of a point, i.e., we have a diagram \begin{equation*} X \xleftarrow{\ \pi\ } {\widetilde{X}} = X_3 \to X_2 \to X_1 \to X_0 = {\mathbb{P}}^2, \end{equation*} where each map $X_i \to X_{i-1}$ is the blowup of a point $P_i \in X_{i-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: The minimal resolution of a sextic du Val del Pezzo surface is rational and is obtained from P^2 by three successive point blowups.

nodes.name: Hyperplane class h
nodes.statement: We denote by $h$ the hyperplane class on ${\mathbb{P}}^2$ and its pullback to ${\widetilde{X}}$.

nodes.name: Exceptional divisors $E_i$ and classes $e_i$
nodes.statement: We denote by $E_i \subset {\widetilde{X}}$ the pullback (i.e., the total preimage) to ${\widetilde{X}}$ of the exceptional divisor of $X_i \to X_{i-1}$ and by $e_i$ its class in $\mathrm{Pic}({\widetilde{X}})$.

nodes.name: Picard lattice of $\widetilde{X}$
nodes.statement: We have $\mathrm{Pic}({\widetilde{X}}) \cong {\mathbb{Z}}\langle h, e_1,e_2,e_3 \rangle$, with $h^2 = 1$, $e_i^2 = -1$, $he_i = e_ie_j = 0$ for all $i \ne j$. Moreover, \begin{equation} K_{\widetilde{X}} = -3h + e_1 + e_2 + e_3 = \pi^*K_X. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Pic of the resolution is the standard rank-4 lattice spanned by h, e_1, e_2, e_3, with $K = -3h + e_1+e_2+e_3 = \pi^*K_X$.
nodes.label: lemma:pic-tx

nodes.name: Canonical class of $\widetilde{X}$
nodes.statement: K_{\widetilde{X}} = -3h + e_1 + e_2 + e_3 = \pi^*K_X.
nodes.label: eq:ktx

nodes.name: Six types of sextic du Val del Pezzo surfaces
nodes.statement: By~\cite[Section~8.4.2]{dolgachev2012cag} there are six possibilities for configurations of the blowup centers and $(-2)$-curves on ${\widetilde{X}}$ (see Table~\ref{table:dp6} below for a picture). \begin{description} \item[Type 0] Neither of $P_i$ lies on the exceptional divisor in $X_{i-1}$ and their images in ${\mathbb{P}}^2$ do not lie on a common line. Then ${\widetilde{X}}$ contains no $(-2)$-curves and $X = {\widetilde{X}}$ is smooth. \item[Type 1] Neither of $P_i$ lies on the exceptional divisor in $X_{i-1}$ but their images in ${\mathbb{P}}^2$ lie on a common line. Then ${\widetilde{X}}$ contains a unique $(-2)$-curve (the strict transform $\Delta_{123}$ of that line) and~$X$ has one~$A_1$ singularity. \item[Type 2] The point $P_2$ lies on the exceptional divisor of $X_1 \to X_0$, the point $P_3$ is away from the exceptional divisors, and the line through $P_1$ in the direction of $P_2$ on ${\mathbb{P}}^2$ does not pass through the image of $P_3$. Then ${\widetilde{X}}$ contains a unique $(-2)$-curve (the strict transform $\Delta_{12}$ of the exceptional divisor of $X_1 \to X_0$) and $X$ has one $A_1$ singularity. \item[Type 3] The point $P_2$ lies on the exceptional divisor of $X_1 \to X_0$, the point $P_3$ is away from the exceptional divisors, but the line through $P_1$ in the direction of $P_2$ on ${\mathbb{P}}^2$ passes through the image of $P_3$. Then ${\widetilde{X}}$ contains two disjoint $(-2)$-curves (the strict transforms $\Delta_{123}$ and $\Delta_{12}$ of the line on~${\mathbb{P}}^2$ and of the exceptional divisor of $X_1 \to X_0$, respectively) and $X$ has two $A_1$ singularities. \item[Type 4] The point $P_2$ lies on the exceptional divisor of $X_1 \to X_0$, the point $P_3$ lies on the exceptional divisor of $X_2 \to X_1$, and the strict transform $L_{12}$ of the line through $P_1$ in the direction of $P_2$ does not contain $P_3$. Then ${\widetilde{X}}$ contains a 2-chain of $(-2)$-curves (the strict transforms $\Delta_{12}$ and $\Delta_{23}$ of the exceptional divisors of $X_1 \to X_0$ and $X_2 \to X_1$, respectively) and $X$ has one $A_2$ singularity. \item[Type 5] The point $P_2$ lies on the exceptional divisor of $X_1 \to X_0$, the point $P_3$ lies on the exceptional divisor of $X_2 \to X_1$, and the strict transform of the line through $P_1$ in the direction of $P_2$ contains $P_3$. Then ${\widetilde{X}}$ contains a 2-chain of $(-2)$-curves and one more $(-2)$-curve disjoint from the chain (the strict transforms $\Delta_{123}$, $\Delta_{12}$ and $\Delta_{23}$ of the line and the exceptional divisors of~$X_1 \to X_0$ and $X_2 \to X_1$ respectively) and $X$ has one $A_2$ singularity and one $A_1$ singularity.
nodes.statement_short: Classification of the configurations of blowup centers and (-2)-curves on the resolution into Types 0-5.

nodes.name: Set of $(-2)$-curves $\boldsymbol\Delta(X)$
nodes.statement: We denote by~${\boldsymbol\Delta} = {\boldsymbol\Delta}(X)$ the set of all $(-2)$-curves on ${\widetilde{X}}$.

nodes.name: Linear systems containing the (-2)-curves
nodes.statement: Note that the $(-2)$ curves (when they exist) on ${\widetilde{X}}$ are contained in the following linear systems: \begin{equation*} \Delta_{12} = E_1 - E_2 \in |e_1 - e_2|, \qquad \Delta_{23} = E_2 - E_3 \in |e_2 - e_3|, \qquad\text{and}\qquad \Delta_{123} \in |h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3|. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: The (-2)-curves are $\Delta_{12}=E_1-E_2$, $\Delta_{23}=E_2-E_3$ and $\Delta_{123}\in|h-e_1-e_2-e_3|$.

nodes.name: Uniqueness and toricity of each type
nodes.statement: In each of these types there is a unique (up to isomorphism) sextic del Pezzo surface. Moreover, the surfaces of types $0$, $2$, $3$, and $5$ are toric (in particular, the surface of type~5 is the weighted projective plane~${\mathbb{P}}(1,2,3)$, see~\cite[Example~5.8]{kawamata2015multi} for an alternative description of its derived category). The surfaces of type~1 and~4 are not toric.
nodes.statement_short: Each type has a unique surface; types 0, 2, 3, 5 are toric (type 5 is P(1,2,3)), types 1 and 4 are not.

nodes.name: Exceptional components $\boldsymbol\Delta$ of a resolution
nodes.statement: Denote by ${\boldsymbol\Delta}$ the set of irreducible components of the exceptional divisor of $\pi$; each of these is a smooth rational curve on ${\widetilde{X}}$.

nodes.name: Properties of pullback and pushforward for rational surface singularities
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a normal surface with rational singularities and let $\pi \colon {\widetilde{X}} \to X$ be its resolution. The functor $\pi^* \colon {\mathbf{D}}^-(X) \to {\mathbf{D}}^-({\widetilde{X}})$ is fully faithful. The functor $\pi_* \colon {\mathbf{D}}^-({\widetilde{X}}) \to {\mathbf{D}}^-(X)$ is its right adjoint, it preserves boundedness, and there is an isomorphism of functors \begin{equation} \pi_* \circ \pi^* \cong \mathrm{id}. \end{equation} Moreover, \begin{equation*} \mathrm{Im} \pi^* = {}^\perp\langle {\mathscr{O}}_\Delta(-1) \rangle_{\Delta \in {\boldsymbol\Delta}} \qquad\text{and}\qquad \mathrm{Ker} \pi_* = \langle {\mathscr{O}}_\Delta(-1) \rangle^\oplus_{\Delta \in {\boldsymbol\Delta}}, \end{equation*} where $\langle - \rangle^\oplus$ denotes the minimal triangulated subcategory closed under infinite direct sums defined in ${\mathbf{D}}^-$.
nodes.statement_short: For a resolution of rational surface singularities, $\pi^*$ is fully faithful, $\pi_*\pi^*\cong\mathrm{id}$, and $\mathrm{Ker}\,\pi_*$ is generated by the $\mathscr{O}_\Delta(-1)$.
assumptions: Let $X$ be a normal surface with rational singularities and let $\pi \colon {\widetilde{X}} \to X$ be its resolution.
conclusions: The functor $\pi^* \colon {\mathbf{D}}^-(X) \to {\mathbf{D}}^-({\widetilde{X}})$ is fully faithful.

The functor $\pi_* \colon {\mathbf{D}}^-({\widetilde{X}}) \to {\mathbf{D}}^-(X)$ is its right adjoint, it preserves boundedness, and there is an isomorphism of functors \begin{equation}\label{eq:pis-pis-id} \pi_* \circ \pi^* \cong \mathrm{id}. \end{equation}

\mathrm{Im} \pi^* = {}^\perp\langle {\mathscr{O}}_\Delta(-1) \rangle_{\Delta \in {\boldsymbol\Delta}} \qquad\text{and}\qquad \mathrm{Ker} \pi_* = \langle {\mathscr{O}}_\Delta(-1) \rangle^\oplus_{\Delta \in {\boldsymbol\Delta}}, \end{equation*}
nodes.label: lemma:pi-properties

nodes.name: $\pi_*\pi^* \cong \mathrm{id}$
nodes.statement: \pi_* \circ \pi^* \cong \mathrm{id}.
nodes.label: eq:pis-pis-id

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.3
nodes.statement: The pullback-pushforward adjunction is standard. By projection formula we have \begin{equation*} \pi_*(\pi^*{\mathscr{F}}) \cong {\mathscr{F}} \otimes \pi_*{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}, \end{equation*} and since $X$ has rational singularities, the canonical morphism ${\mathscr{O}}_X \to \pi_*{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}$ is an isomorphism, hence~\eqref{eq:pis-pis-id} holds. By adjunction it follows that $\pi^*$ is fully faithful. Finally, by~\cite[Lemma~2.1]{bodzenta2015flops} (see also~\cite[Lemma~3.1]{bridgeland} and Lemma~\ref{lemma:spectral} below) and~\cite[Proposition~9.14 and Theorem~9.15]{bodzenta2015flops} the category $\mathrm{Ker}\pi_*$ is generated by sheaves ${\mathscr{O}}_\Delta(-1)$. The description of $\mathrm{Im}\pi^*$ follows by adjunction.
nodes.statement_short: Projection formula plus rationality gives $\pi_*\pi^*\cong\mathrm{id}$; full faithfulness by adjunction; the kernel description is cited from Bodzenta-Bondal.

nodes.name: Adjunction and projection formula give pi_* pi^* = id
nodes.statement: The pullback-pushforward adjunction is standard. By projection formula we have \begin{equation*} \pi_*(\pi^*{\mathscr{F}}) \cong {\mathscr{F}} \otimes \pi_*{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}, \end{equation*} and since $X$ has rational singularities, the canonical morphism ${\mathscr{O}}_X \to \pi_*{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}$ is an isomorphism, hence~\eqref{eq:pis-pis-id} holds.
nodes.statement_short: Adjunction and projection formula give pi_* pi^* = id

nodes.name: Full faithfulness of pi^* by adjunction
nodes.statement: By adjunction it follows that $\pi^*$ is fully faithful.
nodes.statement_short: Full faithfulness of pi^* by adjunction

nodes.name: Kernel of pi_* generated by O_Delta(-1) (cited); image by adjunction
nodes.statement: Finally, by~\cite[Lemma~2.1]{bodzenta2015flops} (see also~\cite[Lemma~3.1]{bridgeland} and Lemma~\ref{lemma:spectral} below) and~\cite[Proposition~9.14 and Theorem~9.15]{bodzenta2015flops} the category $\mathrm{Ker}\pi_*$ is generated by sheaves ${\mathscr{O}}_\Delta(-1)$. The description of $\mathrm{Im}\pi^*$ follows by adjunction.
nodes.statement_short: Kernel of pi_* generated by O_Delta(-1) (cited); image by adjunction

nodes.name: Bridgeland's spectral sequence lemma
nodes.statement: Let $\pi \colon {\widetilde{X}} \to X$ be a proper morphism with fibers of dimension at most~$1$. Let ${\mathscr{F}}$ be a possibly unbounded complex of quasicoherent sheaves on ${\widetilde{X}}$ and let ${\mathscr{H}}^i({\mathscr{F}})$ be its cohomology sheaf in degree $i$. The spectral sequence $R^i\pi_*({\mathscr{H}}^j({\mathscr{F}})) \Rightarrow {\mathscr{H}}^{i+j}(\pi_*({\mathscr{F}}))$ degenerates at the second page, and gives for each $i$ an exact sequence \begin{equation*} 0 \to R^1\pi_*{\mathscr{H}}^{i-1}({\mathscr{F}}) \to {\mathscr{H}}^i(\pi_*({\mathscr{F}})) \to R^0\pi_*{\mathscr{H}}^i({\mathscr{F}}) \to 0. \end{equation*} In particular, if ${\mathscr{H}}^i(\pi_*({\mathscr{F}})) = 0$ for $i \le p$ for some integer $p$, then $\pi_*({\mathscr{H}}^i({\mathscr{F}})) = 0$ for $i \le p - 1$ and \begin{equation*} \pi_*{\mathscr{F}} \cong \pi_*(\tau^{\ge p}{\mathscr{F}}), \end{equation*} where $\tau$ stands for the truncation functor with respect to the canonical filtration.
nodes.statement_short: For a proper map with fibers of dimension at most 1 the pushforward spectral sequence degenerates, giving short exact sequences and a truncation isomorphism.
assumptions: Let $\pi \colon {\widetilde{X}} \to X$ be a proper morphism with fibers of dimension at most~$1$.
Let ${\mathscr{F}}$ be a possibly unbounded complex of quasicoherent sheaves on ${\widetilde{X}}$ and let ${\mathscr{H}}^i({\mathscr{F}})$ be its cohomology sheaf in degree $i$.
conclusions: The spectral sequence $R^i\pi_*({\mathscr{H}}^j({\mathscr{F}})) \Rightarrow {\mathscr{H}}^{i+j}(\pi_*({\mathscr{F}}))$ degenerates at the second page, and gives for each $i$ an exact sequence \begin{equation*} 0 \to R^1\pi_*{\mathscr{H}}^{i-1}({\mathscr{F}}) \to {\mathscr{H}}^i(\pi_*({\mathscr{F}})) \to R^0\pi_*{\mathscr{H}}^i({\mathscr{F}}) \to 0. \end{equation*}

In particular, if ${\mathscr{H}}^i(\pi_*({\mathscr{F}})) = 0$ for $i \le p$ for some integer $p$, then $\pi_*({\mathscr{H}}^i({\mathscr{F}})) = 0$ for $i \le p - 1$ and \begin{equation*} \pi_*{\mathscr{F}} \cong \pi_*(\tau^{\ge p}{\mathscr{F}}), \end{equation*}
nodes.label: lemma:spectral

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.4
nodes.statement: The fibers of $\pi$ are at most 1-dimensional, hence $R^{\ge 2}\pi_* = 0$, and the second page of the spectral sequence looks like \begin{equation*} \xymatrix@R=1ex{ \dots & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & \dots \\ \dots & R^1\pi_*{\mathscr{H}}^{i-2}({\mathscr{F}}) & R^1\pi_*{\mathscr{H}}^{i-1}({\mathscr{F}}) & R^1\pi_*{\mathscr{H}}^{i}({\mathscr{F}}) & R^1\pi_*{\mathscr{H}}^{i+1}({\mathscr{F}}) & \dots \\ \dots & R^0\pi_*{\mathscr{H}}^{i-2}({\mathscr{F}}) & R^0\pi_*{\mathscr{H}}^{i-1}({\mathscr{F}}) \ar[uul]_{d_2} & R^0\pi_*{\mathscr{H}}^{i}({\mathscr{F}}) \ar[uul]_{d_2} & R^0\pi_*{\mathscr{H}}^{i+1}({\mathscr{F}}) \ar[uul]_{d_2} & \dots } \end{equation*} It follows that the spectral sequence degenerates at the second page, and gives the required exact sequences. The vanishing of $\pi_*({\mathscr{H}}^i({\mathscr{F}}))$ for all $i \le p-1$ follows immediately from the exact sequences, and in its turn implies $\pi_*(\tau^{\le p-1}{\mathscr{F}}) = 0$. Applying the pushforward to the canonical truncation triangle~$\tau^{\le p-1}{\mathscr{F}} \to {\mathscr{F}} \to \tau^{\ge p}{\mathscr{F}}$ we obtain the required isomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: Fibers of dimension at most 1 kill $R^{\ge2}\pi_*$, so the second page has two rows and the spectral sequence degenerates; then push forward the truncation triangle.

nodes.name: Second page has only two nonzero rows
nodes.statement: The fibers of $\pi$ are at most 1-dimensional, hence $R^{\ge 2}\pi_* = 0$, and the second page of the spectral sequence looks like \begin{equation*} \xymatrix@R=1ex{ \dots & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & \dots \\ \dots & R^1\pi_*{\mathscr{H}}^{i-2}({\mathscr{F}}) & R^1\pi_*{\mathscr{H}}^{i-1}({\mathscr{F}}) & R^1\pi_*{\mathscr{H}}^{i}({\mathscr{F}}) & R^1\pi_*{\mathscr{H}}^{i+1}({\mathscr{F}}) & \dots \\ \dots & R^0\pi_*{\mathscr{H}}^{i-2}({\mathscr{F}}) & R^0\pi_*{\mathscr{H}}^{i-1}({\mathscr{F}}) \ar[uul]_{d_2} & R^0\pi_*{\mathscr{H}}^{i}({\mathscr{F}}) \ar[uul]_{d_2} & R^0\pi_*{\mathscr{H}}^{i+1}({\mathscr{F}}) \ar[uul]_{d_2} & \dots } \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Second page has only two nonzero rows

nodes.name: Degeneration and exact sequences; vanishing below p
nodes.statement: It follows that the spectral sequence degenerates at the second page, and gives the required exact sequences. The vanishing of $\pi_*({\mathscr{H}}^i({\mathscr{F}}))$ for all $i \le p-1$ follows immediately from the exact sequences, and in its turn implies $\pi_*(\tau^{\le p-1}{\mathscr{F}}) = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Degeneration and exact sequences; vanishing below p

nodes.name: Truncation isomorphism
nodes.statement: Applying the pushforward to the canonical truncation triangle~$\tau^{\le p-1}{\mathscr{F}} \to {\mathscr{F}} \to \tau^{\ge p}{\mathscr{F}}$ we obtain the required isomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: Truncation isomorphism

nodes.name: Essential surjectivity of $\pi_*$
nodes.statement: The functor $\pi_* \colon {\mathbf{D}}({\widetilde{X}}) \to {\mathbf{D}}(X)$ is essentially surjective.
nodes.statement_short: Every bounded complex on X is the pushforward of a bounded complex on the resolution.
conclusions: The functor $\pi_* \colon {\mathbf{D}}({\widetilde{X}}) \to {\mathbf{D}}(X)$ is essentially surjective.
nodes.label: corollary:pis-epi

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 2.5
nodes.statement: Let ${\mathscr{F}} \in {\mathbf{D}}(X)$ and assume that $p$ is such that $\tau^{\le p}({\mathscr{F}}) = 0$. Then ${\mathscr{F}} \cong \pi_*(\pi^*{\mathscr{F}}) \cong \pi_*(\tau^{\ge p}\pi^*{\mathscr{F}})$, and clearly $\tau^{\ge p}\pi^*{\mathscr{F}} \in {\mathbf{D}}({\widetilde{X}})$.
nodes.statement_short: Write $\mathscr{F}\cong\pi_*(\tau^{\ge p}\pi^*\mathscr{F})$ using Lemma 2.3 and Lemma 2.4.

nodes.name: Grothendieck duality
nodes.statement: Let $f \colon X \to Y$ be a proper morphism. The {\sf Grothendieck duality} is a bifunctorial isomorphism \begin{equation} \mathrm{RHom}(f_*{\mathscr{F}},{\mathscr{G}}) \cong \mathrm{RHom}({\mathscr{F}},f^!{\mathscr{G}}), \end{equation} where $f^!$ is the twisted pullback functor (if ${\mathscr{G}}$ is perfect, $f^!{\mathscr{G}} \cong {\mathscr{G}} \otimes \omega^\bullet_{X/Y}$, where $\omega^\bullet_{X/Y} = f^!{\mathscr{O}}_Y$ is the relative dualizing complex). In other words, the twisted pullback functor is right adjoint to the (derived) pushforward.
nodes.statement_short: For proper f the twisted pullback $f^!$ is right adjoint to $f_*$.
assumptions: Let $f \colon X \to Y$ be a proper morphism.
conclusions: The {\sf Grothendieck duality} is a bifunctorial isomorphism \begin{equation}\label{eq:Gd} \mathrm{RHom}(f_*{\mathscr{F}},{\mathscr{G}}) \cong \mathrm{RHom}({\mathscr{F}},f^!{\mathscr{G}}), \end{equation}

nodes.name: Grothendieck duality isomorphism
nodes.statement: \mathrm{RHom}(f_*{\mathscr{F}},{\mathscr{G}}) \cong \mathrm{RHom}({\mathscr{F}},f^!{\mathscr{G}}),
nodes.label: eq:Gd

nodes.name: Serre duality for Gorenstein schemes
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a projective Gorenstein ${\mathsf{k}}$-scheme of dimension $n$. If either ${\mathscr{F}}$ or ${\mathscr{G}}$ is a perfect complex, there is a natural Serre duality isomorphism \begin{equation*} \mathrm{Ext}^i({\mathscr{F}},{\mathscr{G}})^\vee \cong \mathrm{Ext}^{n-i}({\mathscr{G}},{\mathscr{F}} \otimes \omega_X). \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Serre duality on a projective Gorenstein scheme when one of the arguments is perfect.
assumptions: Let $X$ be a projective Gorenstein ${\mathsf{k}}$-scheme of dimension $n$.
If either ${\mathscr{F}}$ or ${\mathscr{G}}$ is a perfect complex
conclusions: there is a natural Serre duality isomorphism \begin{equation*} \mathrm{Ext}^i({\mathscr{F}},{\mathscr{G}})^\vee \cong \mathrm{Ext}^{n-i}({\mathscr{G}},{\mathscr{F}} \otimes \omega_X). \end{equation*}
nodes.label: proposition:serre-gorenstein

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.6
nodes.statement: Let $f \colon X \to \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}})$ be the structure morphism. If ${\mathscr{F}}$ is a locally free sheaf, then we have $\mathrm{Ext}^i({\mathscr{F}},{\mathscr{G}}) \cong H^i(X,{\mathscr{F}}^\vee \otimes {\mathscr{G}})$, and this is a cohomology group of $f_*({\mathscr{F}}^\vee \otimes {\mathscr{G}})$. By Grothendieck duality \begin{equation*} \mathrm{RHom}(f_*({\mathscr{F}}^\vee \otimes {\mathscr{G}}),{\mathsf{k}}) \cong \mathrm{RHom}({\mathscr{F}}^\vee \otimes {\mathscr{G}},f^!({\mathsf{k}})). \end{equation*} Since $X$ is Gorenstein, $f^!({\mathsf{k}}) \cong \omega_X[n]$, hence the right hand side equals $\mathrm{RHom}({\mathscr{F}}^\vee \otimes {\mathscr{G}}, \omega_X[n])$. Since~${\mathscr{F}}$ is locally free, this can be rewritten as $\mathrm{RHom}({\mathscr{G}},{\mathscr{F}} \otimes \omega_X[n])$. Computing the cohomology groups in degree $-i$, we deduce the required duality isomorphism. For arbitrary perfect ${\mathscr{F}}$ the Serre duality follows by using the stupid filtration. Finally, when ${\mathscr{G}}$ is perfect, we replace ${\mathscr{F}}$ by ${\mathscr{G}}$, ${\mathscr{G}}$ by ${\mathscr{F}} \otimes \omega_X$, and $i$ by $n - i$, and deduce the required isomorphism from the previous case.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Grothendieck duality to the structure morphism with $f^!\mathsf{k}=\omega_X[n]$ for locally free F, extend by the stupid filtration, then swap roles.

nodes.name: Reduce Ext to cohomology for locally free F
nodes.statement: Let $f \colon X \to \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}})$ be the structure morphism. If ${\mathscr{F}}$ is a locally free sheaf, then we have $\mathrm{Ext}^i({\mathscr{F}},{\mathscr{G}}) \cong H^i(X,{\mathscr{F}}^\vee \otimes {\mathscr{G}})$, and this is a cohomology group of $f_*({\mathscr{F}}^\vee \otimes {\mathscr{G}})$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce Ext to cohomology for locally free F

nodes.name: Apply Grothendieck duality
nodes.statement: By Grothendieck duality \begin{equation*} \mathrm{RHom}(f_*({\mathscr{F}}^\vee \otimes {\mathscr{G}}),{\mathsf{k}}) \cong \mathrm{RHom}({\mathscr{F}}^\vee \otimes {\mathscr{G}},f^!({\mathsf{k}})). \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Apply Grothendieck duality

nodes.name: Use Gorenstein dualizing sheaf to obtain the duality
nodes.statement: Since $X$ is Gorenstein, $f^!({\mathsf{k}}) \cong \omega_X[n]$, hence the right hand side equals $\mathrm{RHom}({\mathscr{F}}^\vee \otimes {\mathscr{G}}, \omega_X[n])$. Since~${\mathscr{F}}$ is locally free, this can be rewritten as $\mathrm{RHom}({\mathscr{G}},{\mathscr{F}} \otimes \omega_X[n])$. Computing the cohomology groups in degree $-i$, we deduce the required duality isomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: Use Gorenstein dualizing sheaf to obtain the duality

nodes.name: Extend to perfect F via stupid filtration
nodes.statement: For arbitrary perfect ${\mathscr{F}}$ the Serre duality follows by using the stupid filtration.
nodes.statement_short: Extend to perfect F via stupid filtration

nodes.name: Case G perfect by symmetry
nodes.statement: Finally, when ${\mathscr{G}}$ is perfect, we replace ${\mathscr{F}}$ by ${\mathscr{G}}$, ${\mathscr{G}}$ by ${\mathscr{F}} \otimes \omega_X$, and $i$ by $n - i$, and deduce the required isomorphism from the previous case.
nodes.statement_short: Case G perfect by symmetry

nodes.name: Duality functor via the dualizing complex is an equivalence
nodes.statement: It follows from sheafified Grothendieck duality that \begin{equation*} \mathrm{R}\mathscr{H}\mathit{om}(-,\omega^\bullet_{X/{\mathsf{k}}}) \colon {\mathbf{D}}(X)^{\mathrm{opp}} \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } {\mathbf{D}}(X). \end{equation*} is an equivalence of categories.

nodes.name: Derived dual $\mathscr{F}^\vee$
nodes.statement: In case when the scheme $X$ is Gorenstein, the dualizing complex $\omega^\bullet_{X/{\mathsf{k}}}$ is a shift of the canonical line bundle, $\omega^\bullet_{X/{\mathsf{k}}} \cong \omega_X[\dim X]$, and it follows that the usual duality functor \begin{equation*} {\mathscr{F}} \mapsto {\mathscr{F}}^\vee := \mathrm{R}\mathscr{H}\mathit{om}({\mathscr{F}},{\mathscr{O}}_X) \cong \mathrm{R}\mathscr{H}\mathit{om}({\mathscr{F}},\omega_X^\bullet) \otimes \omega_X^{-1}[-\dim X] \end{equation*} is also an equivalence of categories ${\mathbf{D}}(X)^{\mathrm{opp}} \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } {\mathbf{D}}(X)$.
nodes.statement_short: On a Gorenstein scheme the derived dual RHom(F, O_X) is an anti-autoequivalence of D(X).

nodes.name: Three-block exceptional collection on $\widetilde{X}$
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a sextic du Val del Pezzo surface over an algebraically closed field ${\mathsf{k}}$ and let~$\pi \colon {\widetilde{X}} \to X$ be its minimal resolution of singularities. There is a semiorthogonal decomposition \begin{equation} {\mathbf{D}}({\widetilde{X}}) = \langle {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1, {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2, {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3 \rangle, \end{equation} whose components are generated by the following exceptional collections of line bundles \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1 &= \langle {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}} \rangle,\\ {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2 &= \langle {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_1), {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_2), {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_3) \rangle,\\ {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3 &= \langle {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h), {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(2h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3) \rangle. \end{aligned} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $\mathbf{D}(\widetilde{X})$ has a three-block decomposition generated by $\mathscr{O}$, the three $\mathscr{O}(h-e_i)$, and $\mathscr{O}(h)$, $\mathscr{O}(2h-e_1-e_2-e_3)$.
assumptions: Let $X$ be a sextic du Val del Pezzo surface over an algebraically closed field ${\mathsf{k}}$ and let~$\pi \colon {\widetilde{X}} \to X$ be its minimal resolution of singularities.
conclusions: There is a semiorthogonal decomposition \begin{equation} \label{eq:dbtx} {\mathbf{D}}({\widetilde{X}}) = \langle {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1, {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2, {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3 \rangle, \end{equation} whose components are generated by the following exceptional collections of line bundles \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \label{eq:tx-excol} {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1 &= \langle {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}} \rangle,\\ {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2 &= \langle {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_1), {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_2), {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_3) \rangle,\\ {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3 &= \langle {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h), {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(2h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3) \rangle. \end{aligned} \end{equation}
nodes.label: proposition:tx-excol

nodes.name: Decomposition (eq:dbtx) of $\mathbf{D}(\widetilde{X})$
nodes.statement: {\mathbf{D}}({\widetilde{X}}) = \langle {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1, {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2, {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3 \rangle,
nodes.label: eq:dbtx

nodes.name: Exceptional line bundles generating $\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}_i$
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1 &= \langle {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}} \rangle,\\ {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2 &= \langle {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_1), {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_2), {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_3) \rangle,\\ {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3 &= \langle {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h), {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(2h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3) \rangle. \end{aligned}
nodes.label: eq:tx-excol

nodes.name: Dual decomposition of $\mathbf{D}(\widetilde{X})$
nodes.statement: {\mathbf{D}}({\widetilde{X}}) = \langle {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3^\vee, {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2^\vee, {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1^\vee \rangle.
nodes.statement_short: Dualizing (eq:dbtx) gives $\mathbf{D}(\widetilde{X}) = \langle \widetilde{\mathcal{A}}_3^\vee, \widetilde{\mathcal{A}}_2^\vee, \widetilde{\mathcal{A}}_1^\vee\rangle$.
nodes.label: eq:dbtx-dual

nodes.name: Left mutation functor $\mathbb{L}_{\mathcal{A}}$
nodes.statement: Below we denote by ${\mathbb{L}}_{\mathcal{A}}$ the left mutation functor through an admissible subcategory ${\mathcal{A}}$.

nodes.name: Dual decomposition of $\mathbf{D}(\widetilde{X})$ is right mutation-dual
nodes.statement: The semiorthogonal decomposition~\eqref{eq:dbtx-dual} is right mutation-dual to~\eqref{eq:dbtx}, i.e., \begin{equation*} {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1^\vee = {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1, \qquad {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2^\vee = {\mathbb{L}}_{{\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1}({\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2), \quad\text{and}\quad {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3^\vee = {\mathbb{L}}_{{\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1}({\mathbb{L}}_{{\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2}({\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3)) = {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3 \otimes \omega_{\widetilde{X}}. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: The dual decomposition is obtained from (eq:dbtx) by left mutations; its last component is the twist by the canonical bundle.
conclusions: The semiorthogonal decomposition~\eqref{eq:dbtx-dual} is right mutation-dual to~\eqref{eq:dbtx}

\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1^\vee = {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1, \qquad {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2^\vee = {\mathbb{L}}_{{\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1}({\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2), \quad\text{and}\quad {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3^\vee = {\mathbb{L}}_{{\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1}({\mathbb{L}}_{{\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2}({\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3)) = {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3 \otimes \omega_{\widetilde{X}}. \end{equation*}
nodes.label: lemma:dual-sod-tx

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.2
nodes.statement: The claim is trivial for the first component, since ${\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1^\vee = \langle {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}^\vee \rangle = \langle {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}} \rangle = {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1$, and is easy for the last component, since ${\mathbb{L}}_{{\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1}({\mathbb{L}}_{{\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2}({\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3)) = {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3 \otimes \omega_{\widetilde{X}}$ and \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} & {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h) \otimes \omega_{\widetilde{X}} && \cong {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(-2h + e_1 + e_2 + e_3) && \cong {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(2h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3)^\vee,\\ & {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(2h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3) \otimes \omega_{\widetilde{X}} && \cong {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(-h) && \cong {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h)^\vee. \end{aligned} \end{equation} Finally, for the second component we have ${\mathbb{L}}_{{\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1}({\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2) = {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1^\perp \cap {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3^\perp = ({\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1^\vee)^\perp \cap {}^\perp({\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3 \otimes \omega_X) = {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2^\vee$ by Serre duality.
nodes.statement_short: Check component by component: the first is self-dual, the last is the Serre twist computed in (eq:ce3-dual), the middle follows by Serre duality.

nodes.name: Duals of the A3 line bundles twisted by the canonical class
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} & {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h) \otimes \omega_{\widetilde{X}} && \cong {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(-2h + e_1 + e_2 + e_3) && \cong {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(2h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3)^\vee,\\ & {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(2h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3) \otimes \omega_{\widetilde{X}} && \cong {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(-h) && \cong {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h)^\vee. \end{aligned}
nodes.label: eq:ce3-dual

nodes.name: Auslander algebra $\tilde{R}_m$ (notation)
nodes.statement: For $m = 2$ and $m = 3$ we denote by ${\tilde{R}}_m$ the Auslander algebra defined by~\eqref{eq:trm}, and refer to Appendix~\ref{appendix:auslander} for its basic properties, especially note the definition~\eqref{eq:projective-resolution-ei} of the {\sf standard exceptional modules} and Proposition~\ref{proposition:rm-equivalence}.

nodes.name: Components $\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}_i$ are products of Auslander-algebra categories
nodes.statement: The components ${\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i$ of~\eqref{eq:dbtx} are equivalent to products of derived categories of Auslander algebras as indicated in the next table: \begin{equation*} \begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|} \hline \text{Type of $X$} & {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1 & {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2 & {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3 \\ \hline 0 & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \\ \hline 1 & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\tilde{R}}_2) \\ \hline 2 & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\tilde{R}}_2) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \\ \hline 3 & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\tilde{R}}_2) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\tilde{R}}_2) \\ \hline 4 & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\tilde{R}}_3) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \\ \hline 5 & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\tilde{R}}_3) & {\mathbf{D}}({\tilde{R}}_2) \\ \hline \end{array} \end{equation*} This equivalence takes the exceptional line bundles in~\eqref{eq:tx-excol} to the standard exceptional modules over the corresponding Auslander algebra.
nodes.statement_short: Depending on the type of X, each $\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}_i$ is a product of copies of $\mathbf{D}(\mathsf{k})$, $\mathbf{D}(\tilde R_2)$, $\mathbf{D}(\tilde R_3)$.
conclusions: The components ${\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i$ of~\eqref{eq:dbtx} are equivalent to products of derived categories of Auslander algebras as indicated in the next table: \begin{equation*} \begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|} \hline \text{Type of $X$} & {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1 & {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2 & {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3 \\ \hline 0 & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \\ \hline 1 & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\tilde{R}}_2) \\ \hline 2 & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\tilde{R}}_2) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \\ \hline 3 & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\tilde{R}}_2) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\tilde{R}}_2) \\ \hline 4 & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\tilde{R}}_3) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \\ \hline 5 & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\tilde{R}}_3) & {\mathbf{D}}({\tilde{R}}_2) \\ \hline \end{array} \end{equation*}
This equivalence takes the exceptional line bundles in~\eqref{eq:tx-excol} to the standard exceptional modules over the corresponding Auslander algebra.
nodes.label: proposition:tcai-auslander

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.3
nodes.statement: The component ${\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1$ is generated by a single exceptional object, hence is equivalent to ${\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}})$. So, in view of Proposition~\ref{proposition:rm-equivalence} to prove the proposition it is enough to compute $\mathrm{Ext}$-spaces between the exceptional line bundles forming the components ${\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2$ and ${\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3$ of the semiorthogonal decomposition~\eqref{eq:dbtx}. First of all, we have \begin{equation*} \mathrm{Ext}^p({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_i), {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_j)) \cong H^p({\widetilde{X}}, {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(e_i - e_j)). \end{equation*} Assuming $i \ne j$ and using exact sequences (note that $e_i\cdot e_j = 0$ and $e_i^2 = -1$ by Lemma~\ref{lemma:pic-tx}) \begin{equation*} 0 \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(e_i - e_j) \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(e_i) \to {\mathscr{O}}_{E_j} \to 0, \qquad\qquad 0 \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}} \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(e_i) \to {\mathscr{O}}_{E_i}(-1) \to 0, \end{equation*} we obtain an exact sequence \begin{equation*} 0 \to H^0({\widetilde{X}}, {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(e_i - e_j)) \to {\mathsf{k}} \to {\mathsf{k}} \to H^1({\widetilde{X}}, {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(e_i - e_j)) \to 0, \end{equation*} where the middle map is given by the restriction to $E_j$ of the equation of $E_i$. This restriction vanishes if and only if $E_j$ is a component of $E_i$ --- in this case we deduce that $\mathrm{Ext}^\bullet({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_i), {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_j)) \cong {\mathsf{k}} \oplus {\mathsf{k}}[-1]$, and otherwise $\mathrm{Ext}^\bullet({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_i), {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_j)) = 0$. By Proposition~\ref{proposition:rm-equivalence} this gives the required description of ${\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2$ in types from~0 to 3. In the last two types (4 and 5) it remains to check that multiplication map \begin{equation} \mathrm{Ext}^p({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_1),{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_2)) \otimes \mathrm{Ext}^q({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_2),{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_3)) \to \mathrm{Ext}^{p+q}({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_1),{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_3)) \end{equation} is an isomorphism when $p = 0$ or $q = 0$. For this consider exact sequences \begin{equation} 0 \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_1) \xrightarrow{\ \Delta_{12}\ } {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_2) \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\Delta_{12}}(-1) \to 0, \end{equation} \begin{equation} 0 \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_2) \xrightarrow{\ \Delta_{23}\ } {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_3) \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\Delta_{23}}(-1) \to 0, \end{equation} where $\Delta_{12} = E_1 - E_2$ and $\Delta_{23} = E_2 - E_3$. Using Lemma~\ref{lemma:pic-tx}, we compute \begin{equation*} \mathrm{Ext}^\bullet({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_1),{\mathscr{O}}_{\Delta_{23}}(-1)) \cong H^\bullet(\Delta_{23},{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(e_1 - h)\vert_{\Delta_{23}} \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{\Delta_{23}}(-1)) = H^\bullet(\Delta_{23},{\mathscr{O}}_{\Delta_{23}}(-1)) = 0. \end{equation*} Applying the functor $\mathrm{Ext}^\bullet({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_1),-)$ to~\eqref{eq:e23}, we deduce that~\eqref{eq:multiplication-ext-tx} is an isomorphism for~$q = 0$. Similarly, by Serre duality $\mathrm{Ext}^\bullet({\mathscr{O}}_{\Delta_{12}}(-1),{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_3))$ is dual to $\mathrm{Ext}^\bullet({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(e_1 + e_2 - 2h),{\mathscr{O}}_{\Delta_{12}}(-1))$, and a computation similar to the above shows it is zero. Applying the functor $\mathrm{Ext}^\bullet(-,{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_3))$ to~\eqref{eq:e12}, we deduce that~~\eqref{eq:multiplication-ext-tx} is an isomorphism for $p = 0$. To describe ${\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3$ we only need to compute \begin{equation*} \mathrm{Ext}^p({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h), {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(2h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3)) \cong H^p({\widetilde{X}}, {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3)). \end{equation*} Using exact sequences \begin{align*} 0 \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_1) \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h) &\to {\mathscr{O}}_{E_1} \to 0,\\ 0 \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_1 - e_2) \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_1) &\to {\mathscr{O}}_{E_2} \to 0,\\ 0 \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3) \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_1 - e_2) &\to {\mathscr{O}}_{E_3} \to 0, \end{align*} we conclude that $H^\bullet({\widetilde{X}}, {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3)) = 0$ if the three centers of the blowups are not contained on a line (i.e., in types~0, 2, and 4), and $H^0({\widetilde{X}}, {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3)) = H^1({\widetilde{X}}, {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3)) = {\mathsf{k}}$ otherwise. By Proposition~\ref{proposition:rm-equivalence} this describes ${\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce via Proposition A.3 to computing Ext-spaces between the exceptional line bundles. Exact sequences on the blowup show Ext is k+k[-1] exactly when a (-2)-curve links the bundles, and the multiplication maps are isomorphisms.

nodes.name: A1 is D(k)
nodes.statement: The component ${\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1$ is generated by a single exceptional object, hence is equivalent to ${\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}})$.
nodes.statement_short: A1 is D(k)

nodes.name: Reduce to computing Ext-spaces via Proposition A.3
nodes.statement: So, in view of Proposition~\ref{proposition:rm-equivalence} to prove the proposition it is enough to compute $\mathrm{Ext}$-spaces between the exceptional line bundles forming the components ${\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2$ and ${\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3$ of the semiorthogonal decomposition~\eqref{eq:dbtx}.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to computing Ext-spaces via Proposition A.3

nodes.name: Compute Ext between O(h-e_i) and O(h-e_j) via exact sequences
nodes.statement: First of all, we have \begin{equation*} \mathrm{Ext}^p({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_i), {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_j)) \cong H^p({\widetilde{X}}, {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(e_i - e_j)). \end{equation*} Assuming $i \ne j$ and using exact sequences (note that $e_i\cdot e_j = 0$ and $e_i^2 = -1$ by Lemma~\ref{lemma:pic-tx}) \begin{equation*} 0 \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(e_i - e_j) \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(e_i) \to {\mathscr{O}}_{E_j} \to 0, \qquad\qquad 0 \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}} \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(e_i) \to {\mathscr{O}}_{E_i}(-1) \to 0, \end{equation*} we obtain an exact sequence \begin{equation*} 0 \to H^0({\widetilde{X}}, {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(e_i - e_j)) \to {\mathsf{k}} \to {\mathsf{k}} \to H^1({\widetilde{X}}, {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(e_i - e_j)) \to 0, \end{equation*} where the middle map is given by the restriction to $E_j$ of the equation of $E_i$. This restriction vanishes if and only if $E_j$ is a component of $E_i$ --- in this case we deduce that $\mathrm{Ext}^\bullet({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_i), {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_j)) \cong {\mathsf{k}} \oplus {\mathsf{k}}[-1]$, and otherwise $\mathrm{Ext}^\bullet({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_i), {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_j)) = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Compute Ext between O(h-e_i) and O(h-e_j) via exact sequences

nodes.name: Description of A2 in types 0-3
nodes.statement: By Proposition~\ref{proposition:rm-equivalence} this gives the required description of ${\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2$ in types from~0 to 3.
nodes.statement_short: Description of A2 in types 0-3

nodes.name: Remaining: multiplication maps in types 4, 5
nodes.statement: In the last two types (4 and 5) it remains to check that multiplication map \begin{equation} \mathrm{Ext}^p({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_1),{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_2)) \otimes \mathrm{Ext}^q({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_2),{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_3)) \to \mathrm{Ext}^{p+q}({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_1),{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_3)) \end{equation} is an isomorphism when $p = 0$ or $q = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Remaining: multiplication maps in types 4, 5

nodes.name: Multiplication map on Ext between the A2 line bundles
nodes.statement: \mathrm{Ext}^p({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_1),{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_2)) \otimes \mathrm{Ext}^q({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_2),{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_3)) \to \mathrm{Ext}^{p+q}({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_1),{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_3))
nodes.label: eq:multiplication-ext-tx

nodes.name: Exact sequences realizing Delta_12 and Delta_23
nodes.statement: For this consider exact sequences \begin{equation} 0 \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_1) \xrightarrow{\ \Delta_{12}\ } {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_2) \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\Delta_{12}}(-1) \to 0, \end{equation} \begin{equation} 0 \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_2) \xrightarrow{\ \Delta_{23}\ } {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_3) \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\Delta_{23}}(-1) \to 0, \end{equation} where $\Delta_{12} = E_1 - E_2$ and $\Delta_{23} = E_2 - E_3$.
nodes.statement_short: Exact sequences realizing Delta_12 and Delta_23

nodes.name: Exact sequence for $\Delta_{12}$
nodes.statement: 0 \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_1) \xrightarrow{\ \Delta_{12}\ } {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_2) \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\Delta_{12}}(-1) \to 0,
nodes.label: eq:e12

nodes.name: Exact sequence for $\Delta_{23}$
nodes.statement: 0 \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_2) \xrightarrow{\ \Delta_{23}\ } {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_3) \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\Delta_{23}}(-1) \to 0,
nodes.label: eq:e23

nodes.name: Multiplication isomorphism for q = 0
nodes.statement: Using Lemma~\ref{lemma:pic-tx}, we compute \begin{equation*} \mathrm{Ext}^\bullet({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_1),{\mathscr{O}}_{\Delta_{23}}(-1)) \cong H^\bullet(\Delta_{23},{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(e_1 - h)\vert_{\Delta_{23}} \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{\Delta_{23}}(-1)) = H^\bullet(\Delta_{23},{\mathscr{O}}_{\Delta_{23}}(-1)) = 0. \end{equation*} Applying the functor $\mathrm{Ext}^\bullet({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_1),-)$ to~\eqref{eq:e23}, we deduce that~\eqref{eq:multiplication-ext-tx} is an isomorphism for~$q = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Multiplication isomorphism for q = 0

nodes.name: Multiplication isomorphism for p = 0 via Serre duality
nodes.statement: Similarly, by Serre duality $\mathrm{Ext}^\bullet({\mathscr{O}}_{\Delta_{12}}(-1),{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_3))$ is dual to $\mathrm{Ext}^\bullet({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(e_1 + e_2 - 2h),{\mathscr{O}}_{\Delta_{12}}(-1))$, and a computation similar to the above shows it is zero. Applying the functor $\mathrm{Ext}^\bullet(-,{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_3))$ to~\eqref{eq:e12}, we deduce that~~\eqref{eq:multiplication-ext-tx} is an isomorphism for $p = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Multiplication isomorphism for p = 0 via Serre duality

nodes.name: Compute Ext between O(h) and O(2h-e_1-e_2-e_3) by type
nodes.statement: To describe ${\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3$ we only need to compute \begin{equation*} \mathrm{Ext}^p({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h), {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(2h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3)) \cong H^p({\widetilde{X}}, {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3)). \end{equation*} Using exact sequences \begin{align*} 0 \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_1) \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h) &\to {\mathscr{O}}_{E_1} \to 0,\\ 0 \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_1 - e_2) \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_1) &\to {\mathscr{O}}_{E_2} \to 0,\\ 0 \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3) \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_1 - e_2) &\to {\mathscr{O}}_{E_3} \to 0, \end{align*} we conclude that $H^\bullet({\widetilde{X}}, {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3)) = 0$ if the three centers of the blowups are not contained on a line (i.e., in types~0, 2, and 4), and $H^0({\widetilde{X}}, {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3)) = H^1({\widetilde{X}}, {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3)) = {\mathsf{k}}$ otherwise.
nodes.statement_short: Compute Ext between O(h) and O(2h-e_1-e_2-e_3) by type

nodes.name: Description of A3
nodes.statement: By Proposition~\ref{proposition:rm-equivalence} this describes ${\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3$.
nodes.statement_short: Description of A3

nodes.name: Exact sequence for $\Delta_{123}$
nodes.statement: 0 \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h) \xrightarrow{\ \Delta_{123}\ } {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(2h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3) \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\Delta_{123}}(-1) \to 0.
nodes.label: eq:e123

nodes.name: (-2)-curve sheaves correspond to simple modules
nodes.statement: Comparing exact sequences~\eqref{eq:resolution-simple} of standard exceptional modules over an Auslander algebra with the exact sequences~\eqref{eq:e12}, \eqref{eq:e23} and~\eqref{eq:e123}, and taking into account that the equivalence of Proposition~\ref{proposition:tcai-auslander} takes the exceptional line bundles generating ${\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i$ to the standard exceptional modules over the corresponding Auslander algebras, we conclude that the sheaves~${\mathscr{O}}_\Delta(-1)$ go to the corresponding simple modules. For instance, for a surface of type 5, when we have the maximal number of $(-2)$-curves on ${\widetilde{X}}$, and when ${\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2 \cong {\mathbf{D}}({\tilde{R}}_3)$, ${\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3 \cong {\mathbf{D}}({\tilde{R}}_2)$, the sheaves ${\mathscr{O}}_{\Delta_{12}}(-1)$ and~${\mathscr{O}}_{\Delta_{23}}(-1)$ go to $S_1$ and $S_2$ in ${\mathbf{D}}({\tilde{R}}_3)$, and the sheaf ${\mathscr{O}}_{\Delta_{123}}(-1)$ goes to $S_1$ in ${\mathbf{D}}({\tilde{R}}_2)$.
nodes.statement_short: Under the equivalences of Proposition 3.3 the sheaves $\mathscr{O}_\Delta(-1)$ go to simple modules of the Auslander algebras.
nodes.label: remark:delta-simples

nodes.name: Semiorthogonal decomposition of a sextic du Val del Pezzo surface
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a sextic du Val del Pezzo surface over an algebraically closed field~${\mathsf{k}}$, and let $\pi \colon {\widetilde{X}} \to X$ be its minimal resolution of singularities. Then there is a unique semiorthogonal decomposition \begin{equation} {\mathbf{D}}(X) = \langle {\mathcal{A}}_1, {\mathcal{A}}_2, {\mathcal{A}}_3 \rangle, \end{equation} such that $\pi_*({\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i) = {\mathcal{A}}_i$ and $\pi^*({\mathcal{A}}_i \cap {\mathbf{D}}^\mathrm{perf}(X)) \subset {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i$, where ${\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i$ are the components of~\eqref{eq:dbtx}. The components~${\mathcal{A}}_i$ are admissible with projection functors of finite cohomological amplitude, and are equivalent to products of derived categories of finite-dimensional algebras as indicated in the next table: \begin{equation*} \begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|} \hline \text{Type of $X$} & {\mathcal{A}}_1 & {\mathcal{A}}_2 & {\mathcal{A}}_3 \\ \hline 0 & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \\ \hline 1 & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^2) \\ \hline 2 & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^2) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \\ \hline 3 & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^2) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^2) \\ \hline 4 & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^3) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \\ \hline 5 & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^3) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^2) \\ \hline \end{array} \end{equation*} The categories ${\mathcal{A}}_i^\mathrm{perf} := {\mathcal{A}}_i \cap {\mathbf{D}}^\mathrm{perf}(X)$ form a semiorthogonal decomposition of the perfect category \begin{equation*} {\mathbf{D}}^\mathrm{perf}(X) = \langle {\mathcal{A}}_1^\mathrm{perf}, {\mathcal{A}}_2^\mathrm{perf}, {\mathcal{A}}_3^\mathrm{perf} \rangle. \end{equation*}
nodes.section: 3.2 Semiorthogonal decomposition for a sextic del Pezzo surface
nodes.statement_short: $\mathbf{D}(X)$ has a unique three-component decomposition descended from the resolution, with components equivalent to products of $\mathbf{D}(\mathsf{k}[t]/t^m)$; it restricts to perfect complexes.
assumptions: Let $X$ be a sextic du Val del Pezzo surface over an algebraically closed field~${\mathsf{k}}$, and let $\pi \colon {\widetilde{X}} \to X$ be its minimal resolution of singularities.
conclusions: Then there is a unique semiorthogonal decomposition \begin{equation}\label{eq:dbx} {\mathbf{D}}(X) = \langle {\mathcal{A}}_1, {\mathcal{A}}_2, {\mathcal{A}}_3 \rangle, \end{equation} such that $\pi_*({\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i) = {\mathcal{A}}_i$ and $\pi^*({\mathcal{A}}_i \cap {\mathbf{D}}^\mathrm{perf}(X)) \subset {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i$, where ${\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i$ are the components of~\eqref{eq:dbtx}.

The components~${\mathcal{A}}_i$ are admissible with projection functors of finite cohomological amplitude, and are equivalent to products of derived categories of finite-dimensional algebras as indicated in the next table: \begin{equation*} \begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|} \hline \text{Type of $X$} & {\mathcal{A}}_1 & {\mathcal{A}}_2 & {\mathcal{A}}_3 \\ \hline 0 & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \\ \hline 1 & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^2) \\ \hline 2 & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^2) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \\ \hline 3 & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^2) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^2) \\ \hline 4 & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^3) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \times {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) \\ \hline 5 & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^3) & {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^2) \\ \hline \end{array} \end{equation*}

The categories ${\mathcal{A}}_i^\mathrm{perf} := {\mathcal{A}}_i \cap {\mathbf{D}}^\mathrm{perf}(X)$ form a semiorthogonal decomposition of the perfect category \begin{equation*} {\mathbf{D}}^\mathrm{perf}(X) = \langle {\mathcal{A}}_1^\mathrm{perf}, {\mathcal{A}}_2^\mathrm{perf}, {\mathcal{A}}_3^\mathrm{perf} \rangle. \end{equation*}
nodes.label: theorem:dbx

nodes.name: Decomposition (eq:dbx) of $\mathbf{D}(X)$
nodes.statement: {\mathbf{D}}(X) = \langle {\mathcal{A}}_1, {\mathcal{A}}_2, {\mathcal{A}}_3 \rangle,
nodes.section: 3.2 Semiorthogonal decomposition for a sextic del Pezzo surface
nodes.label: eq:dbx

nodes.name: Extension of (eq:dbtx) to $\mathbf{D}^-(\widetilde{X})$
nodes.statement: Since ${\widetilde{X}}$ is smooth, every component ${\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i$ of ${\mathbf{D}}({\widetilde{X}})$ is admissible, hence~\eqref{eq:dbtx} is a strong semiorthogonal decomposition in the sense of~\cite[Definition~2.6]{kuznetsov2011base}. Therefore, by~\cite[Proposition~4.2]{kuznetsov2011base} it extends to a semiorthogonal decomposition of the bounded above derived category \begin{equation} {\mathbf{D}}^-({\widetilde{X}}) = \langle {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1^-, {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2^-, {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3^- \rangle. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 3.2 Semiorthogonal decomposition for a sextic del Pezzo surface
nodes.statement_short: Since the resolution is smooth, the decomposition is strong and extends to the bounded above derived category (Kuznetsov base change).

nodes.name: Decomposition of $\mathbf{D}^-(\widetilde{X})$
nodes.statement: {\mathbf{D}}^-({\widetilde{X}}) = \langle {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1^-, {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2^-, {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3^- \rangle.
nodes.section: 3.2 Semiorthogonal decomposition for a sextic del Pezzo surface
nodes.label: eq:dbtx-

nodes.name: Subsets $\boldsymbol\Delta_2, \boldsymbol\Delta_3$ of $(-2)$-curves
nodes.statement: We denote by ${\boldsymbol\Delta}_2 \subset {\boldsymbol\Delta}$ the subset formed by those of the curves $\Delta_{12}$ and $\Delta_{23}$ that are defined on ${\widetilde{X}}$ and by ${\boldsymbol\Delta}_3 \subset {\boldsymbol\Delta}$ its complement.
nodes.section: 3.2 Semiorthogonal decomposition for a sextic del Pezzo surface

nodes.name: Intersections of $\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}_i^-$ with $\mathrm{Ker}\,\pi_*$
nodes.statement: We have \begin{equation*} {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1^- \cap \mathrm{Ker} \pi_* = 0, \qquad {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2^- \cap \mathrm{Ker} \pi_* = \langle {\mathscr{O}}_{\Delta}(-1) \rangle^\oplus_{\Delta \in {\boldsymbol\Delta}_2}, \quad\text{and}\quad {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3^- \cap \mathrm{Ker} \pi_* = \langle {\mathscr{O}}_{\Delta}(-1) \rangle^\oplus_{\Delta \in {\boldsymbol\Delta}_3}. \end{equation*} Moreover, for any ${\mathscr{F}} \in \mathrm{Ker}\pi_* \subset {\mathbf{D}}^-({\widetilde{X}})$ there is a canonical direct sum decomposition \begin{equation*} {\mathscr{F}} = {\mathscr{F}}_2 \oplus {\mathscr{F}}_3 \end{equation*} with ${\mathscr{F}}_j \in {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_j^- \cap \mathrm{Ker} \pi_*$.
nodes.section: 3.2 Semiorthogonal decomposition for a sextic del Pezzo surface
nodes.statement_short: The kernel of $\pi_*$ splits as a direct sum of parts lying in $\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}_2^-$ and $\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}_3^-$, generated by the $(-2)$-curves of $\boldsymbol\Delta_2$ and $\boldsymbol\Delta_3$.
conclusions: We have \begin{equation*} {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1^- \cap \mathrm{Ker} \pi_* = 0, \qquad {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2^- \cap \mathrm{Ker} \pi_* = \langle {\mathscr{O}}_{\Delta}(-1) \rangle^\oplus_{\Delta \in {\boldsymbol\Delta}_2}, \quad\text{and}\quad {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3^- \cap \mathrm{Ker} \pi_* = \langle {\mathscr{O}}_{\Delta}(-1) \rangle^\oplus_{\Delta \in {\boldsymbol\Delta}_3}. \end{equation*}

Moreover, for any ${\mathscr{F}} \in \mathrm{Ker}\pi_* \subset {\mathbf{D}}^-({\widetilde{X}})$ there is a canonical direct sum decomposition \begin{equation*} {\mathscr{F}} = {\mathscr{F}}_2 \oplus {\mathscr{F}}_3 \end{equation*} with ${\mathscr{F}}_j \in {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_j^- \cap \mathrm{Ker} \pi_*$.
nodes.label: lemma:ker-pis

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.6
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lemma:pi-properties} an object ${\mathscr{F}} \in {\mathbf{D}}^-({\widetilde{X}})$ is in $\mathrm{Ker}\pi_*$ if and only if every its cohomology sheaf~${\mathscr{H}}^j({\mathscr{F}})$ is an iterated extension of sheaves ${\mathscr{O}}_\Delta(-1)$ where $\Delta$ run over the set ${\boldsymbol\Delta}$ of all $(-2)$-curves on~${\widetilde{X}}$. Note that ${\mathscr{O}}_\Delta(-1) \in {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2$ for $\Delta \in {\boldsymbol\Delta}_2$ by~\eqref{eq:e12} and~\eqref{eq:e23}, while ${\mathscr{O}}_\Delta(-1) \in {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3$ for $\Delta \in {\boldsymbol\Delta}_3$ by~\eqref{eq:e123}. Moreover, the subcategories generated by the sheaves ${\mathscr{O}}_\Delta(-1)$ with $\Delta \in {\boldsymbol\Delta}_2$ and $\Delta \in {\boldsymbol\Delta}_3$ are completely orthogonal, since the supports of these sheaves do not intersect. This last observation shows that any ${\mathscr{F}} \in \mathrm{Ker}\pi_*$ decomposes as ${\mathscr{F}}_2 \oplus {\mathscr{F}}_3$ with the required properties (just take ${\mathscr{F}}_2$ and ${\mathscr{F}}_3$ to be the components of ${\mathscr{F}}$ supported on the union of the curves $\Delta$ from ${\boldsymbol\Delta}_2$ and ${\boldsymbol\Delta}_3$ respectively).
nodes.section: 3.2 Semiorthogonal decomposition for a sextic del Pezzo surface
nodes.statement_short: Kernel objects have cohomology built from $\mathscr{O}_\Delta(-1)$; these lie in $\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}_2$ or $\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}_3$ and have disjoint supports, giving the splitting.

nodes.name: Kernel objects have cohomology built from O_Delta(-1)
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lemma:pi-properties} an object ${\mathscr{F}} \in {\mathbf{D}}^-({\widetilde{X}})$ is in $\mathrm{Ker}\pi_*$ if and only if every its cohomology sheaf~${\mathscr{H}}^j({\mathscr{F}})$ is an iterated extension of sheaves ${\mathscr{O}}_\Delta(-1)$ where $\Delta$ run over the set ${\boldsymbol\Delta}$ of all $(-2)$-curves on~${\widetilde{X}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Kernel objects have cohomology built from O_Delta(-1)
nodes.section: 3.2 Semiorthogonal decomposition for a sextic del Pezzo surface

nodes.name: Locate O_Delta(-1) in A2 or A3; disjoint supports give orthogonality
nodes.statement: Note that ${\mathscr{O}}_\Delta(-1) \in {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2$ for $\Delta \in {\boldsymbol\Delta}_2$ by~\eqref{eq:e12} and~\eqref{eq:e23}, while ${\mathscr{O}}_\Delta(-1) \in {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3$ for $\Delta \in {\boldsymbol\Delta}_3$ by~\eqref{eq:e123}. Moreover, the subcategories generated by the sheaves ${\mathscr{O}}_\Delta(-1)$ with $\Delta \in {\boldsymbol\Delta}_2$ and $\Delta \in {\boldsymbol\Delta}_3$ are completely orthogonal, since the supports of these sheaves do not intersect.
nodes.statement_short: Locate O_Delta(-1) in A2 or A3; disjoint supports give orthogonality
nodes.section: 3.2 Semiorthogonal decomposition for a sextic del Pezzo surface

nodes.name: Splitting by supports
nodes.statement: This last observation shows that any ${\mathscr{F}} \in \mathrm{Ker}\pi_*$ decomposes as ${\mathscr{F}}_2 \oplus {\mathscr{F}}_3$ with the required properties (just take ${\mathscr{F}}_2$ and ${\mathscr{F}}_3$ to be the components of ${\mathscr{F}}$ supported on the union of the curves $\Delta$ from ${\boldsymbol\Delta}_2$ and ${\boldsymbol\Delta}_3$ respectively).
nodes.statement_short: Splitting by supports
nodes.section: 3.2 Semiorthogonal decomposition for a sextic del Pezzo surface

nodes.name: Orthogonality $\mathrm{Hom}(\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}_i^-, \widetilde{\mathcal{A}}_j^-\cap\mathrm{Ker}\,\pi_*) = 0$
nodes.statement: We have $\mathrm{Hom}({\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i^-,{\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_j^- \cap \mathrm{Ker} \pi_*) = 0$ for any $i \ne j$.
nodes.section: 3.2 Semiorthogonal decomposition for a sextic del Pezzo surface
nodes.statement_short: The generating line bundles of one component restrict trivially to the (-2)-curves belonging to another.
assumptions: for any $i \ne j$
conclusions: We have $\mathrm{Hom}({\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i^-,{\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_j^- \cap \mathrm{Ker} \pi_*) = 0$
nodes.label: lemma:ker-pis-orthogonality

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.7
nodes.statement: Since ${\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i^-$ is generated by an exceptional collection of line bundles and ${\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_j^- \cap \mathrm{Ker} \pi_*$ is generated by sheaves ${\mathscr{O}}_\Delta(-1)$ for $\Delta \in {\boldsymbol\Delta}_j$, it is enough to check that any of the line bundles generating ${\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i^-$ restricts trivially to any curve $\Delta$ from ${\boldsymbol\Delta}_j$. For $i = 1$ this is evident; for $i = 2$ we have $(h-e_k)\cdot \Delta_{123} = (h - e_k)(h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3) = 1 - 1 = 0$, and for $i = 3$ we have $h\cdot (e_k - e_l) = 0$ and $(2h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3) \cdot (e_k - e_l) = 1 - 1 = 0$.
nodes.section: 3.2 Semiorthogonal decomposition for a sextic del Pezzo surface
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to checking that each generating line bundle has degree zero on the relevant (-2)-curves, then compute intersection numbers.

nodes.name: Projection functors $\tilde\alpha_i$
nodes.statement: Denote by $\tilde\alpha_i$ the projection functors of the decomposition~\eqref{eq:dbtx-}.

nodes.name: Semiorthogonal decomposition of $\mathbf{D}^-(X)$

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.8
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lemma:pi-properties} the functor $\pi^* \colon {\mathbf{D}}^-(X) \to {\mathbf{D}}^-({\widetilde{X}})$ is fully faithful, hence the subcategories ${\mathcal{A}}_i^-$ are semiorthogonal. Let us prove~\eqref{eq:pis-ai}. For this take any object ${\mathscr{F}} \in {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i^-$ and consider the standard triangle \begin{equation*} \pi^*(\pi_*{\mathscr{F}}) \to {\mathscr{F}} \to {\mathscr{G}}. \end{equation*} Then, of course, ${\mathscr{G}} \in \mathrm{Ker}\pi_*$. By Lemma~\ref{lemma:ker-pis} we have ${\mathscr{G}} = {\mathscr{G}}_2 \oplus {\mathscr{G}}_3$ with~${\mathscr{G}}_j \in {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_j^- \cap \mathrm{Ker} \pi_*$. If~$j \ne i$ then~$\mathrm{Ext}^\bullet({\mathscr{F}},{\mathscr{G}}_j) = 0$ by Lemma~\ref{lemma:ker-pis-orthogonality} and $\mathrm{Ext}^\bullet(\pi^*(\pi_*{\mathscr{F}}),{\mathscr{G}}_j) = 0$ since ${\mathscr{G}}_j \in \mathrm{Ker} \pi_*$. It follows from the above triangle that $\mathrm{Hom}({\mathscr{G}},{\mathscr{G}}_j) = 0$, hence ${\mathscr{G}}_j = 0$ since it is a direct summand of ${\mathscr{G}}$. Therefore we have ${\mathscr{G}} \in {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i^-$, hence $\pi^*(\pi_*{\mathscr{F}}) \in {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i^-$, hence $\pi_*{\mathscr{F}} \in {\mathcal{A}}_i^-$ by definition of the latter. This proves an inclusion $\pi_*({\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i^-) \subset {\mathcal{A}}_i^-$. The other inclusion follows from~\eqref{eq:pis-pis-id}. Now let us decompose any ${\mathscr{F}} \in {\mathbf{D}}^-(X)$. For this take ${\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}} := \pi^*({\mathscr{F}}) \in {\mathbf{D}}^-({\widetilde{X}})$ and consider its decomposition with respect to~\eqref{eq:dbtx-}. It is given by a chain of morphisms \begin{equation*} 0 = {\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}_3 \rightarrow {\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}_2 \rightarrow {\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}_1 \rightarrow {\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}_0 = {\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}, \end{equation*} whose cones are $\tilde\alpha_i({\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}) \in {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i^-$. Pushing it forward to $X$, we obtain a chain of morphisms \begin{equation*} 0 = \pi_*({\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}_3) \rightarrow \pi_*({\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}_2) \rightarrow \pi_*({\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}_1) \rightarrow \pi_*({\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}_0) = \pi_*({\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}) \cong {\mathscr{F}}, \end{equation*} whose cones are $\pi_*(\tilde\alpha_i({\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}})) \cong \pi_*(\tilde\alpha_i(\pi^*{\mathscr{F}})) \in \pi_*({\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i^-) = {\mathcal{A}}_i^-$. This proves the semiorthogonal decomposition and shows that its projection functors are given by~\eqref{eq:alpha}.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.9
nodes.statement: For the first claim it is enough to check that the projection functors $\alpha_i$ preserve boundedness. Take any ${\mathscr{F}} \in {\mathbf{D}}^{[a,b]}(X)$ and consider $\pi^*({\mathscr{F}}) \in {\mathbf{D}}^{(-\infty,b]}({\widetilde{X}})$. By projection formula $\pi_*(\pi^*({\mathscr{F}})) \cong {\mathscr{F}}$, hence by Lemma~\ref{lemma:spectral} we have $\tau^{\le a-1}(\pi^*({\mathscr{F}})) \in \mathrm{Ker} \pi_*$. Consider the triangle \begin{equation*} \tilde\alpha_i(\tau^{\le a-1}(\pi^*({\mathscr{F}}))) \to \tilde\alpha_i(\pi^*({\mathscr{F}})) \to \tilde\alpha_i(\tau^{\ge a}(\pi^*({\mathscr{F}}))) \end{equation*} obtained by applying the projection functor $\tilde\alpha_i$ to the canonical truncation triangle. By Lemma~\ref{lemma:ker-pis} the functor $\tilde\alpha_i$ preserves~$\mathrm{Ker}\pi_*$, hence the first term of the triangle is in $\mathrm{Ker} \pi_*$. Therefore, applying the pushforward we obtain an isomorphism \begin{equation*} \alpha_i({\mathscr{F}}) = \pi_*(\tilde\alpha_i(\pi^*({\mathscr{F}}))) \cong \pi_*(\tilde\alpha_i(\tau^{\ge a}(\pi^*({\mathscr{F}}))). \end{equation*} So, it remains to note that $\tau^{\ge a}(\pi^*({\mathscr{F}})) \in {\mathbf{D}}^{[a,b]}({\widetilde{X}})$, hence $\pi_*(\tilde\alpha_i(\tau^{\ge a}(\pi^*({\mathscr{F}})))$ is bounded, since both $\tilde\alpha_i$ and $\pi_*$ preserve boundedness. Moreover, if the cohomological amplitude of $\tilde\alpha_i$ is $(p,q)$ (it is finite since~${\widetilde{X}}$ is smooth, see~\cite[Proposition~2.5]{kuznetsov2008resolution}), then $\pi_*(\tilde\alpha_i(\tau^{\ge a}(\pi^*({\mathscr{F}}))) \in {\mathbf{D}}^{[a+p,b+q+1]}(X)$. In particular, $\alpha_i$ has finite cohomological amplitude. Let us prove the last claim. By~\eqref{eq:pis-ai} we have $\pi_*({\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i) \subset {\mathcal{A}}_i^-$, and since $\pi_*$ preserves boundedness, we have $\pi_*({\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i) \subset {\mathcal{A}}_i$. To check that this inclusion is an equality, take any ${\mathscr{F}} \in {\mathcal{A}}_i$. By Corollary~\ref{corollary:pis-epi} there exists ${\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}} \in {\mathbf{D}}({\widetilde{X}})$ such that ${\mathscr{F}} \cong \pi_*({\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}})$. Let ${\mathscr{G}}$ be the cone of the natural morphism $\pi^*{\mathscr{F}} \to {\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}$. Then ${\mathscr{G}} \in \mathrm{Ker} \pi_*$. Moreover, $\tilde\alpha_i({\mathscr{G}}) \in \mathrm{Ker} \pi_*$ by Lemma~\ref{lemma:ker-pis}, hence applying the functor $\pi_* \circ \tilde\alpha_i$ to the distinguished triangle $\pi^*{\mathscr{F}} \to {\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}} \to {\mathscr{G}}$, we deduce an isomorphism ${\mathscr{F}} \cong \alpha_i({\mathscr{F}}) \cong \pi_*(\tilde\alpha_i({\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}))$, and it remains to note that $\tilde\alpha_i({\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}) \in {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.10
nodes.statement: By definition $\gamma \circ \pi_{m*} = \pi_* \circ \tilde\gamma \circ \pi_m^* \circ \pi_{m*}$, so for commutativity of the first diagram it is enough to check that for any $M \in {\mathbf{D}}^-({\tilde{R}}_m)$ the cone of the canonical morphism $\pi_m^*(\pi_{m*}M) \to M$ is killed by the functor $\pi_* \circ \tilde\gamma$. But this cone, by Proposition~\ref{proposition:auslander-localization} is contained in the subcategory generated by the simple modules $S_1,\dots,S_{m-1}$ over ${\tilde{R}}_m$. By Remark~\ref{remark:delta-simples} the functor $\tilde\gamma$ takes these modules to sheaves ${\mathscr{O}}_\Delta(-1)$ for appropriate $(-2)$-curves $\Delta$ on ${\widetilde{X}}$, and the functor $\pi_*$ kills every ${\mathscr{O}}_\Delta(-1)$ by Lemma~\ref{lemma:pi-properties}. For commutativity of the second diagram note that by Proposition~\ref{proposition:auslander-localization} the image of the functor~$\pi_m^*$ is the left orthogonal ${}^\perp\langle S_1,\dots, S_{m-1} \rangle \subset {\mathbf{D}}^-({\tilde{R}}_m)$ of the subcategory generated by the simple modules. Therefore, using Lemma~\ref{lemma:ker-pis-orthogonality} and Remark~\ref{remark:delta-simples} we deduce that the image of $\tilde\gamma \circ \pi_m^*$ is contained in the left orthogonal ${}^\perp \langle {\mathscr{O}}_\Delta(-1) \rangle \subset {\mathbf{D}}^-({\widetilde{X}})$ of the subcategory generated by all $(-2)$-curves $\Delta$. Hence, by Lemma~\ref{lemma:pi-properties} it is contained in the image of $\pi^* \colon {\mathbf{D}}^-(X) \to {\mathbf{D}}^-({\widetilde{X}})$. Thus, the functor $\pi^* \circ \pi_*$ is identical on the image of $\tilde\gamma \circ \pi_m^*$, hence $\tilde\gamma \circ \pi_m^* \cong \pi^* \circ \pi_* \circ \tilde\gamma \circ \pi_m^* \cong \pi^* \circ \gamma$, and so the second diagram commutes. Let us show that $\gamma$ is fully faithful. Indeed, by commutativity of the second diagram in~\eqref{eq:gamma-tgamma}, this follows from full faithfulness of the functors $\pi_m^*$ (Proposition~\ref{proposition:auslander-localization}), $\tilde\gamma$ (Proposition~\ref{proposition:tcai-auslander}), and $\pi^*$ (Lemma~\ref{lemma:pi-properties}). Finally, let us show that $\gamma$ preserves boundedness. Indeed, take any $N \in {\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^m)$. By Proposition~\ref{proposition:auslander-localization} there exists $M \in {\mathbf{D}}({\tilde{R}}_m)$ such that $N \cong \pi_{m*}(M)$. Then $\gamma(N) = \gamma(\pi_{m*}(M))$ and by commutativity of the first diagram this is the same as $\pi_*(\tilde\gamma(M))$. We know that $\tilde\gamma(M)$ is bounded by Proposition~\ref{proposition:tcai-auslander}, hence so is $\pi_*(\tilde\gamma(M)) = \gamma(N)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.11
nodes.statement: By definition $\gamma_j = \pi_* \circ \tilde\gamma_j \circ \pi_{m_j}^*$ and its image is contained in $\pi_*({\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i^-) = {\mathcal{A}}_i^-$. Moreover, since $\gamma_j$ preserves boundedness, it actually is in ${\mathcal{A}}_i$. To see that the images of $\gamma_j$ are orthogonal, it is enough to check orthogonality of the images of functors $\pi^* \circ \gamma_j = \tilde\gamma_j \circ \pi_{m_j}^*$, which follows immediately from Proposition~\ref{proposition:tcai-auslander}. Therefore, ${\mathscr{F}} \cong \pi_*({\mathscr{G}}) \cong \oplus \pi_*({\mathscr{G}}_j)$. Moreover, $\pi_*({\mathscr{G}}_j) \in \pi_*(\tilde\gamma_j({\mathbf{D}}({\tilde{R}}_{m_j}))) = \gamma_j({\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^m))$, hence objects ${\mathscr{F}}_j = \pi_*({\mathscr{G}}_j)$ give the required decomposition of ${\mathscr{F}}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.12
nodes.statement: Consider the semiorthogonal decompositions \begin{equation*} {\mathbf{D}}({\widetilde{X}}) = \langle {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3 \otimes \omega_{\widetilde{X}}, {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1, {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2 \rangle \qquad\text{and}\qquad {\mathbf{D}}({\widetilde{X}}) = \langle {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_2 \otimes \omega_{\widetilde{X}}, {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_3 \otimes \omega_{\widetilde{X}}, {\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_1 \rangle, \end{equation*} obtained from~\eqref{eq:dbtx} by mutations. Since $\omega_{\widetilde{X}} \cong \pi^*\omega_X$ and $\omega_X$ is a line bundle on $X$, we have \begin{equation*} \pi_*({\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i \otimes \omega_{\widetilde{X}}) = \pi_*({\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i) \otimes \omega_X = {\mathcal{A}}_i \otimes \omega_X, \end{equation*} hence the arguments of this subsection also prove semiorthogonal decompositions \begin{equation} {\mathbf{D}}(X) = \langle {\mathcal{A}}_3 \otimes \omega_X, {\mathcal{A}}_1, {\mathcal{A}}_2 \rangle \qquad\text{and}\qquad {\mathbf{D}}(X) = \langle {\mathcal{A}}_2 \otimes \omega_X, {\mathcal{A}}_3 \otimes \omega_X, {\mathcal{A}}_1 \rangle. \end{equation} Since the twist by $\omega_X$ is an autoequivalence of ${\mathbf{D}}(X)$, these decompositions together with~\eqref{eq:dbx} show that each ${\mathcal{A}}_i$ is admissible. Indeed, (up to a twist) each ${\mathcal{A}}_i$ appears in one of the three decompositions on the left, and in one on the right, hence it is both left and right admissible.

nodes.name: Decomposition of $\mathbf{D}(X)$ into derived categories of zero-dimensional schemes
nodes.statement: For every sextic du Val del Pezzo surface $X$ over an algebraically closed field ${\mathsf{k}}$ there are zero-dimensional Gorenstein schemes $Z_1$, $Z_2$, $Z_3$ of lengths $1$, $3$, and $2$ respectively, such that ${\mathcal{A}}_i \cong {\mathbf{D}}(Z_i)$ and \begin{equation} {\mathbf{D}}(X) = \langle {\mathbf{D}}(Z_1), {\mathbf{D}}(Z_2), {\mathbf{D}}(Z_3) \rangle. \end{equation} The scheme structure of $Z_i$ depends on the type of $X$ as follows: \begin{equation*} \begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|} \hline \text{Type of $X$} & Z_1 & Z_2 & Z_3 \\ \hline 0 & \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}) & \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}) \sqcup \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}) \sqcup \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}) & \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}) \sqcup \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}) \\ \hline 1 & \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}) & \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}) \sqcup \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}) \sqcup \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}) & \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^2) \\ \hline 2 & \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}) & \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^2) \sqcup \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}) & \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}) \sqcup \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}) \\ \hline 3 & \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}) & \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^2) \sqcup \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}) & \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^2) \\ \hline 4 & \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}) & \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^3) & \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}) \sqcup \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}) \\ \hline 5 & \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}) & \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^3) & \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^2) \\ \hline \end{array} \end{equation*}
