nodes.statement_short: D(X) decomposes into derived categories of zero-dimensional Gorenstein schemes of lengths 1, 3, 2 whose structure depends on the type.
assumptions: For every sextic du Val del Pezzo surface $X$ over an algebraically closed field ${\mathsf{k}}$
conclusions: there are zero-dimensional Gorenstein schemes $Z_1$, $Z_2$, $Z_3$ of lengths $1$, $3$, and $2$ respectively, such that ${\mathcal{A}}_i \cong {\mathbf{D}}(Z_i)$ and \begin{equation} \label{eq:dbx-dz} {\mathbf{D}}(X) = \langle {\mathbf{D}}(Z_1), {\mathbf{D}}(Z_2), {\mathbf{D}}(Z_3) \rangle. \end{equation}

The scheme structure of $Z_i$ depends on the type of $X$ as follows: \begin{equation*} \begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|} \hline \text{Type of $X$} & Z_1 & Z_2 & Z_3 \\ \hline 0 & \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}) & \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}) \sqcup \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}) \sqcup \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}) & \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}) \sqcup \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}) \\ \hline 1 & \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}) & \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}) \sqcup \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}) \sqcup \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}) & \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^2) \\ \hline 2 & \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}) & \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^2) \sqcup \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}) & \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}) \sqcup \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}) \\ \hline 3 & \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}) & \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^2) \sqcup \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}) & \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^2) \\ \hline 4 & \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}) & \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^3) & \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}) \sqcup \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}) \\ \hline 5 & \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}) & \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^3) & \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^2) \\ \hline \end{array} \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Dual decomposition of $\mathbf{D}(X)$
nodes.statement: If $X$ is a sextic del Pezzo surface over an algebraically closed field, there is a semiorthogonal decomposition \begin{equation} {\mathbf{D}}(X) = \langle {\mathcal{A}}_3^\vee, {\mathcal{A}}_2^\vee, {\mathcal{A}}_1^\vee \rangle, \end{equation} where \begin{equation*} {\mathcal{A}}_i^\vee := \{ {\mathscr{F}} \in {\mathbf{D}}(X) \mid {\mathscr{F}}^\vee \in {\mathcal{A}}_i \} \cong {\mathbf{D}}(Z_i), \end{equation*} and ${\mathcal{A}}_i$ are the components of~\eqref{eq:dbx}. Moreover, this semiorthogonal decomposition is right mutation-dual to~\eqref{eq:dbx}, i.e., ${\mathcal{A}}_1^\vee = {\mathcal{A}}_1$, ${\mathcal{A}}_2^\vee = {\mathbb{L}}_{{\mathcal{A}}_1}({\mathcal{A}}_2)$ and ${\mathcal{A}}_3^\vee = {\mathbb{L}}_{{\mathcal{A}}_1}({\mathbb{L}}_{{\mathcal{A}}_2}({\mathcal{A}}_3))$.

nodes.statement_short: Dualizing (eq:dbx) gives a decomposition with components equivalent to D(Z_i), which is the right mutation-dual of (eq:dbx).

Moreover, this semiorthogonal decomposition is right mutation-dual to~\eqref{eq:dbx}, i.e., ${\mathcal{A}}_1^\vee = {\mathcal{A}}_1$, ${\mathcal{A}}_2^\vee = {\mathbb{L}}_{{\mathcal{A}}_1}({\mathcal{A}}_2)$ and ${\mathcal{A}}_3^\vee = {\mathbb{L}}_{{\mathcal{A}}_1}({\mathbb{L}}_{{\mathcal{A}}_2}({\mathcal{A}}_3))$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.14
nodes.statement: As we discussed in Section~\ref{subsection:duality}, the functor ${\mathscr{F}} \mapsto {\mathscr{F}}^\vee$ is an equivalence ${\mathbf{D}}(X)^{\mathrm{opp}} \to {\mathbf{D}}(X)$ (since~$X$ is Gorenstein). When applied to the semiorthogonal decomposition of Corollary~\ref{corollary:dbx-z2-z3}, it gives~\eqref{eq:dbx-dual} with~${\mathcal{A}}_i^\vee \cong {\mathbf{D}}(Z_i)^{\mathrm{opp}}$. Since $Z_1$, $Z_2$ and $Z_3$ are themselves Gorenstein, we have ${\mathbf{D}}(Z_i)^{\mathrm{opp}} \cong {\mathbf{D}}(Z_i)$. Finally, let us prove mutation-duality of~\eqref{eq:dbx-dual} and~\eqref{eq:dbx}. It follows from~\eqref{eq:alpha} that ${\mathbb{L}}_{{\mathcal{A}}_i} \circ \pi_* \cong \pi_* \circ {\mathbb{L}}_{{\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i}$ and ${\mathbb{L}}_{{\widetilde{{\mathcal{A}}}}_i} \circ \pi^* \cong \pi^* \circ {\mathbb{L}}_{{\mathcal{A}}_i}$. So, the required result follows easily from Lemma~\ref{lemma:dual-sod-tx}.

nodes.name: Sheaves on $Y \times \mathrm{Spec}(\mathsf{k}[t]/t^m)$ and flatness criterion
nodes.statement: Let $Z = \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^m)$. For any scheme $Y$ we have an equivalence \begin{equation*} \mathrm{coh}(Y \times Z) \cong \mathrm{coh}(Y,{\mathscr{O}}_Y[t]/t^m), \end{equation*} where the right hand side is the category of coherent sheaves ${\mathscr{F}}$ on $Y$ with an operator $t \colon {\mathscr{F}} \to {\mathscr{F}}$ such that $t^m = 0$. An object $({\mathscr{F}},t) \in \mathrm{coh}(Y,{\mathscr{O}}_Y[t]/t^m)$ considered as a sheaf on $Y \times Z$ is flat over $Z$ if and only if all the maps in the next chain of epimorphisms \begin{equation} \xymatrix@1{{\mathscr{F}}/(t{\mathscr{F}}) \ar@{->>}[r]^-t & (t{\mathscr{F}})/(t^2{\mathscr{F}}) \ar@{->>}[r]^-t & \ \dots\ \ar@{->>}[r]^-t & (t^{m-1}{\mathscr{F}})/(t^m{\mathscr{F}})} \end{equation} are isomorphisms.
nodes.statement_short: Coherent sheaves on $Y\times Z$ are sheaves with a nilpotent operator t; flatness over Z means the successive t-quotient maps are isomorphisms.
assumptions: Let $Z = \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^m)$.
For any scheme $Y$
conclusions: we have an equivalence \begin{equation*} \mathrm{coh}(Y \times Z) \cong \mathrm{coh}(Y,{\mathscr{O}}_Y[t]/t^m), \end{equation*} where the right hand side is the category of coherent sheaves ${\mathscr{F}}$ on $Y$ with an operator $t \colon {\mathscr{F}} \to {\mathscr{F}}$ such that $t^m = 0$.

An object $({\mathscr{F}},t) \in \mathrm{coh}(Y,{\mathscr{O}}_Y[t]/t^m)$ considered as a sheaf on $Y \times Z$ is flat over $Z$ if and only if all the maps in the next chain of epimorphisms \begin{equation}\label{eq:t-quotients} \xymatrix@1{{\mathscr{F}}/(t{\mathscr{F}}) \ar@{->>}[r]^-t & (t{\mathscr{F}})/(t^2{\mathscr{F}}) \ar@{->>}[r]^-t & \ \dots\ \ar@{->>}[r]^-t & (t^{m-1}{\mathscr{F}})/(t^m{\mathscr{F}})} \end{equation} are isomorphisms.
nodes.label: lemma:sheaves-y-z

nodes.name: Chain of t-quotient epimorphisms

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.15
nodes.statement: The first part follows immediately from an identification $Y \times Z = \mathrm{Spec}_Y({\mathscr{O}}_Y[t]/t^m)$. To verify flatness, we should compute the derived pullback functors for the embedding $Y \to Y \times Z$ corresponding to the unique closed point of~$Z$. Using the standard resolution \begin{equation*} \dots \xrightarrow{\ t^{m-1}\ } {\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^m \xrightarrow{\ t\ } {\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^m \xrightarrow{\ t^{m-1}\ } {\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^m \xrightarrow{\ t\ } {\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^m \xrightarrow{\ \ \ } {\mathsf{k}} \to 0 \end{equation*} we see that $({\mathscr{F}},t)$ is flat over $Z$ if and only if the complex \begin{equation*} \dots \xrightarrow{\ t^{m-1}\ } {\mathscr{F}} \xrightarrow{\ t\ } {\mathscr{F}} \xrightarrow{\ t^{m-1}\ } {\mathscr{F}} \xrightarrow{\ t\ } {\mathscr{F}} \xrightarrow{\ t^{m-1}\ } \dots \end{equation*} is exact. This means that $\mathrm{Ker}({\mathscr{F}} \xrightarrow{\ t\ } {\mathscr{F}}) = t^{m-1}{\mathscr{F}}$ and $\mathrm{Ker}({\mathscr{F}} \xrightarrow{\ t^{m-1}\ } {\mathscr{F}}) = t{\mathscr{F}}$. The second equality implies that the composition of all maps in~\eqref{eq:t-quotients} is an isomorphism, hence so is each of them. On the other hand, if all the maps in~\eqref{eq:t-quotients} are isomorphisms then both equalities above easily follow. This proves the required criterion of flatness.
nodes.statement_short: Identify $Y\times Z$ with a relative spectrum; test flatness with the periodic resolution of the residue field and translate exactness into the quotient-chain criterion.

nodes.name: Equivalence by relative Spec; reduce flatness to derived pullback

This means that $\mathrm{Ker}({\mathscr{F}} \xrightarrow{\ t\ } {\mathscr{F}}) = t^{m-1}{\mathscr{F}}$ and $\mathrm{Ker}({\mathscr{F}} \xrightarrow{\ t^{m-1}\ } {\mathscr{F}}) = t{\mathscr{F}}$.

nodes.name: Embedding functors $\gamma_Z$
nodes.statement: In what follows for a connected component $Z$ of $Z_d$ we denote by $\gamma_Z$ the embedding functor (constructed in Proposition~\ref{proposition:gamma}) \begin{equation*} \gamma_Z \colon {\mathbf{D}}(Z) \hookrightarrow {\mathbf{D}}(X), \end{equation*} By definition~\eqref{def:gamma} we have $\gamma_Z = \pi_* \circ \tilde\gamma_Z \circ \pi_m^*$, where $\pi_m^* \colon {\mathbf{D}}^-(Z) \to {\mathbf{D}}^-({\tilde{R}}_m)$ is the categorical resolution of the scheme $Z = \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^m)$ described in~\eqref{eq:pms}, and $\tilde\gamma_Z \colon {\mathbf{D}}({\tilde{R}}_m) \to {\mathbf{D}}({\widetilde{X}})$ is the embedding of Proposition~\ref{proposition:tcai-auslander}. Then \begin{equation*} \gamma_{Z_2} = \bigoplus_{Z \subset Z_2} \gamma_Z \qquad\text{and}\qquad \gamma_{Z_3} = \bigoplus_{Z \subset Z_3} \gamma_Z, \end{equation*} (Proposition~\ref{proposition:sod-cai}) with the sum over all connected components in both cases.
nodes.statement_short: For a component Z of $Z_d$, $\gamma_Z = \pi_*\tilde\gamma_Z\pi_m^*$, and $\gamma_{Z_d}$ is the sum over components.

nodes.name: Images $\mathscr{E}_z$ of points of $Z_d$
nodes.statement_short: The image $\mathscr{E}_z$ of a point of $Z_d$ is the pushforward of an explicit line bundle; it is globally generated with $d$ sections and no higher cohomology.
conclusions: If $z$ is the unique closed ${\mathsf{k}}$-point of $Z_1$ then $\gamma_{Z_1}({\mathscr{O}}_z) \cong {\mathscr{O}}_X \cong \pi_*{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}$.

Let $z \in Z_2$ be a closed ${\mathsf{k}}$-point and let ${\mathscr{E}}_z := \gamma_{Z_2}({\mathscr{O}}_z) \in {\mathbf{D}}(X)$ be the corresponding object. Then \begin{itemize} \item[(a)] if the component of $Z_2$ containing $z$ is reduced and corresponds to the $i$-th blowup center, then \begin{equation*} {\mathscr{E}}_z \cong \pi_*{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_i); \end{equation*} \item[(b)] if the component of $Z_2$ containing $z$ has length $2$ then \begin{equation*} {\mathscr{E}}_z \cong \pi_*{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_1) \cong \pi_*{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_2); \end{equation*} \item[(c)] if the component of $Z_2$ containing $z$ has length $3$, then \begin{equation*} {\mathscr{E}}_z \cong \pi_*{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_1) \cong \pi_*{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_2) \cong \pi_*{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_3). \end{equation*}

Let $z \in Z_3$ be a closed ${\mathsf{k}}$-point and let ${\mathscr{E}}_z := \gamma_{Z_3}({\mathscr{O}}_z) \in {\mathbf{D}}(X)$ be the corresponding object. Then \begin{itemize} \item[(a)] if the component of $Z_3$ containing $z$ is reduced then \begin{equation*} {\mathscr{E}}_z \cong \pi_*{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h) \qquad\text{or}\qquad {\mathscr{E}}_z \cong \pi_*{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(2h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3); \end{equation*} \item[(b)] if the component of $Z_3$ containing $z$ has length $2$ then \begin{equation*} {\mathscr{E}}_z \cong \pi_*{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h) \cong \pi_*{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(2h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3). \end{equation*}

In all these cases, ${\mathscr{E}}_z$ is a globally generated sheaf, and if $z \in Z_d$ then \begin{equation*} \dim H^0(X,{\mathscr{E}}_z) = d \qquad\text{and}\qquad H^{i}(X,{\mathscr{E}}_z) = 0 \quad\text{for $i \ne 0$}. \end{equation*}
nodes.label: lemma:e-z-small

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.16
nodes.statement: The statements (1), (2), and~(3) follow directly from the first commutative diagram in~\eqref{eq:gamma-tgamma}, isomorphism~$\pi_{m*}(S_0) \cong {\mathscr{O}}_z$ proved in Proposition~\ref{proposition:auslander-localization}, and the fact that the simple module $S_0$ coincides with the standard exceptional module $E_0$ (see~\eqref{eq:resolution-simple}), so that by Proposition~\ref{proposition:tcai-auslander} the functor $\tilde\gamma$ takes it to one of the line bundles in~\eqref{eq:tx-excol}. Going over the possible cases gives for~${\mathscr{E}}_z$ the first isomorphisms. The other isomorphisms of sheaves in case of non-reduced components follow from exact sequences~\eqref{eq:e12}, \eqref{eq:e23} and~\eqref{eq:e123} respectively. In cases $(1)$, $(2a)$ and $(3a)$ the global generation is easy (the corresponding sheaves are already globally generated on ${\widetilde{X}}$; extending their evaluation homomorphisms to exact sequences and pushing them forward to $X$ it is easy to see that their pushforwards are also globally generated). In cases $(2b)$, $(2c)$, and~$(3b)$ the same argument shows that $\pi_*{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_1)$, $\pi_*{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_3)$ and $\pi_*{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h)$ are globally generated, and for the remaining two sheaves we can use the corresponding isomorphisms. The cohomology computation reduces to a computation on ${\widetilde{X}}$ which is straightforward.
nodes.statement_short: Push the simple module $S_0=E_0$ through the commutative diagram to get a line bundle, compare non-reduced cases via the exact sequences, and check global generation and cohomology on the resolution.

nodes.name: First isomorphisms from the diagram and S_0 = E_0
nodes.statement: The statements (1), (2), and~(3) follow directly from the first commutative diagram in~\eqref{eq:gamma-tgamma}, isomorphism~$\pi_{m*}(S_0) \cong {\mathscr{O}}_z$ proved in Proposition~\ref{proposition:auslander-localization}, and the fact that the simple module $S_0$ coincides with the standard exceptional module $E_0$ (see~\eqref{eq:resolution-simple}), so that by Proposition~\ref{proposition:tcai-auslander} the functor $\tilde\gamma$ takes it to one of the line bundles in~\eqref{eq:tx-excol}. Going over the possible cases gives for~${\mathscr{E}}_z$ the first isomorphisms.

nodes.statement: The other isomorphisms of sheaves in case of non-reduced components follow from exact sequences~\eqref{eq:e12}, \eqref{eq:e23} and~\eqref{eq:e123} respectively. In cases $(1)$, $(2a)$ and $(3a)$ the global generation is easy (the corresponding sheaves are already globally generated on ${\widetilde{X}}$; extending their evaluation homomorphisms to exact sequences and pushing them forward to $X$ it is easy to see that their pushforwards are also globally generated). nodes.label: def:fez

nodes.name: Length $\ell(Z)$
nodes.statement: We denote by~$\ell(Z)$ the length of~$Z$.

nodes.name: Bundles $\mathfrak{E}_Z$ and $\widetilde{\mathfrak{E}}_Z$
nodes.statement: Both ${\mathfrak{E}}_Z$ and ${\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_Z$ are vector bundles of rank~$\ell(Z)$ on~$X$ and~${\widetilde{X}}$ respectively, and \begin{equation} {\mathfrak{E}}_Z \cong \pi_*({\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_Z). \end{equation} Moreover, ${\mathfrak{E}}_Z$ is an iterated extension of the sheaf ${\mathscr{E}}_z$, where $z$ is the closed point of~$Z$. In particular, the bundle ${\mathfrak{E}}_Z$ is globally generated with $\dim H^0(X,{\mathfrak{E}}_Z) = d\ell(Z)$ and $H^i(X,{\mathfrak{E}}_Z) = 0$ for $i \ne 0$.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathfrak{E}_Z$ and its pullback are vector bundles of rank $\ell(Z)$, iterated extensions of $\mathscr{E}_z$, globally generated with $d\ell(Z)$ sections.
conclusions: Both ${\mathfrak{E}}_Z$ and ${\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_Z$ are vector bundles of rank~$\ell(Z)$ on~$X$ and~${\widetilde{X}}$ respectively, and \begin{equation} \label{eq:ez-pullback} {\mathfrak{E}}_Z \cong \pi_*({\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_Z). \end{equation}
Moreover, ${\mathfrak{E}}_Z$ is an iterated extension of the sheaf ${\mathscr{E}}_z$, where $z$ is the closed point of~$Z$.
In particular, the bundle ${\mathfrak{E}}_Z$ is globally generated with $\dim H^0(X,{\mathfrak{E}}_Z) = d\ell(Z)$ and $H^i(X,{\mathfrak{E}}_Z) = 0$ for $i \ne 0$.
nodes.label: proposition:e-z-big

nodes.name: $\mathfrak{E}_Z \cong \pi_*(\widetilde{\mathfrak{E}}_Z)$
nodes.statement: {\mathfrak{E}}_Z \cong \pi_*({\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_Z).

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.17
nodes.statement: First, by commutativity of~\eqref{eq:gamma-tgamma} we have ${\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_Z \cong \tilde\gamma_Z(\pi_m^*({\mathscr{O}}_Z))$. Furthermore, $\pi_m^*({\mathscr{O}}_Z) \cong P_0$, the principal projective module, see~\eqref{eq:pms}, so that \begin{equation} {\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_Z \cong \tilde\gamma_Z(P_0). \end{equation} By~\eqref{eq:projective-resolution-ei} the module $P_0$ is an iterated extension of the standard exceptional modules $E_i$, hence $\tilde\gamma_Z(P_0)$ is an iterated extension of $\tilde\gamma_Z(E_i)$, and as it is explained in the proof of Proposition~\ref{proposition:tcai-auslander} these are line bundles on ${\widetilde{X}}$. More precisely, if $Z$ is reduced, then \begin{equation*} {\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_Z \cong {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_i)\quad\text{for some $i$},\quad\text{or}\quad {\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_Z \cong {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h),\quad\text{or}\quad {\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_Z \cong {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(2h-e_1-e_2-e_3), \end{equation*} depending on whether $Z$ is a component of $Z_2$ or of $Z_3$. Furthermore, if $Z$ has length~2 then we have exact sequences \begin{equation} 0 \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_2) \to {\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_Z \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_1) \to 0, \end{equation} when $Z$ is a component of $Z_2$, or \begin{equation} 0 \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(2h-e_1-e_2-e_3) \to {\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_Z \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h) \to 0, \end{equation} when $Z$ is a component of $Z_3$. Finally, if $Z$ has length~3 we have two exact sequences \begin{equation} 0 \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_3) \to {\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_Z \to {\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}'_Z \to 0, \qquad\text{where}\qquad 0 \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_2) \to {\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}'_Z \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_1) \to 0. \end{equation} In all cases ${\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_Z$ is evidently a vector bundle of rank~$\ell(Z)$, and since ${\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_Z \cong \pi^*{\mathfrak{E}}_Z$, it follows that ${\mathfrak{E}}_Z$ is also a vector bundle of the same rank~$\ell(Z)$. Finally, since $Z \cong \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^m)$, the sheaf ${\mathscr{O}}_Z$ is an iterated extension of the sheaf ${\mathscr{O}}_z$, where $z$ is the closed point of $Z$, hence ${\mathfrak{E}}_Z = \gamma_Z({\mathscr{O}}_Z)$ is an iterated extension of the sheaf ${\mathscr{E}}_z = \gamma_Z({\mathscr{O}}_z)$. Now the last part of Lemma~\ref{lemma:e-z-small} implies the last part of the proposition.
nodes.statement_short: Identify the pullback with $\tilde\gamma_Z(P_0)$, an iterated extension of line bundles; list the extensions by length, deduce local freeness, and get cohomology from Lemma 3.16.

nodes.name: Pullback equals gamma~_Z(P_0)

Furthermore, $\pi_m^*({\mathscr{O}}_Z) \cong P_0$, the principal projective module, see~\eqref{eq:pms}, so that \begin{equation} {\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_Z \cong \tilde\gamma_Z(P_0). \end{equation}

nodes.statement: 0 \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_2) \to {\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_Z \to {\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_1) \to 0,

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.18
nodes.statement: Let $Z \cong \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^m) \subset Z_d$ be a connected component. We apply Lemma~\ref{lemma:sheaves-y-z} to construct a sheaf ${\mathscr{E}}_Z$ on~$X \times Z$ such that ${\mathfrak{E}}_Z \cong p_{X*}{\mathscr{E}}_Z$. For this, first, note that the filtration on ${\mathscr{O}}_Z$ induced by the natural action of the ring ${\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^m$ has quotients isomorphic to ${\mathscr{O}}_z$, where $z$ is the closed point of $Z$, hence the induced filtration on ${\mathfrak{E}}_Z \cong \gamma_Z({\mathscr{O}}_Z)$ has quotients isomorphic to $\gamma({\mathscr{O}}_z) = {\mathscr{E}}_z$, i.e., \begin{equation} (t^i{\mathfrak{E}}_Z)/(t^{i+1}{\mathfrak{E}}_Z) \cong {\mathscr{E}}_z. \end{equation} It is clear that the epimorphisms between these quotients induced by $t$ have to be isomorphisms, hence the sheaf ${\mathscr{E}}_Z$ associated with ${\mathfrak{E}}_Z$ is flat over~$Z$ by Lemma~\ref{lemma:sheaves-y-z}. Next, we define ${\mathscr{E}}_{Z_d}$ as the sum ${\mathscr{E}}_{Z_d} := \bigoplus {\mathscr{E}}_Z$ over connected components $Z \subset Z_d$. Then the first part of the proposition holds. It remains to show that the functors $\gamma_{Z_d}$ are Fourier--Mukai. The functor $\tilde\gamma_Z \colon {\mathbf{D}}({\tilde{R}}_m) \to {\mathbf{D}}({\widetilde{X}})$ by construction (which is explained in Proposition~\ref{proposition:tcai-auslander} and is based on Proposition~\ref{proposition:rm-equivalence}) is a Fourier--Mukai functor. By~\eqref{def:gamma} the functor $\gamma_Z \colon {\mathbf{D}}(Z) \to {\mathbf{D}}(X)$ is also a Fourier--Mukai functor. Since the scheme $Z$ is affine, the kernel object defining the functor $\gamma_Z$ can be identified with the sheaf $\gamma_Z({\mathscr{O}}_Z) \cong {\mathfrak{E}}_Z \in {\mathbf{D}}(X)$ with its natural module structure over ${\mathsf{k}}[Z] = {\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^m$, which corresponds to the sheaf ${\mathscr{E}}_Z$ by its definition above. The last claim follows from this by dualization (note that Grothendieck duality implies that the equivalence of Lemma~\ref{lemma:sheaves-y-z} is compatible with dualization, since the dualizing complex of $Z$ is trivial).
nodes.statement_short: Build the kernel on each component from the t-filtration of $\mathfrak{E}_Z$ via Lemma 3.15; Fourier-Mukai property comes from the construction of $\tilde\gamma_Z$ and affineness of Z; dualize for the last claim.

nodes.statement: Denote \begin{equation*} \chi({\mathscr{F}},{\mathscr{G}}) = \sum (-1)^i \dim \mathrm{Ext}^i({\mathscr{F}},{\mathscr{G}}) \qquad\text{and}\qquad r({\mathscr{F}}) = \sum (-1)^i \mathrm{rk}({\mathscr{H}}^i({\mathscr{F}})) \end{equation*} (assuming the sums are actually finite).

nodes.statement: For any ${\mathscr{F}} \in {\mathbf{D}}(X)$ we have \begin{alignat*}{2} \chi({\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_2},{\mathscr{F}}) &= 2 &&\chi({\mathscr{O}}_X,{\mathscr{F}}) + \chi({\mathscr{O}}_X,{\mathscr{F}}(K_X)) - 3r({\mathscr{F}}),\\ \chi({\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3},{\mathscr{F}}) &= &&\chi({\mathscr{O}}_X,{\mathscr{F}}) + \chi({\mathscr{O}}_X,{\mathscr{F}}(K_X)) - 2r({\mathscr{F}}). \end{alignat*}

assumptions: For any ${\mathscr{F}} \in {\mathbf{D}}(X)$
conclusions: \chi({\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_2},{\mathscr{F}}) &= 2 &&\chi({\mathscr{O}}_X,{\mathscr{F}}) + \chi({\mathscr{O}}_X,{\mathscr{F}}(K_X)) - 3r({\mathscr{F}}),\\ \chi({\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3},{\mathscr{F}}) &= &&\chi({\mathscr{O}}_X,{\mathscr{F}}) + \chi({\mathscr{O}}_X,{\mathscr{F}}(K_X)) - 2r({\mathscr{F}}).

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.20
nodes.statement: By Corollary~\ref{corollary:pis-epi} we can write ${\mathscr{F}} = \pi_*{\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}$ for some ${\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}} \in {\mathbf{D}}({\widetilde{X}})$, hence by adjunction \begin{equation*} \chi({\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_d}, {\mathscr{F}}) = \chi({\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_d},\pi_*{\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}) = \chi(\pi^*{\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_d},{\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}) = \chi({\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_{Z_d},{\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}). \end{equation*} As it is explained in Proposition~\ref{proposition:e-z-big} the bundle ${\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_{Z_2}$ is an extension (possibly trivial) of the line bundles~${\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_i)$ for $i = 1,2,3$, hence \begin{equation*} \mathrm{ch}({\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_{Z_2}) = \sum \mathrm{ch}({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_i)) = 3 + (3h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3) = 3 - K_{\widetilde{X}} = 2\mathrm{ch}({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}) + \mathrm{ch}(\omega_{\widetilde{X}}^{-1}) - 3\mathrm{ch}({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{P}}), \end{equation*} where ${\widetilde{P}}$ is a general point on ${\widetilde{X}}$. Therefore, by Riemann--Roch and adjunction we have \begin{equation*} \chi({\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_{Z_2},{\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}) = 2\chi({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}},{\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}) + \chi(\omega_{\widetilde{X}}^{-1},{\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}) - 3\chi({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{P}},{\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}) = 2\chi({\mathscr{O}}_X,{\mathscr{F}}) + \chi(\omega_X^{-1},{\mathscr{F}}) - 3\chi({\mathscr{O}}_{\pi({\widetilde{P}})},{\mathscr{F}}), \end{equation*} which gives the first equality. Similarly, for ${\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_{Z_3}$ we have \begin{equation*} \mathrm{ch}({\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_{Z_3}) = \mathrm{ch}({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h)) + \mathrm{ch}({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(2h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3)) = \mathrm{ch}({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}) + \mathrm{ch}(\omega_{\widetilde{X}}^{-1}) - 2\mathrm{ch}({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{P}}), \end{equation*} and using Riemann--Roch and adjunction in the same way as before, we finish the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Lift F to the resolution, compute the Chern characters of the pulled-back bundles as sums of line bundles, and apply Riemann-Roch and adjunction.

nodes.name: Reduce to the resolution by adjunction
nodes.statement: By Corollary~\ref{corollary:pis-epi} we can write ${\mathscr{F}} = \pi_*{\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}$ for some ${\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}} \in {\mathbf{D}}({\widetilde{X}})$, hence by adjunction \begin{equation*} \chi({\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_d}, {\mathscr{F}}) = \chi({\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_d},\pi_*{\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}) = \chi(\pi^*{\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_d},{\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}) = \chi({\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_{Z_d},{\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}). \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the resolution by adjunction

nodes.name: Chern character of pulled-back E_{Z_2}
nodes.statement: As it is explained in Proposition~\ref{proposition:e-z-big} the bundle ${\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_{Z_2}$ is an extension (possibly trivial) of the line bundles~${\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_i)$ for $i = 1,2,3$, hence \begin{equation*} \mathrm{ch}({\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_{Z_2}) = \sum \mathrm{ch}({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_i)) = 3 + (3h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3) = 3 - K_{\widetilde{X}} = 2\mathrm{ch}({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}) + \mathrm{ch}(\omega_{\widetilde{X}}^{-1}) - 3\mathrm{ch}({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{P}}), \end{equation*} where ${\widetilde{P}}$ is a general point on ${\widetilde{X}}$.

nodes.name: First equality by Riemann-Roch
nodes.statement: Therefore, by Riemann--Roch and adjunction we have \begin{equation*} \chi({\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_{Z_2},{\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}) = 2\chi({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}},{\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}) + \chi(\omega_{\widetilde{X}}^{-1},{\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}) - 3\chi({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{P}},{\widetilde{{\mathscr{F}}}}) = 2\chi({\mathscr{O}}_X,{\mathscr{F}}) + \chi(\omega_X^{-1},{\mathscr{F}}) - 3\chi({\mathscr{O}}_{\pi({\widetilde{P}})},{\mathscr{F}}), \end{equation*} which gives the first equality.

nodes.name: Second equality similarly

nodes.name: Pushforwards of the universal kernels are vector bundles
nodes.statement: The pushforwards $p_{2*}{\mathscr{E}}_{Z_2}$ and $p_{3*}{\mathscr{E}}_{Z_3}$ are vector bundles on $Z_2$ and $Z_3$ of rank $2$ and $3$ respectively. Similarly, the pushforward $p_{23*}(p_{X2}^*{\mathscr{E}}_{Z_2}^\vee \otimes p_{X3}^*{\mathscr{E}}_{Z_3})$ is a line bundle on $Z_2 \times Z_3$.

conclusions: The pushforwards $p_{2*}{\mathscr{E}}_{Z_2}$ and $p_{3*}{\mathscr{E}}_{Z_3}$ are vector bundles on $Z_2$ and $Z_3$ of rank $2$ and $3$ respectively.
the pushforward $p_{23*}(p_{X2}^*{\mathscr{E}}_{Z_2}^\vee \otimes p_{X3}^*{\mathscr{E}}_{Z_3})$ is a line bundle on $Z_2 \times Z_3$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.21
nodes.statement: Let $Z \cong \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^m)$ be a connected component of $Z_d$ with $d \in \{2,3\}$ with closed point~$z$. Consider the fiber square \begin{equation*} \xymatrix{ X \times Z \ar[r]^-{p_Z} \ar[d]_{p_X} & Z \ar[d] \\ X \ar[r] & \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}) } \end{equation*} The pushforward to $\mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}})$ of $p_{Z*}{\mathscr{E}}_{Z}$ equals the pushforward of $p_{X*}({\mathscr{E}}_{Z}) \cong {\mathfrak{E}}_Z$, i.e.~$H^\bullet(X,{\mathfrak{E}}_{Z})$ with its natural ${\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^m$-module structure. So, by Lemma~\ref{lemma:sheaves-y-z} to check that $p_{Z*}{\mathscr{E}}_{Z}$ is a vector bundle it is enough to show that the natural epimorphisms between the quotient spaces $(t^iH^0(X,{\mathfrak{E}}_{Z}))/(t^{i+1}H^0(X,{\mathfrak{E}}_{Z}))$ are isomorphisms (the other cohomology groups of ${\mathfrak{E}}_Z$ vanish by Proposition~\ref{proposition:e-z-big}). By~\eqref{eq:fez-quotients} all these quotients are isomorphic to $H^0(X,{\mathscr{E}}_z)$, hence $d$-dimensional by Lemma~\ref{lemma:e-z-small}, hence the epimorphisms $t$ between them are isomorphisms. This proves that $p_{Z*}{\mathscr{E}}_{Z}$ is locally free of rank~$d$ on $Z$. For the second statement, let $Z \subset Z_2$ and $Z' \subset Z_3$ be connected components, $Z \cong \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^m)$, and~$Z' \cong \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}[t']/(t')^{m'})$. Under an analogue of Lemma~\ref{lemma:sheaves-y-z} the sheaf $p_{23*}(p_{X2}^*{\mathscr{E}}_{Z_2}^\vee \otimes p_{X3}^*{\mathscr{E}}_{Z_3})$ corresponds to the vector space $H^\bullet(X,{\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_2}^\vee \otimes {\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3})$ with its natural bifiltration. So, we have to check that the operators $t$ and $t'$ induce isomorphisms between the quotients of this bifiltration. Since \begin{equation*} H^\bullet(X,{\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_2}^\vee \otimes {\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3}) \cong \mathrm{Ext}^\bullet({\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_2},{\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3}) \cong \mathrm{Ext}^\bullet(\pi^*{\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_2},\pi^*{\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3}) \cong \mathrm{Ext}^\bullet({\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_{Z_2},{\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_{Z_3}), \end{equation*} and the bifiltration is induced by the defining exact sequences~\eqref{eq:tcez-12}, \eqref{eq:tcez-12-23} and~\eqref{eq:tcez-123} of ${\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_Z$ and ${\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_{Z'}$, it is enough to compute $\mathrm{Ext}$-spaces between the corresponding line bundles on ${\widetilde{X}}$. A direct computation gives \begin{alignat*}{3} & \mathrm{Ext}^\bullet({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_i),{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h)) &&\cong H^\bullet({\widetilde{X}},{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(e_i)) &&= {\mathsf{k}},\\ & \mathrm{Ext}^\bullet({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_i),{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(2h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3)) &&\cong H^\bullet({\widetilde{X}},{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_j - e_k)) &&= {\mathsf{k}}, \end{alignat*} therefore, the epimorphisms $t$ and $t'$ between them are isomorphisms, and the sheaf $p_{23*}(p_{X2}^*{\mathscr{E}}_{Z_2}^\vee \otimes p_{X3}^*{\mathscr{E}}_{Z_3})$ is locally free of rank 1 on $Z \times Z'$. Summing up over all connected components completes the proof of the lemma.

nodes.statement_short: Reduce to quotient maps on H^0

nodes.name: Quotients d-dimensional, so locally free of rank d
nodes.statement: By~\eqref{eq:fez-quotients} all these quotients are isomorphic to $H^0(X,{\mathscr{E}}_z)$, hence $d$-dimensional by Lemma~\ref{lemma:e-z-small}, hence the epimorphisms $t$ between them are isomorphisms. This proves that $p_{Z*}{\mathscr{E}}_{Z}$ is locally free of rank~$d$ on $Z$.
nodes.statement_short: Quotients d-dimensional, so locally free of rank d

nodes.name: Fix components Z, Z'
nodes.statement: For the second statement, let $Z \subset Z_2$ and $Z' \subset Z_3$ be connected components, $Z \cong \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}[t]/t^m)$, and~$Z' \cong \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}}[t']/(t')^{m'})$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix components Z, Z'

nodes.name: Reduce to bifiltration quotients
nodes.statement: Under an analogue of Lemma~\ref{lemma:sheaves-y-z} the sheaf $p_{23*}(p_{X2}^*{\mathscr{E}}_{Z_2}^\vee \otimes p_{X3}^*{\mathscr{E}}_{Z_3})$ corresponds to the vector space $H^\bullet(X,{\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_2}^\vee \otimes {\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3})$ with its natural bifiltration. So, we have to check that the operators $t$ and $t'$ induce isomorphisms between the quotients of this bifiltration.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to bifiltration quotients

nodes.name: Reduce to Ext between line bundles on the resolution
nodes.statement: Since \begin{equation*} H^\bullet(X,{\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_2}^\vee \otimes {\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3}) \cong \mathrm{Ext}^\bullet({\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_2},{\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3}) \cong \mathrm{Ext}^\bullet(\pi^*{\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_2},\pi^*{\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3}) \cong \mathrm{Ext}^\bullet({\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_{Z_2},{\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_{Z_3}), \end{equation*} and the bifiltration is induced by the defining exact sequences~\eqref{eq:tcez-12}, \eqref{eq:tcez-12-23} and~\eqref{eq:tcez-123} of ${\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_Z$ and ${\widetilde{{\mathfrak{E}}}}_{Z'}$, it is enough to compute $\mathrm{Ext}$-spaces between the corresponding line bundles on ${\widetilde{X}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to Ext between line bundles on the resolution

nodes.name: Ext spaces are one-dimensional; line bundle
nodes.statement: A direct computation gives \begin{alignat*}{3} & \mathrm{Ext}^\bullet({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_i),{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h)) &&\cong H^\bullet({\widetilde{X}},{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(e_i)) &&= {\mathsf{k}},\\ & \mathrm{Ext}^\bullet({\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h-e_i),{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(2h - e_1 - e_2 - e_3)) &&\cong H^\bullet({\widetilde{X}},{\mathscr{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(h - e_j - e_k)) &&= {\mathsf{k}}, \end{alignat*} therefore, the epimorphisms $t$ and $t'$ between them are isomorphisms, and the sheaf $p_{23*}(p_{X2}^*{\mathscr{E}}_{Z_2}^\vee \otimes p_{X3}^*{\mathscr{E}}_{Z_3})$ is locally free of rank 1 on $Z \times Z'$. Summing up over all connected components completes the proof of the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Ext spaces are one-dimensional; line bundle

nodes.name: Gluing bimodules of the decomposition
nodes.statement: The above lemma can be interpreted as a computation of the gluing bimodules (cf.~\cite[Section~2.2]{kuznetsov2015categorical}) between the components of~\eqref{eq:dbx}. It says that ${\mathbf{D}}(X)$ is the gluing of ${\mathbf{D}}({\mathsf{k}})$, ${\mathbf{D}}(Z_2)$, and ${\mathbf{D}}(Z_3)$ with the gluing bimodules being ${\mathsf{k}}[Z_2]^{\oplus 2}$, ${\mathsf{k}}[Z_2 \times Z_3]$, and ${\mathsf{k}}[Z_3]^{\oplus 3}$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 3.21 computes the gluing bimodules between D(k), D(Z_2), D(Z_3).

nodes.name: Anticanonical Hilbert polynomial $h_{\mathscr{F}}$
nodes.statement: For a sheaf ${\mathscr{F}}$ on $X$ we denote by \begin{equation*} h_{\mathscr{F}}(t) := \chi({\mathscr{F}}(-tK_X)) \in {\mathbb{Z}}[t], \end{equation*} the Hilbert polynomial of ${\mathscr{F}}$ with respect to the anticanonical polarization of $X$.

nodes.name: Leading coefficient of the Hilbert polynomial
nodes.statement: This is a quadratic polynomial with the leading coefficient equal to $r({\mathscr{F}})\cdot K_X^2/2 = 3r({\mathscr{F}})$.

nodes.name: Polynomials $h_d(t)$
nodes.statement: h_d(t) := (3t + d)(t+1) \in {\mathbb{Z}}[t].
nodes.label: eq:hd

nodes.name: Inequalities between the $h_d$
nodes.statement: h_4(t) > h_3(t) > h_2(t) > h_{{\mathscr{O}}_X}(t) > h_4(t-1) > h_3(t-1) > h_2(t-1) \qquad\text{for all $t \gg 0$.}
nodes.statement_short: For large t the polynomials are ordered h_4 > h_3 > h_2 > h_{O_X} > shifted ones; stated as an elementary verification.
nodes.label: eq:hd-inequalities

nodes.name: Semistability of sheaves with Hilbert polynomial $h_d$
nodes.statement: A sheaf ${\mathscr{F}}$ on $X$ with Hilbert polynomial $h_d(t)$ is Gieseker semistable if and only if it is Gieseker stable and if and only if it is torsion-free.
nodes.statement_short: For Hilbert polynomial h_d, Gieseker semistable, stable and torsion-free are equivalent.
assumptions: A sheaf ${\mathscr{F}}$ on $X$ with Hilbert polynomial $h_d(t)$
conclusions: is Gieseker semistable if and only if it is Gieseker stable and if and only if it is torsion-free.
nodes.label: lemma:hd-stable

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.1
nodes.statement: As we observed above, the leading monomial of $h_d({\mathscr{F}})$ being $3t^2$ means that $r({\mathscr{F}}) = 1$. Therefore, such a sheaf ${\mathscr{F}}$ could (and will) be destabilized only by a subsheaf of rank~0, i.e., by a torsion sheaf. Thus, ${\mathscr{F}}$ is (semi)stable if and only if it is torsion-free.
nodes.statement_short: Rank one forces destabilizing subsheaves to be torsion, so (semi)stability equals torsion-freeness.

nodes.name: Leading term gives rank 1
nodes.statement: As we observed above, the leading monomial of $h_d({\mathscr{F}})$ being $3t^2$ means that $r({\mathscr{F}}) = 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Leading term gives rank 1

nodes.name: Only torsion subsheaves can destabilize
nodes.statement: Therefore, such a sheaf ${\mathscr{F}}$ could (and will) be destabilized only by a subsheaf of rank~0, i.e., by a torsion sheaf.
nodes.statement_short: Only torsion subsheaves can destabilize

nodes.name: Equivalence with torsion-freeness
nodes.statement: Thus, ${\mathscr{F}}$ is (semi)stable if and only if it is torsion-free.
nodes.statement_short: Equivalence with torsion-freeness

nodes.name: Hilbert polynomials and stability of $\mathscr{E}_z$ and $\mathscr{E}_z^\vee$
nodes.statement: Let $d \in \{2, 3\}$. For any closed point $z \in Z_d$ the sheaf ${\mathscr{E}}_z$ is stable with $h_{{\mathscr{E}}_z}(t) = h_d(t)$. Its derived dual~${\mathscr{E}}_z^\vee$ is a stable sheaf with $h_{{\mathscr{E}}_z^\vee}(t) = h_d(-t-1) = h_{6-d}(t-1)$. Furthermore, the sheaf ${\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_d}$ is semistable with $h_{{\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_d}} = \ell(Z_d)h_d$.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathscr{E}_z$ is stable with Hilbert polynomial $h_d$, its dual is a stable sheaf with polynomial $h_{6-d}(t-1)$, and $\mathfrak{E}_{Z_d}$ is semistable.
conclusions: For any closed point $z \in Z_d$ the sheaf ${\mathscr{E}}_z$ is stable with $h_{{\mathscr{E}}_z}(t) = h_d(t)$.
Its derived dual~${\mathscr{E}}_z^\vee$ is a stable sheaf with $h_{{\mathscr{E}}_z^\vee}(t) = h_d(-t-1) = h_{6-d}(t-1)$.
Furthermore, the sheaf ${\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_d}$ is semistable with $h_{{\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_d}} = \ell(Z_d)h_d$.
nodes.label: lemma:hilbert-fz

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.2
nodes.statement: As we already mentioned, $r({\mathscr{E}}_z) = 1$ implies the leading monomial of $h_{{\mathscr{E}}_z}$ equals $3t^2$. So, to show an equality of polynomials $h_{{\mathscr{E}}_z} = h_d$ it is enough to check that they take the same values at points~$t = 0$ and~$t = -1$. In other words, we have to check that \begin{equation*} \chi(X,{\mathscr{E}}_z) = h_d(0) = d \qquad\text{and}\qquad \chi(X,{\mathscr{E}}_z \otimes \omega_X) = h_d(-1) = 0. \end{equation*} The first is proved in Lemma~\ref{lemma:e-z-small}, and the second follows from ${\mathscr{E}}_z \in {\mathcal{A}}_d$ and decompositions~\eqref{eq:dbx-other}. The sheaf ${\mathscr{E}}_z$ is torsion free since by Lemma~\ref{lemma:e-z-small} it is the direct image of a line bundle under a dominant map $\pi$, hence is stable by Lemma~\ref{lemma:hd-stable}. Furthermore, it follows from Proposition~\ref{proposition:e-z-big} that ${\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_d}$ is semistable with the same reduced Hilbert polynomial. To show that ${\mathscr{E}}_z^\vee$ is a sheaf, consider the connected component $Z$ of~$Z_d$ containing~$z$ and note that the sheaf ${\mathfrak{E}}_Z$ is filtered by ${\mathscr{E}}_z$, hence ${\mathfrak{E}}_Z^\vee$ is filtered by ${\mathscr{E}}_z^\vee$. But ${\mathfrak{E}}_Z$ is locally free by Proposition~\ref{proposition:e-z-big}, hence~${\mathfrak{E}}_Z^\vee$ is a sheaf, hence ${\mathscr{E}}_z^\vee$ is a sheaf as well. Stability of ${\mathscr{E}}_z^\vee$ is proved in the same way as that of ${\mathscr{E}}_z$; and the fact that its Hilbert polynomial equals $h_d(-t-1)$ follows easily from Serre duality (Proposition~\ref{proposition:serre-gorenstein}).
nodes.statement_short: Match two values of the quadratic Hilbert polynomials using Lemma 3.16 and (eq:dbx-other); torsion-freeness gives stability; dual is a sheaf because the bundle is filtered by E_z; Serre duality for the dual polynomial.

nodes.name: Leading term 3t^2
nodes.statement: As we already mentioned, $r({\mathscr{E}}_z) = 1$ implies the leading monomial of $h_{{\mathscr{E}}_z}$ equals $3t^2$.
nodes.statement_short: Leading term 3t^2

nodes.name: Reduce to values at t = 0 and t = -1
nodes.statement: So, to show an equality of polynomials $h_{{\mathscr{E}}_z} = h_d$ it is enough to check that they take the same values at points~$t = 0$ and~$t = -1$. In other words, we have to check that \begin{equation*} \chi(X,{\mathscr{E}}_z) = h_d(0) = d \qquad\text{and}\qquad \chi(X,{\mathscr{E}}_z \otimes \omega_X) = h_d(-1) = 0. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to values at t = 0 and t = -1

nodes.name: Values from Lemma 3.16 and (eq:dbx-other)
nodes.statement: The first is proved in Lemma~\ref{lemma:e-z-small}, and the second follows from ${\mathscr{E}}_z \in {\mathcal{A}}_d$ and decompositions~\eqref{eq:dbx-other}.
nodes.statement_short: Values from Lemma 3.16 and (eq:dbx-other)

nodes.name: Torsion-free hence stable
nodes.statement: The sheaf ${\mathscr{E}}_z$ is torsion free since by Lemma~\ref{lemma:e-z-small} it is the direct image of a line bundle under a dominant map $\pi$, hence is stable by Lemma~\ref{lemma:hd-stable}.
nodes.statement_short: Torsion-free hence stable

nodes.name: Semistability of E_{Z_d}
nodes.statement: Furthermore, it follows from Proposition~\ref{proposition:e-z-big} that ${\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_d}$ is semistable with the same reduced Hilbert polynomial.
nodes.statement_short: Semistability of E_{Z_d}

nodes.name: Dual of E_z is a sheaf via filtration of locally free E_Z
nodes.statement: To show that ${\mathscr{E}}_z^\vee$ is a sheaf, consider the connected component $Z$ of~$Z_d$ containing~$z$ and note that the sheaf ${\mathfrak{E}}_Z$ is filtered by ${\mathscr{E}}_z$, hence ${\mathfrak{E}}_Z^\vee$ is filtered by ${\mathscr{E}}_z^\vee$. But ${\mathfrak{E}}_Z$ is locally free by Proposition~\ref{proposition:e-z-big}, hence~${\mathfrak{E}}_Z^\vee$ is a sheaf, hence ${\mathscr{E}}_z^\vee$ is a sheaf as well.
nodes.statement_short: Dual of E_z is a sheaf via filtration of locally free E_Z

nodes.name: Dual stability and Hilbert polynomial via Serre duality
nodes.statement: Stability of ${\mathscr{E}}_z^\vee$ is proved in the same way as that of ${\mathscr{E}}_z$; and the fact that its Hilbert polynomial equals $h_d(-t-1)$ follows easily from Serre duality (Proposition~\ref{proposition:serre-gorenstein}).
nodes.statement_short: Dual stability and Hilbert polynomial via Serre duality

nodes.name: Moduli space $\mathscr{M}_d(X)$
nodes.statement: {\mathscr{M}}_d(X) := {\mathscr{M}}_{X,-K_X}(h_d)
nodes.statement_short: $\mathscr{M}_d(X)$ is the moduli space of Gieseker semistable sheaves on X with Hilbert polynomial $h_d$.
nodes.label: eq:mdx

nodes.name: Closed points of $\mathscr{M}_d(X)$
nodes.statement: Let ${\mathscr{F}}$ be a torsion free sheaf on $X$ whose Hilbert polynomial is $h_d(t)$ with $d \in \{2, 3, 4 \}$. $(i)$ If $d \in \{2, 3\}$ there is a unique closed point $z \in Z_d$ such that ${\mathscr{F}} \cong {\mathscr{E}}_z$. \newline $(ii)$ If $d \in \{3, 4\}$ there is a unique closed point $z \in Z_{6-d}$ such that ${\mathscr{F}} \cong {\mathscr{E}}_z^\vee \otimes \omega_X^{-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Torsion-free sheaves with polynomial $h_d$ are exactly the $\mathscr{E}_z$ (d=2,3) or twisted duals $\mathscr{E}_z^\vee\otimes\omega_X^{-1}$ (d=3,4).
assumptions: Let ${\mathscr{F}}$ be a torsion free sheaf on $X$ whose Hilbert polynomial is $h_d(t)$ with $d \in \{2, 3, 4 \}$.
conclusions: If $d \in \{2, 3\}$ there is a unique closed point $z \in Z_d$ such that ${\mathscr{F}} \cong {\mathscr{E}}_z$.
If $d \in \{3, 4\}$ there is a unique closed point $z \in Z_{6-d}$ such that ${\mathscr{F}} \cong {\mathscr{E}}_z^\vee \otimes \omega_X^{-1}$.
nodes.label: lemma:md-points

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.3
nodes.statement: First, assume $d = 2$. Let us show that ${\mathscr{F}} \in {\mathcal{A}}_2$. By Corollary~\ref{corollary:a-as-orthogonals} for this we should check that~$\mathrm{Ext}^\bullet({\mathscr{F}},{\mathscr{O}}_X) = \mathrm{Ext}^\bullet({\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3},{\mathscr{F}}) = 0$. By Lemma~\ref{lemma:hd-stable} the sheaf ${\mathscr{F}}$ is stable. By Lemma~\ref{lemma:hilbert-fz} and~\eqref{eq:hd-inequalities}, we have $\frac1{\ell(Z_3)}h_{{\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3}}(t) > h_{\mathscr{F}}(t) > h_{{\mathscr{O}}_X}(t)$, hence by semistability \begin{equation*} \mathrm{Hom}({\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3},{\mathscr{F}}) = \mathrm{Hom}({\mathscr{F}},{\mathscr{O}}_X) = 0. \end{equation*} Similarly, $\frac1{\ell(Z_3)}h_{{\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3}}(t-1) < h_{\mathscr{F}}(t) < h_{{\mathscr{O}}_X}(t+1)$, hence \begin{equation*} \mathrm{Hom}({\mathscr{F}},{\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3}(K_X)) = \mathrm{Hom}({\mathscr{O}}_X(-K_X),{\mathscr{F}}) = 0. \end{equation*} By Serre duality on $X$ (note that ${\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3}$ is locally free and use Proposition~\ref{proposition:serre-gorenstein}) we deduce \begin{equation*} \mathrm{Ext}^2({\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3},{\mathscr{F}}) = \mathrm{Ext}^2({\mathscr{F}},{\mathscr{O}}_X) = 0. \end{equation*} Since (again by Serre duality and local freeness of ${\mathscr{O}}_X$ and ${\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3}$) we can have nontrivial $\mathrm{Ext}^p({\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3},{\mathscr{F}})$ and~$\mathrm{Ext}^p({\mathscr{F}},{\mathscr{O}}_X)$ only for $p \in \{0,1,2\}$, it remains to check that \begin{equation*} \chi({\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3},{\mathscr{F}}) = \chi(X,{\mathscr{F}}(K_X)) = 0. \end{equation*} The second equality here just follows from $h_{\mathscr{F}}(-1) = h_2(-1) = 0$, and the first follows from Lemma~\ref{lemma:chi-ez-f} and $h_2(0) + h_2(-1) - 2 = 0$. Thus, we have shown that ${\mathscr{F}} \in {\mathcal{A}}_2 \cong {\mathbf{D}}(Z_2)$. Since $Z_2$ is a zero-dimensional scheme, any object in~${\mathbf{D}}(Z_2)$ is isomorphic to an iterated extension of shifts of structure sheaves of closed points in~$Z_2$. By Lemma~\ref{lemma:e-z-small} these sheaves correspond to sheaves~${\mathscr{E}}_z \in {\mathcal{A}}_2$, hence ${\mathscr{F}}$ is an extension of shifts of those. Since ${\mathscr{F}}$ is a pure sheaf of rank equal to~1, we conclude that ${\mathscr{F}} \cong {\mathscr{E}}_z$ for a closed point $z \in Z_2$. The case $d = 3$ is treated similarly. The same argument with~${\mathcal{A}}_2$ and~${\mathcal{A}}_3$ replaced by~${\mathcal{A}}_2^\vee \otimes \omega_X^{-1}$ and~${\mathcal{A}}_3^\vee \otimes \omega_X^{-1}$ and~\eqref{eq:dbx} replaced by a twist of~\eqref{eq:dbx-dual} proves part~$(ii)$.
nodes.statement_short: For d = 2 show F lies in A_2 by orthogonality checks (slope comparison, Serre duality, Euler characteristic via Lemma 3.20); then a rank-1 pure object of D(Z_2) is a point sheaf. Other cases by symmetry and the dual decomposition.

nodes.name: Case d = 2
nodes.statement: First, assume $d = 2$. Let us show that ${\mathscr{F}} \in {\mathcal{A}}_2$. By Corollary~\ref{corollary:a-as-orthogonals} for this we should check that~$\mathrm{Ext}^\bullet({\mathscr{F}},{\mathscr{O}}_X) = \mathrm{Ext}^\bullet({\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3},{\mathscr{F}}) = 0$. By Lemma~\ref{lemma:hd-stable} the sheaf ${\mathscr{F}}$ is stable. By Lemma~\ref{lemma:hilbert-fz} and~\eqref{eq:hd-inequalities}, we have $\frac1{\ell(Z_3)}h_{{\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3}}(t) > h_{\mathscr{F}}(t) > h_{{\mathscr{O}}_X}(t)$, hence by semistability \begin{equation*} \mathrm{Hom}({\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3},{\mathscr{F}}) = \mathrm{Hom}({\mathscr{F}},{\mathscr{O}}_X) = 0. \end{equation*} Similarly, $\frac1{\ell(Z_3)}h_{{\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3}}(t-1) < h_{\mathscr{F}}(t) < h_{{\mathscr{O}}_X}(t+1)$, hence \begin{equation*} \mathrm{Hom}({\mathscr{F}},{\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3}(K_X)) = \mathrm{Hom}({\mathscr{O}}_X(-K_X),{\mathscr{F}}) = 0. \end{equation*} By Serre duality on $X$ (note that ${\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3}$ is locally free and use Proposition~\ref{proposition:serre-gorenstein}) we deduce \begin{equation*} \mathrm{Ext}^2({\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3},{\mathscr{F}}) = \mathrm{Ext}^2({\mathscr{F}},{\mathscr{O}}_X) = 0. \end{equation*} Since (again by Serre duality and local freeness of ${\mathscr{O}}_X$ and ${\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3}$) we can have nontrivial $\mathrm{Ext}^p({\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3},{\mathscr{F}})$ and~$\mathrm{Ext}^p({\mathscr{F}},{\mathscr{O}}_X)$ only for $p \in \{0,1,2\}$, it remains to check that \begin{equation*} \chi({\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3},{\mathscr{F}}) = \chi(X,{\mathscr{F}}(K_X)) = 0. \end{equation*} The second equality here just follows from $h_{\mathscr{F}}(-1) = h_2(-1) = 0$, and the first follows from Lemma~\ref{lemma:chi-ez-f} and $h_2(0) + h_2(-1) - 2 = 0$. Thus, we have shown that ${\mathscr{F}} \in {\mathcal{A}}_2 \cong {\mathbf{D}}(Z_2)$. Since $Z_2$ is a zero-dimensional scheme, any object in~${\mathbf{D}}(Z_2)$ is isomorphic to an iterated extension of shifts of structure sheaves of closed points in~$Z_2$. By Lemma~\ref{lemma:e-z-small} these sheaves correspond to sheaves~${\mathscr{E}}_z \in {\mathcal{A}}_2$, hence ${\mathscr{F}}$ is an extension of shifts of those. Since ${\mathscr{F}}$ is a pure sheaf of rank equal to~1, we conclude that ${\mathscr{F}} \cong {\mathscr{E}}_z$ for a closed point $z \in Z_2$. The case $d = 3$ is treated similarly.
nodes.statement_short: Case d = 2

nodes.name: Show F lies in A_2
nodes.statement: Let us show that ${\mathscr{F}} \in {\mathcal{A}}_2$. By Corollary~\ref{corollary:a-as-orthogonals} for this we should check that~$\mathrm{Ext}^\bullet({\mathscr{F}},{\mathscr{O}}_X) = \mathrm{Ext}^\bullet({\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3},{\mathscr{F}}) = 0$. By Lemma~\ref{lemma:hd-stable} the sheaf ${\mathscr{F}}$ is stable. By Lemma~\ref{lemma:hilbert-fz} and~\eqref{eq:hd-inequalities}, we have $\frac1{\ell(Z_3)}h_{{\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3}}(t) > h_{\mathscr{F}}(t) > h_{{\mathscr{O}}_X}(t)$, hence by semistability \begin{equation*} \mathrm{Hom}({\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3},{\mathscr{F}}) = \mathrm{Hom}({\mathscr{F}},{\mathscr{O}}_X) = 0. \end{equation*} Similarly, $\frac1{\ell(Z_3)}h_{{\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3}}(t-1) < h_{\mathscr{F}}(t) < h_{{\mathscr{O}}_X}(t+1)$, hence \begin{equation*} \mathrm{Hom}({\mathscr{F}},{\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3}(K_X)) = \mathrm{Hom}({\mathscr{O}}_X(-K_X),{\mathscr{F}}) = 0. \end{equation*} By Serre duality on $X$ (note that ${\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3}$ is locally free and use Proposition~\ref{proposition:serre-gorenstein}) we deduce \begin{equation*} \mathrm{Ext}^2({\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3},{\mathscr{F}}) = \mathrm{Ext}^2({\mathscr{F}},{\mathscr{O}}_X) = 0. \end{equation*} Since (again by Serre duality and local freeness of ${\mathscr{O}}_X$ and ${\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3}$) we can have nontrivial $\mathrm{Ext}^p({\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3},{\mathscr{F}})$ and~$\mathrm{Ext}^p({\mathscr{F}},{\mathscr{O}}_X)$ only for $p \in \{0,1,2\}$, it remains to check that \begin{equation*} \chi({\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3},{\mathscr{F}}) = \chi(X,{\mathscr{F}}(K_X)) = 0. \end{equation*} The second equality here just follows from $h_{\mathscr{F}}(-1) = h_2(-1) = 0$, and the first follows from Lemma~\ref{lemma:chi-ez-f} and $h_2(0) + h_2(-1) - 2 = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Show F lies in A_2

nodes.name: Reduce to two Ext vanishings
nodes.statement: By Corollary~\ref{corollary:a-as-orthogonals} for this we should check that~$\mathrm{Ext}^\bullet({\mathscr{F}},{\mathscr{O}}_X) = \mathrm{Ext}^\bullet({\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3},{\mathscr{F}}) = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to two Ext vanishings

nodes.name: Hom vanishing by comparing reduced Hilbert polynomials
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lemma:hd-stable} the sheaf ${\mathscr{F}}$ is stable. By Lemma~\ref{lemma:hilbert-fz} and~\eqref{eq:hd-inequalities}, we have $\frac1{\ell(Z_3)}h_{{\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3}}(t) > h_{\mathscr{F}}(t) > h_{{\mathscr{O}}_X}(t)$, hence by semistability \begin{equation*} \mathrm{Hom}({\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3},{\mathscr{F}}) = \mathrm{Hom}({\mathscr{F}},{\mathscr{O}}_X) = 0. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Hom vanishing by comparing reduced Hilbert polynomials

nodes.name: Further Hom vanishing
nodes.statement: Similarly, $\frac1{\ell(Z_3)}h_{{\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3}}(t-1) < h_{\mathscr{F}}(t) < h_{{\mathscr{O}}_X}(t+1)$, hence \begin{equation*} \mathrm{Hom}({\mathscr{F}},{\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3}(K_X)) = \mathrm{Hom}({\mathscr{O}}_X(-K_X),{\mathscr{F}}) = 0. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Further Hom vanishing

nodes.name: Ext^2 vanishing by Serre duality
nodes.statement: By Serre duality on $X$ (note that ${\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3}$ is locally free and use Proposition~\ref{proposition:serre-gorenstein}) we deduce \begin{equation*} \mathrm{Ext}^2({\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3},{\mathscr{F}}) = \mathrm{Ext}^2({\mathscr{F}},{\mathscr{O}}_X) = 0. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Ext^2 vanishing by Serre duality

nodes.name: Remains: Euler characteristics vanish
nodes.statement: Since (again by Serre duality and local freeness of ${\mathscr{O}}_X$ and ${\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3}$) we can have nontrivial $\mathrm{Ext}^p({\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3},{\mathscr{F}})$ and~$\mathrm{Ext}^p({\mathscr{F}},{\mathscr{O}}_X)$ only for $p \in \{0,1,2\}$, it remains to check that \begin{equation*} \chi({\mathfrak{E}}_{Z_3},{\mathscr{F}}) = \chi(X,{\mathscr{F}}(K_X)) = 0. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Remains: Euler characteristics vanish

nodes.name: Euler characteristics via Lemma 3.20
nodes.statement: The second equality here just follows from $h_{\mathscr{F}}(-1) = h_2(-1) = 0$, and the first follows from Lemma~\ref{lemma:chi-ez-f} and $h_2(0) + h_2(-1) - 2 = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Euler characteristics via Lemma 3.20

nodes.name: F is a point sheaf E_z
nodes.statement: Thus, we have shown that ${\mathscr{F}} \in {\mathcal{A}}_2 \cong {\mathbf{D}}(Z_2)$. Since $Z_2$ is a zero-dimensional scheme, any object in~${\mathbf{D}}(Z_2)$ is isomorphic to an iterated extension of shifts of structure sheaves of closed points in~$Z_2$. By Lemma~\ref{lemma:e-z-small} these sheaves correspond to sheaves~${\mathscr{E}}_z \in {\mathcal{A}}_2$, hence ${\mathscr{F}}$ is an extension of shifts of those. Since ${\mathscr{F}}$ is a pure sheaf of rank equal to~1, we conclude that ${\mathscr{F}} \cong {\mathscr{E}}_z$ for a closed point $z \in Z_2$. The case $d = 3$ is treated similarly.
nodes.statement_short: F is a point sheaf E_z

nodes.name: Part (ii) via the dual decomposition
nodes.statement: The same argument with~${\mathcal{A}}_2$ and~${\mathcal{A}}_3$ replaced by~${\mathcal{A}}_2^\vee \otimes \omega_X^{-1}$ and~${\mathcal{A}}_3^\vee \otimes \omega_X^{-1}$ and~\eqref{eq:dbx} replaced by a twist of~\eqref{eq:dbx-dual} proves part~$(ii)$.
nodes.statement_short: Part (ii) via the dual decomposition

nodes.name: Morphism $p_S \colon M \to S$
nodes.statement: Let $p_S \colon M \to S$ be a morphism of schemes.

nodes.name: Fibers $M_s$ and embeddings $i_{M_s}$
nodes.statement: For each geometric point $s \in S$ we denote by $M_s$ the scheme-theoretic fiber of $M$ over $s$ and by~$i_{M_s} \colon M_s \hookrightarrow M$ its embedding.

nodes.name: Embedding $i_s$
nodes.statement: The embedding $s \hookrightarrow S$ is denoted simply by $i_s$.

nodes.name: Fiberwise criteria for families
nodes.statement: Assume ${\mathscr{F}} \in {\mathbf{D}}^-(M)$ and $M$ is proper over $S$, and in $(ii)$ and $(iii)$ that $M$ is flat over $S$. \begin{enumerate} \item[$(i)$] If $i_{M_s}^*({\mathscr{F}}) \in {\mathbf{D}}^{\le p_0}(M_s)$ for some integer $p_0$ and all geometric points $s \in S$, then ${\mathscr{F}} \in {\mathbf{D}}^{\le p_0}(M)$. In particular, if $i_{M_s}^*({\mathscr{F}}) = 0$ for all geometric points $s \in S$, then ${\mathscr{F}} = 0$. \item[$(ii)$] If for all geometric points $s \in S$ the pullback $i_{M_s}^*({\mathscr{F}})$ is a pure sheaf such that $H^k(M_s, i_{M_s}^*{\mathscr{F}}) = 0$ for all~$k \ne 0$ and $\dim H^0(M_s,i_{M_s}^*{\mathscr{F}}) = r$ for a constant $r$, then $p_{S*}({\mathscr{F}})$ is a vector bundle of rank~$r$ on~$S$. \item[$(iii)$] If for any geometric point $s \in S$ there is a point $m \in M_s$ such that $i_{M_s}^*({\mathscr{F}}) \cong {\mathscr{O}}_m$, then there is a unique section $\varphi \colon S \to M$ of the projection $p_S$ and a line bundle ${\mathscr{L}} \in \mathrm{Pic}(S)$ such that ${\mathscr{F}} \cong \varphi_*{\mathscr{L}}$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Fiberwise criteria: vanishing and amplitude are detected on fibers; fiberwise cohomologically constant pure sheaves push forward to vector bundles; fiberwise point sheaves are pushforwards of line bundles along sections.
assumptions: Assume ${\mathscr{F}} \in {\mathbf{D}}^-(M)$ and $M$ is proper over $S$, and in $(ii)$ and $(iii)$ that $M$ is flat over $S$.
conclusions: If $i_{M_s}^*({\mathscr{F}}) \in {\mathbf{D}}^{\le p_0}(M_s)$ for some integer $p_0$ and all geometric points $s \in S$, then ${\mathscr{F}} \in {\mathbf{D}}^{\le p_0}(M)$. In particular, if $i_{M_s}^*({\mathscr{F}}) = 0$ for all geometric points $s \in S$, then ${\mathscr{F}} = 0$.

If for all geometric points $s \in S$ the pullback $i_{M_s}^*({\mathscr{F}})$ is a pure sheaf such that $H^k(M_s, i_{M_s}^*{\mathscr{F}}) = 0$ for all~$k \ne 0$ and $\dim H^0(M_s,i_{M_s}^*{\mathscr{F}}) = r$ for a constant $r$, then $p_{S*}({\mathscr{F}})$ is a vector bundle of rank~$r$ on~$S$.

If for any geometric point $s \in S$ there is a point $m \in M_s$ such that $i_{M_s}^*({\mathscr{F}}) \cong {\mathscr{O}}_m$, then there is a unique section $\varphi \colon S \to M$ of the projection $p_S$ and a line bundle ${\mathscr{L}} \in \mathrm{Pic}(S)$ such that ${\mathscr{F}} \cong \varphi_*{\mathscr{L}}$.
nodes.label: lemma:fiberwise

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.4
nodes.statement: $(i)$ Let ${\mathscr{H}}^k({\mathscr{F}})$ be the top nonzero cohomology sheaf of ${\mathscr{F}}$; by assumption it is a coherent sheaf on $M$. Let $s \in S$ be a geometric point in the image of the support of~${\mathscr{H}}^k({\mathscr{F}})$ under the map $p_S \colon M \to S$. The spectral sequence \begin{equation} L_qi_{M_s}^*{\mathscr{H}}^p({\mathscr{F}}) \Rightarrow {\mathscr{H}}^{p-q}(i_{M_s}^*{\mathscr{F}}) \end{equation} implies that ${\mathscr{H}}^k(i_{M_s}^*{\mathscr{F}}) \cong L_0i_{M_s}^*{\mathscr{H}}^k({\mathscr{F}}) \ne 0$, hence $k \le p_0$. $(ii)$ Set ${\mathscr{G}} := p_{S*}({\mathscr{F}})$. By base change we have an isomorphism \begin{equation*} H^\bullet(M_s,i_{M_s}^*({\mathscr{F}})) \cong i_s^* ({\mathscr{G}}). \end{equation*} By assumption, the left hand side is a vector space of dimension $r$ in degree $0$. By~$(i)$ we have ${\mathscr{G}} \in {\mathbf{D}}^{\le 0}(S)$. Moreover the spectral sequence~\eqref{eq:spectral} with $M = S$ and ${\mathscr{F}} = {\mathscr{G}}$ \begin{equation*} L_q i_s^* {\mathscr{H}}^p({\mathscr{G}}) \Rightarrow {\mathscr{H}}^{p-q}(i_s^*({\mathscr{G}})) \cong H^{p-q}(M_s, i_{M_s}^*({\mathscr{F}})) \end{equation*} shows that $L_0i_s^*{\mathscr{H}}^0({\mathscr{G}}) \cong H^0(M,i_{M_s}^*{\mathscr{F}})$ and $L_1i_s^*{\mathscr{H}}^0({\mathscr{G}}) = 0$. Therefore, by Serre's criterion the sheaf~${\mathscr{H}}^0({\mathscr{G}})$ is a vector bundle of rank~$r$. Looking again at the spectral sequence, we see that the canonical map ${\mathscr{G}} \to {\mathscr{H}}^0({\mathscr{G}})$ induces an isomorphism $i_s^*{\mathscr{G}} \to i_s^*({\mathscr{H}}^0({\mathscr{G}}))$ for each $s \in S$, hence by part $(i)$ we have an isomorphism ${\mathscr{G}} \cong {\mathscr{H}}^0({\mathscr{G}})$. Thus $p_{S*}({\mathscr{F}}) = {\mathscr{G}}$ is a vector bundle of rank $r$. $(iii)$ By part $(i)$ we have ${\mathscr{F}} \in {\mathbf{D}}^{\le 0}(M)$ and by part~$(ii)$ we know that $p_{S*}({\mathscr{F}})$ is a line bundle. Denote it by ${\mathscr{L}}$. Then replacing the object ${\mathscr{F}}$ by~${\mathscr{F}} \otimes p_S^*{\mathscr{L}}^{-1}$, we may assume that $p_{S*}({\mathscr{F}}) \cong {\mathscr{O}}_S$. We have by adjunction a map ${\mathscr{O}}_{M} = p_S^*{\mathscr{O}}_S \to {\mathscr{F}} \to {\mathscr{H}}^0({\mathscr{F}})$ that restricts to the fiber $M_s$ over a geometric point~\mbox{$s \in S$} as the natural map ${\mathscr{O}}_{M_s} \to {\mathscr{O}}_m$. Therefore, it is fiberwise surjective, hence by part $(i)$ applied to its cone it is surjective on $M$. So, ${\mathscr{H}}^0({\mathscr{F}}) \cong {\mathscr{O}}_\Gamma$ is the structure sheaf of a closed subscheme $\Gamma \subset M$. By the assumption for each geometric point $s \in S$ we have $i_s^*{\mathscr{O}}_\Gamma \cong {\mathscr{O}}_m$. Therefore the map $p_S\vert_\Gamma \colon \Gamma \to S$ is finite and flat of degree~1. By $(ii)$ we have $p_{S*}{\mathscr{O}}_\Gamma \cong {\mathscr{O}}_S$, so it follows that the map $p_S\vert_\Gamma \colon \Gamma \to S$ is an isomorphism. Therefore, $\Gamma$ is the image of a section $\varphi \colon S \to M$ of the morphism $p_S$. The above argument proves ${\mathscr{H}}^0({\mathscr{F}}) \cong {\mathscr{O}}_\Gamma \cong \varphi_*{\mathscr{O}}_S$. Restricting the triangle $\tau^{\le -1}{\mathscr{F}} \to {\mathscr{F}} \to {\mathscr{H}}^0({\mathscr{F}})$ to an arbitrary fiber $M_s$ we deduce that $i_{M_s}^*(\tau^{\le -1}{\mathscr{F}}) = 0$ for any $s \in S$, hence $\tau^{\le -1}{\mathscr{F}} = 0$ by part $(i)$. Therefore ${\mathscr{F}} \cong \varphi_*{\mathscr{O}}_S$.
nodes.statement_short: (i) by the base change spectral sequence on the top cohomology sheaf; (ii) by base change, Serre's criterion and (i); (iii) the adjunction map is fiberwise surjective, so H^0 is the structure sheaf of a degree-one finite flat subscheme, i.e. a section.

nodes.name: Part (iii)
nodes.statement: $(iii)$ By part $(i)$ we have ${\mathscr{F}} \in {\mathbf{D}}^{\le 0}(M)$ and by part~$(ii)$ we know that $p_{S*}({\mathscr{F}})$ is a line bundle. Denote it by ${\mathscr{L}}$. Then replacing the object ${\mathscr{F}}$ by~${\mathscr{F}} \otimes p_S^*{\mathscr{L}}^{-1}$, we may assume that $p_{S*}({\mathscr{F}}) \cong {\mathscr{O}}_S$. We have by adjunction a map ${\mathscr{O}}_{M} = p_S^*{\mathscr{O}}_S \to {\mathscr{F}} \to {\mathscr{H}}^0({\mathscr{F}})$ that restricts to the fiber $M_s$ over a geometric point~\mbox{$s \in S$} as the natural map ${\mathscr{O}}_{M_s} \to {\mathscr{O}}_m$. Therefore, it is fiberwise surjective, hence by part $(i)$ applied to its cone it is surjective on $M$. So, ${\mathscr{H}}^0({\mathscr{F}}) \cong {\mathscr{O}}_\Gamma$ is the structure sheaf of a closed subscheme $\Gamma \subset M$. By the assumption for each geometric point $s \in S$ we have $i_s^*{\mathscr{O}}_\Gamma \cong {\mathscr{O}}_m$. Therefore the map $p_S\vert_\Gamma \colon \Gamma \to S$ is finite and flat of degree~1. Therefore, $\Gamma$ is the image of a section $\varphi \colon S \to M$ of the morphism $p_S$. The above argument proves ${\mathscr{H}}^0({\mathscr{F}}) \cong {\mathscr{O}}_\Gamma \cong \varphi_*{\mathscr{O}}_S$. Restricting the triangle $\tau^{\le -1}{\mathscr{F}} \to {\mathscr{F}} \to {\mathscr{H}}^0({\mathscr{F}})$ to an arbitrary fiber $M_s$ we deduce that $i_{M_s}^*(\tau^{\le -1}{\mathscr{F}}) = 0$ for any $s \in S$, hence $\tau^{\le -1}{\mathscr{F}} = 0$ by part $(i)$. Therefore ${\mathscr{F}} \cong \varphi_*{\mathscr{O}}_S$.

nodes.name: Fine moduli spaces $\mathscr{M}_d(X)$
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a sextic du Val del Pezzo surface over an algebraically closed field ${\mathsf{k}}$. The moduli spaces ${\mathscr{M}}_2(X)$, ${\mathscr{M}}_3(X)$, and ${\mathscr{M}}_4(X)$ are fine moduli spaces. Moreover, \newline$(i)$ ${\mathscr{M}}_2(X) \cong {\mathscr{M}}_4(X) \cong Z_2$ and the sheaves ${\mathscr{E}}_{Z_2}$ and ${\mathscr{E}}_{Z_2}^\vee \otimes \omega_X^{-1}$ are the corresponding universal families; \newline$(ii)$ ${\mathscr{M}}_3(X) \cong Z_3$ and the sheaves ${\mathscr{E}}_{Z_3}$ and ${\mathscr{E}}_{Z_3}^\vee \otimes \omega_X^{-1}$ are two universal families for this moduli problem.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathscr{M}_2(X)\cong\mathscr{M}_4(X)\cong Z_2$ and $\mathscr{M}_3(X)\cong Z_3$ are fine moduli spaces with universal families $\mathscr{E}_{Z_d}$ and their twisted duals.
assumptions: Let $X$ be a sextic du Val del Pezzo surface over an algebraically closed field ${\mathsf{k}}$.
conclusions: The moduli spaces ${\mathscr{M}}_2(X)$, ${\mathscr{M}}_3(X)$, and ${\mathscr{M}}_4(X)$ are fine moduli spaces.
${\mathscr{M}}_2(X) \cong {\mathscr{M}}_4(X) \cong Z_2$ and the sheaves ${\mathscr{E}}_{Z_2}$ and ${\mathscr{E}}_{Z_2}^\vee \otimes \omega_X^{-1}$ are the corresponding universal families;
${\mathscr{M}}_3(X) \cong Z_3$ and the sheaves ${\mathscr{E}}_{Z_3}$ and ${\mathscr{E}}_{Z_3}^\vee \otimes \omega_X^{-1}$ are two universal families for this moduli problem.
nodes.label: theorem:moduli

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.5
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be an arbitrary base scheme and ${\mathscr{F}}$ a coherent sheaf on $X \times S$ flat over $S$ and such that for any geometric point $s \in S$ the restriction ${\mathscr{F}}_s = i_{X \times s}^*({\mathscr{F}})$ is a semistable (i.e., torsion free) sheaf with Hilbert polynomial~$h_d(t)$ for $d \in \{2,3\}$. By Lemma~\ref{lemma:md-points} it follows that \begin{equation*} {\mathscr{F}}_s \cong {\mathscr{E}}_z \end{equation*} for a unique closed point $z \in Z_d$. Consider the semiorthogonal decomposition \begin{equation} {\mathbf{D}}(X \times S) = \langle {\mathcal{A}}_{1S}, {\mathcal{A}}_{2S}, {\mathcal{A}}_{3S} \rangle = \langle {\mathbf{D}}(S), {\mathbf{D}}(Z_2 \times S), {\mathbf{D}}(Z_3 \times S) \rangle, \end{equation} obtained by the base change $S \to \mathrm{Spec}({\mathsf{k}})$ (\cite[Theorem~5.6]{kuznetsov2011base}) from~\eqref{eq:dbx-dz} (the second equality follows from \cite[Theorem~6.4]{kuznetsov2011base} and Proposition~\ref{proposition:fm-zd}). Since by Proposition~\ref{proposition:fm-zd} the embedding functors of~\eqref{eq:dbx-dz} are the Fourier--Mukai functors given by the sheaves ${\mathscr{E}}_{Z_d}$, the embedding functors of~\eqref{eq:dbx-s} are given by the pullbacks ${\mathscr{E}}_{Z_d} \boxtimes {\mathscr{O}}_S$ of ${\mathscr{E}}_{Z_d}$ via the maps $X \times Z_d \times S \to X \times Z_d$. For any ${\mathscr{F}} \in {\mathbf{D}}(X \times S)$, a geometric point $s \in S$, and each $d' \in \{1,2,3\}$ we have by~\cite[(11)]{kuznetsov2011base} an isomorphism \begin{equation*} i_{Z_{d'} \times s}^*(\alpha_{d'S}({\mathscr{F}})) \cong \alpha_{d'}(i_{X \times s}^*({\mathscr{F}})) \in {\mathbf{D}}(Z_{d'}), \end{equation*} where $\alpha_{d'} \colon {\mathbf{D}}(X) \to {\mathbf{D}}(Z_{d'})$ and $\alpha_{d'S} \colon {\mathbf{D}}(X \times S) \to {\mathbf{D}}(Z_{d'} \times S)$ are the projection functors of the semiorthogonal decompositions~\eqref{eq:dbx-dz} and~\eqref{eq:dbx-s} respectively. Using this isomorphism for the sheaf~${\mathscr{F}}$ we started with, and taking into account Lemma~\ref{lemma:e-z-small}, we conclude that \begin{equation*} i_{Z_{d'} \times s}^*(\alpha_{d'S}({\mathscr{F}})) \cong \alpha_{d'}({\mathscr{F}}_s) \cong \alpha_{d'}({\mathscr{E}}_z) \cong \begin{cases} {\mathscr{O}}_z, & \text{if $d' = d$},\\ 0, & \text{otherwise}. \end{cases} \end{equation*} By Lemma~\ref{lemma:fiberwise}$(i)$ it follows that $\alpha_{d'S}({\mathscr{F}}) = 0$ when $d' \ne d$, hence \begin{equation*} {\mathscr{F}} \cong \Phi_{{\mathscr{E}}_{Z_d} \boxtimes {\mathscr{O}}_S}({\mathscr{F}}_d) \end{equation*} for some object ${\mathscr{F}}_d \in {\mathbf{D}}(Z_d \times S)$. Moreover, the object ${\mathscr{F}}_d$ is such that for any geometric point~$s \in S$ we have $i_{Z_d \times s}^*({\mathscr{F}}_d) \cong {\mathscr{O}}_z$ for some closed point~$z \in Z_d$. By Lemma~\ref{lemma:fiberwise}$(iii)$ it follows that ${\mathscr{F}}_d \cong \Gamma_{f_d*}{\mathscr{L}}$, where $f_d \colon S \to Z_d$ is a morphism, $\Gamma_{f_d} \colon S \to Z_d \times S$ is its graph, and ${\mathscr{L}}$ is a line bundle on $S$. Therefore \begin{equation*} {\mathscr{F}} \cong \Phi_{{\mathscr{E}}_{Z_d} \boxtimes {\mathscr{O}}_S}(\Gamma_{f_d*}{\mathscr{L}}) \cong (\mathrm{id}_X \times f_d)^*{\mathscr{E}}_{Z_d} \otimes p_S^*{\mathscr{L}}. \end{equation*} This precisely means that the moduli functor ${\mathscr{M}}_d(X)$ we are interested in is represented by the scheme~$Z_d$, and that ${\mathscr{E}}_{Z_d}$ is a universal sheaf. This proves the statement about~${\mathscr{M}}_2(X)$ and the first statement about~${\mathscr{M}}_3(X)$. The same argument applied to the dual semiorthogonal decomposition~\eqref{eq:dbx-dual} instead of~\eqref{eq:dbx-dz} proves the statement about~${\mathscr{M}}_4(X)$ and the second statement about~${\mathscr{M}}_3(X)$.
nodes.statement_short: Decompose a flat family of such sheaves with respect to the base-changed decomposition; fiberwise projections are point sheaves, so by Lemma 4.4 the family is the pullback of the universal kernel along a map S -> Z_d.
