nodes.label: eq:sod-dpx-perf

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5.11
nodes.statement: The functor $\Phi_d$ has finite cohomological amplitude because the sheaf ${\mathscr{E}}_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d}$ is flat over ${\mathscr{Z}}_d$ by Lemma~\ref{lemma:ezd-tor-ext} (in fact, since $p \colon {\mathscr{X}} \times_S {\mathscr{Z}}_d \to {\mathscr{X}}$ is finite, the functor $\Phi_d$ is exact). The functor $\Phi_d^!$ has finite cohomological amplitude because the sheaf ${\mathscr{E}}_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d}$ has finite $\mathrm{Ext}$-amplitude over ${\mathscr{Z}}_d$ by Lemma~\ref{lemma:ezd-tor-ext} (in fact, since $p_d \colon {\mathscr{X}} \times_S {\mathscr{Z}}_d \to {\mathscr{Z}}_d$ is flat of relative dimension 2, the cohomological amplitude of the functor $\Phi_d^!$ equals $(0,2)$). Thus $\Phi_d \circ \Phi_d^!$ has finite cohomological amplitude. Since the projection functors of~\eqref{eq:sod-dp6} can be expressed as combinations of these functors (see the proof of Theorem~\ref{theorem:sod-dp6}), it follows that the projection functors also have finite cohomological amplitude. To show that the components of~\eqref{eq:sod-dp6} are admissible, note that we have two more decompositions \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} {\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{X}}) &= \langle {\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{Z}}_3,\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_3}) \otimes \omega_{{\mathscr{X}}/S}, {\mathbf{D}}(S), {\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{Z}}_2, \beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2}) \rangle, \\ {\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{X}}) &= \langle {\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{Z}}_2, \beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2}) \otimes \omega_{{\mathscr{X}}/S}, {\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{Z}}_3,\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_3}) \otimes \omega_{{\mathscr{X}}/S}, {\mathbf{D}}(S) \rangle. \end{aligned} \end{equation} Indeed, they can be established by the same argument as~\eqref{eq:sod-dp6} starting with the semiorthogonal decompositions~\eqref{eq:dbx-other} instead of~\eqref{eq:dbx}. Since $\omega_{{\mathscr{X}}/S}$ is invertible, the two above decompositions together with~\eqref{eq:sod-dp6} prove admissibility of all components (each of them appears on the left in one decomposition and on the right in another). The functors $\Phi_d$ preserve perfectness by Lemma~\ref{lemma:phi-d-shriek}. It remains to prove~\eqref{eq:sod-dpx-perf}. For this note that the functors $\Phi_d$ have left adjoints $\Phi_d^*$ because the components of~\eqref{eq:sod-dp6} are admissible. Since the functors $\Phi_d$ commute with arbitrary direct sums, it follows from~\cite[Theorem~5.1]{neeman1996grothendieck} that the functors $\Phi_d^*$ preserve perfectness. Since the projection functors of~\eqref{eq:sod-dp6} can be expressed as combinations of $\Phi_d \circ \Phi_d^*$, they preserve perfectness, hence a restriction of~\eqref{eq:sod-dp6} gives~\eqref{eq:sod-dpx-perf}.

nodes.statement_short: Bound amplitudes of $\Phi_d$ and $\Phi_d^!$; admissibility from two further decompositions twisted by $\omega_{\mathscr{X}/S}$; perfectness of left adjoints via Neeman.

Since $\omega_{{\mathscr{X}}/S}$ is invertible, the two above decompositions together with~\eqref{eq:sod-dp6} prove admissibility of all components (each of them appears on the left in one decomposition and on the right in another).
nodes.statement_short: Admissibility via two twisted decompositions
nodes.section: 5.2 Some properties of the semiorthogonal decomposition

nodes.name: Two more decompositions of $\mathbf{D}(\mathscr{X})$
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} {\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{X}}) &= \langle {\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{Z}}_3,\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_3}) \otimes \omega_{{\mathscr{X}}/S}, {\mathbf{D}}(S), {\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{Z}}_2, \beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2}) \rangle, \\ {\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{X}}) &= \langle {\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{Z}}_2, \beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2}) \otimes \omega_{{\mathscr{X}}/S}, {\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{Z}}_3,\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_3}) \otimes \omega_{{\mathscr{X}}/S}, {\mathbf{D}}(S) \rangle. \end{aligned}
nodes.section: 5.2 Some properties of the semiorthogonal decomposition
nodes.label: eq:more-sod-cx

nodes.name: Phi_d preserve perfectness
nodes.statement: The functors $\Phi_d$ preserve perfectness by Lemma~\ref{lemma:phi-d-shriek}.
nodes.statement_short: Phi_d preserve perfectness
nodes.section: 5.2 Some properties of the semiorthogonal decomposition

nodes.name: Remaining: perfect decomposition
nodes.statement: It remains to prove~\eqref{eq:sod-dpx-perf}.
nodes.statement_short: Remaining: perfect decomposition
nodes.section: 5.2 Some properties of the semiorthogonal decomposition

nodes.name: Left adjoints preserve perfectness; restrict decomposition
nodes.statement: For this note that the functors $\Phi_d$ have left adjoints $\Phi_d^*$ because the components of~\eqref{eq:sod-dp6} are admissible. Since the functors $\Phi_d$ commute with arbitrary direct sums, it follows from~\cite[Theorem~5.1]{neeman1996grothendieck} that the functors $\Phi_d^*$ preserve perfectness. Since the projection functors of~\eqref{eq:sod-dp6} can be expressed as combinations of $\Phi_d \circ \Phi_d^*$, they preserve perfectness, hence a restriction of~\eqref{eq:sod-dp6} gives~\eqref{eq:sod-dpx-perf}.
nodes.statement_short: Left adjoints preserve perfectness; restrict decomposition
nodes.section: 5.2 Some properties of the semiorthogonal decomposition

nodes.name: Relative duality functor $\mathrm{D}_{\mathscr{X}/S}$
nodes.statement: Therefore, the relative duality functor \begin{equation*} {\mathrm{D}}_{{\mathscr{X}}/S}({\mathscr{F}}) := \mathrm{R}\mathscr{H}\mathit{om}({\mathscr{F}} , f^*\omega_S^\bullet) \end{equation*} is an anti-autoequivalence of the category ${\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{X}})$ (see Section~\ref{subsection:duality}).
nodes.section: 5.2 Some properties of the semiorthogonal decomposition
nodes.statement_short: The relative duality functor RHom(-, f^* omega_S) is an anti-autoequivalence of D(X) since f is Gorenstein.

nodes.name: Dual decomposition for families
nodes.statement: The relative duality functor gives a semiorthogonal decomposition \begin{equation} {\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{X}}) = \langle {\mathrm{D}}_{{\mathscr{X}}/S}({\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{Z}}_3,\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_3})), {\mathrm{D}}_{{\mathscr{X}}/S}({\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{Z}}_2,\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2})), {\mathrm{D}}_{{\mathscr{X}}/S}({\mathbf{D}}(S)) \rangle, \end{equation} whose components are equivalent to ${\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{Z}}_3,\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_3})$, ${\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{Z}}_2,\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2})$, and ${\mathbf{D}}(S)$ respectively. Moreover, this decomposition is right mutation-dual to~\eqref{eq:sod-dp6}.
nodes.section: 5.2 Some properties of the semiorthogonal decomposition
nodes.statement_short: Relative duality turns (eq:sod-dp6) into a decomposition that is its right mutation-dual.
conclusions: The relative duality functor gives a semiorthogonal decomposition \begin{equation} \label{eq:sod-dp6-dual} {\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{X}}) = \langle {\mathrm{D}}_{{\mathscr{X}}/S}({\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{Z}}_3,\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_3})), {\mathrm{D}}_{{\mathscr{X}}/S}({\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{Z}}_2,\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2})), {\mathrm{D}}_{{\mathscr{X}}/S}({\mathbf{D}}(S)) \rangle, \end{equation} whose components are equivalent to ${\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{Z}}_3,\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_3})$, ${\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{Z}}_2,\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2})$, and ${\mathbf{D}}(S)$ respectively.
Moreover, this decomposition is right mutation-dual to~\eqref{eq:sod-dp6}.
nodes.label: proposition:sod-dual

nodes.name: Dual family decomposition
nodes.statement: {\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{X}}) = \langle {\mathrm{D}}_{{\mathscr{X}}/S}({\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{Z}}_3,\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_3})), {\mathrm{D}}_{{\mathscr{X}}/S}({\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{Z}}_2,\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2})), {\mathrm{D}}_{{\mathscr{X}}/S}({\mathbf{D}}(S)) \rangle,
nodes.section: 5.2 Some properties of the semiorthogonal decomposition
nodes.label: eq:sod-dp6-dual

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5.12
nodes.statement: Since ${\mathrm{D}}_{{\mathscr{X}}/S}$ is an anti-autoequivalence, \eqref{eq:sod-dp6-dual} is a semiorthogonal decomposition. Consider also the right mutation-dual decomposition \begin{equation*} {\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{X}}) = \langle {\mathbb{L}}_1({\mathbb{L}}_2(\Phi_3({\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{Z}}_3,\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_3}))), {\mathbb{L}}_1(\Phi_2({\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{Z}}_2,\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2}))), \Phi_1({\mathbf{D}}(S)) \rangle, \end{equation*} where ${\mathbb{L}}_1$ and ${\mathbb{L}}_2$ are the mutation functors through the first and the second components of~\eqref{eq:dbcx-again} (they are well-defined because the components of the decomposition are admissible). By base change together with Proposition~\ref{proposition:dbx-dual} and Lemma~\ref{lemma:fiberwise}, these two decompositions coincide. In particular, the components of~\eqref{eq:sod-dp6-dual} are equivalent to ${\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{Z}}_3,\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_3})$, ${\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{Z}}_2,\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2})$, and ${\mathbf{D}}(S)$ respectively.
nodes.section: 5.2 Some properties of the semiorthogonal decomposition
nodes.statement_short: Duality gives a decomposition; compare with the right mutation-dual one fiberwise via Proposition 3.14 and Lemma 4.4.

nodes.name: Dual is a decomposition
nodes.statement: Since ${\mathrm{D}}_{{\mathscr{X}}/S}$ is an anti-autoequivalence, \eqref{eq:sod-dp6-dual} is a semiorthogonal decomposition.
nodes.statement_short: Dual is a decomposition
nodes.section: 5.2 Some properties of the semiorthogonal decomposition

nodes.name: Mutation-dual decomposition
nodes.statement: Consider also the right mutation-dual decomposition \begin{equation*} {\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{X}}) = \langle {\mathbb{L}}_1({\mathbb{L}}_2(\Phi_3({\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{Z}}_3,\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_3}))), {\mathbb{L}}_1(\Phi_2({\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{Z}}_2,\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2}))), \Phi_1({\mathbf{D}}(S)) \rangle, \end{equation*} where ${\mathbb{L}}_1$ and ${\mathbb{L}}_2$ are the mutation functors through the first and the second components of~\eqref{eq:dbcx-again} (they are well-defined because the components of the decomposition are admissible).

nodes.name: Both coincide fiberwise, hence globally
nodes.statement: By base change together with Proposition~\ref{proposition:dbx-dual} and Lemma~\ref{lemma:fiberwise}, these two decompositions coincide. In particular, the components of~\eqref{eq:sod-dp6-dual} are equivalent to ${\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{Z}}_3,\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_3})$, ${\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{Z}}_2,\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2})$, and ${\mathbf{D}}(S)$ respectively.

nodes.name: Regularity criterion
nodes.statement: Let ${\mathscr{X}} \to S$ be a du Val family of sextic del Pezzo surfaces. The total space ${\mathscr{X}}$ of the family is regular if and only if all three schemes $S$, ${\mathscr{Z}}_2$ and ${\mathscr{Z}}_3$ are regular.
nodes.statement_short: The total space is regular iff S, $\mathscr{Z}_2$ and $\mathscr{Z}_3$ are regular.
assumptions: Let ${\mathscr{X}} \to S$ be a du Val family of sextic del Pezzo surfaces.
conclusions: The total space ${\mathscr{X}}$ of the family is regular if and only if all three schemes $S$, ${\mathscr{Z}}_2$ and ${\mathscr{Z}}_3$ are regular.
nodes.label: proposition:smoothness

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5.13
nodes.statement: Consider decompositions~\eqref{eq:dbcx-again} and~\eqref{eq:sod-dpx-perf}. If ${\mathscr{X}}$ is regular then ${\mathbf{D}}^\mathrm{perf}({\mathscr{X}}) = {\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{X}})$, hence it follows that ${\mathbf{D}}^\mathrm{perf}(S) = {\mathbf{D}}(S)$ and ${\mathbf{D}}^\mathrm{perf}({\mathscr{Z}}_d,\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d}) = {\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{Z}}_d,\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d})$ for $d = 2,3$, which means that $S$ and ${\mathscr{Z}}_d$ are regular. The other implication is analogous.
nodes.statement_short: Regularity means perfect = bounded; compare the decompositions of D and D^perf componentwise.

nodes.name: Use both decompositions
nodes.statement: Consider decompositions~\eqref{eq:dbcx-again} and~\eqref{eq:sod-dpx-perf}.
nodes.statement_short: Use both decompositions

nodes.name: Regular total space gives regular S, Z_d
nodes.statement: If ${\mathscr{X}}$ is regular then ${\mathbf{D}}^\mathrm{perf}({\mathscr{X}}) = {\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{X}})$, hence it follows that ${\mathbf{D}}^\mathrm{perf}(S) = {\mathbf{D}}(S)$ and ${\mathbf{D}}^\mathrm{perf}({\mathscr{Z}}_d,\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d}) = {\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{Z}}_d,\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d})$ for $d = 2,3$, which means that $S$ and ${\mathscr{Z}}_d$ are regular.
nodes.statement_short: Regular total space gives regular S, Z_d

nodes.name: Converse analogously
nodes.statement: The other implication is analogous.
nodes.statement_short: Converse analogously

nodes.name: Smoothness criterion for the family
nodes.statement: Note also that a du Val family of sextic del Pezzo surfaces ${\mathscr{X}} \to S$ is smooth over $S$ if and only if the maps ${\mathscr{Z}}_2 \to S$ and ${\mathscr{Z}}_3 \to S$ are smooth (i.e.\ unramified). Indeed, this follows from Corollary~\ref{corollary:S-s} and the description of the fibers~$Z_d$ of ${\mathscr{Z}}_d \to S$ in Corollary~\ref{corollary:dbx-z2-z3}.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathscr{X}\to S$ is smooth iff $\mathscr{Z}_2\to S$ and $\mathscr{Z}_3\to S$ are unramified.
nodes.label: remark:smoothness

nodes.name: Extension of isomorphisms of $\mathscr{Z}_d$
nodes.statement: Let ${\mathscr{X}} \to S$ and ${\mathscr{X}}' \to S$ be two du Val families of sextic del Pezzo surfaces with regular total spaces ${\mathscr{X}}$ and ${\mathscr{X}}'$. Assume there is a dense open subset $S_0 \subset S$ such that for some $d \in \{2,3\}$ there is an $S_0$-isomorphism $\varphi_0 \colon {\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}_0/S_0) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }{\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}'_0/S_0)$, where ${\mathscr{X}}_0 = {\mathscr{X}} \times_S S_0$ and~${\mathscr{X}}'_0 = {\mathscr{X}}' \times_S S_0$. Then~$\varphi_0$ extends to an isomorphism $\varphi \colon {\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}/S) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } {\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}'/S)$ over $S$. Moreover, if we have an equality of Brauer classes $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}_0/S_0)} = \varphi_0^*\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}'_0/S_0)}$ then it extends to $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}/S)} = \varphi^*\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}'/S)}$.
nodes.statement_short: For regular total spaces, an isomorphism of $\mathscr{Z}_d$ over a dense open subset extends over S, along with equality of Brauer classes.
assumptions: Let ${\mathscr{X}} \to S$ and ${\mathscr{X}}' \to S$ be two du Val families of sextic del Pezzo surfaces with regular total spaces ${\mathscr{X}}$ and ${\mathscr{X}}'$.

Assume there is a dense open subset $S_0 \subset S$ such that for some $d \in \{2,3\}$ there is an $S_0$-isomorphism $\varphi_0 \colon {\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}_0/S_0) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }{\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}'_0/S_0)$, where ${\mathscr{X}}_0 = {\mathscr{X}} \times_S S_0$ and~${\mathscr{X}}'_0 = {\mathscr{X}}' \times_S S_0$.
conclusions: Then~$\varphi_0$ extends to an isomorphism $\varphi \colon {\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}/S) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } {\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}'/S)$ over $S$.

Moreover, if we have an equality of Brauer classes $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}_0/S_0)} = \varphi_0^*\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}'_0/S_0)}$ then it extends to $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}/S)} = \varphi^*\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}'/S)}$.
nodes.label: corollary:birational-isomorphism-zd

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 5.15
nodes.statement: For the first part note, that ${\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ is regular by Proposition~\ref{proposition:smoothness}, and in particular normal. Hence it is isomorphic to the normal closure of $S$ in the field of rational functions on ${\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}_0/S_0)$. The same argument works for ${\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}'/S)$, hence $\varphi_0$ extends to an isomorphism $\varphi$. The second claim is evident because the restriction morphisms $\mathrm{Br}({\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}/S)) \to \mathrm{Br}({\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}_0/S_0))$ and~$\mathrm{Br}({\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}'/S)) \to \mathrm{Br}({\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}'_0/S_0))$ of the Brauer groups are injective.
nodes.statement_short: Regular hence normal, so Z_d is the normal closure of S in its function field; Brauer groups of regular schemes inject into those of open subsets.

nodes.name: Z_d is the normal closure of S, so phi_0 extends
nodes.statement: For the first part note, that ${\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ is regular by Proposition~\ref{proposition:smoothness}, and in particular normal. Hence it is isomorphic to the normal closure of $S$ in the field of rational functions on ${\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}_0/S_0)$. The same argument works for ${\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}'/S)$, hence $\varphi_0$ extends to an isomorphism $\varphi$.
nodes.statement_short: Z_d is the normal closure of S, so phi_0 extends

nodes.name: Brauer classes by injectivity of restriction
nodes.statement: The second claim is evident because the restriction morphisms $\mathrm{Br}({\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}/S)) \to \mathrm{Br}({\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}_0/S_0))$ and~$\mathrm{Br}({\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}'/S)) \to \mathrm{Br}({\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}'_0/S_0))$ of the Brauer groups are injective.
nodes.statement_short: Brauer classes by injectivity of restriction

nodes.name: Relative Hilbert schemes $F_d(\mathscr{X}/S)$
nodes.statement: Let $F_d({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ be the relative Hilbert scheme of subschemes in the fibers of ${\mathscr{X}}$ over $S$ with Hilbert polynomial $h'_d(t)$ defined by~\eqref{eq:hdprime}.

nodes.name: Relative Hilbert schemes of lines, conics and cubics
nodes.statement: For each $1 \le d \le 3$ the scheme $F_d({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ is flat over $S$, and \begin{itemize} \item $F_1({\mathscr{X}}/S) \cong {\mathscr{Z}}_2 \times_S {\mathscr{Z}}_3$, \item $F_2({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ is an \'etale locally trivial ${\mathbb{P}}^1$-bundle over ${\mathscr{Z}}_2$, and \item $F_3({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ is an \'etale locally trivial ${\mathbb{P}}^2$-bundle over ${\mathscr{Z}}_3$. \end{itemize} Moreover, $F_2({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ and $F_3({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ are Severi--Brauer varieties over~${\mathscr{Z}}_2$ and~${\mathscr{Z}}_3$ associated with the Brauer classes $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2}$ and $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_3}$, respectively.
nodes.statement_short: $F_1 \cong \mathscr{Z}_2\times_S\mathscr{Z}_3$; $F_2$, $F_3$ are Severi-Brauer varieties over $\mathscr{Z}_2$, $\mathscr{Z}_3$ for the Brauer classes $\beta$.
assumptions: For each $1 \le d \le 3$
conclusions: the scheme $F_d({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ is flat over $S$, and \begin{itemize} \item $F_1({\mathscr{X}}/S) \cong {\mathscr{Z}}_2 \times_S {\mathscr{Z}}_3$, \item $F_2({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ is an \'etale locally trivial ${\mathbb{P}}^1$-bundle over ${\mathscr{Z}}_2$, and \item $F_3({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ is an \'etale locally trivial ${\mathbb{P}}^2$-bundle over ${\mathscr{Z}}_3$. \end{itemize}

Moreover, $F_2({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ and $F_3({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ are Severi--Brauer varieties over~${\mathscr{Z}}_2$ and~${\mathscr{Z}}_3$ associated with the Brauer classes $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2}$ and $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_3}$, respectively.
nodes.label: proposition:fd-md

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5.16
nodes.statement: Assume $d \in \{2,3\}$. The construction of the morphism $F_d(X) \to Z_d$ from Proposition~\ref{proposition:fd-zd} works well in an arbitrary du Val family of sextic del Pezzo surfaces and provides a morphism~\mbox{$F_d({\mathscr{X}}/S) \to {\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}/S)$}. Moreover, it identifies $F_d({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ with the projectivization of the (twisted) vector bundle $p_{d*}{\mathscr{E}}_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d}$, where~${\mathscr{E}}_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d}$ is the (twisted) universal sheaf on the product ${\mathscr{X}} \times_S {\mathscr{Z}}_d$ and~$p_{d} \colon {\mathscr{X}} \times_S {\mathscr{Z}}_d \to {\mathscr{Z}}_d$ is the projection. This is equivalent to the statement of the proposition. For $d = 1$ also a relative version of the argument of Proposition~\ref{proposition:fd-zd} works.
nodes.statement_short: The construction of Proposition 4.9 works in families and identifies F_d with the projectivization of the twisted bundle $p_{d*}\mathscr{E}_{\mathscr{Z}_d}$.

nodes.name: Case d = 2, 3: relative version of Proposition 4.9
nodes.statement: Assume $d \in \{2,3\}$. The construction of the morphism $F_d(X) \to Z_d$ from Proposition~\ref{proposition:fd-zd} works well in an arbitrary du Val family of sextic del Pezzo surfaces and provides a morphism~\mbox{$F_d({\mathscr{X}}/S) \to {\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}/S)$}.
nodes.statement_short: Case d = 2, 3: relative version of Proposition 4.9

nodes.name: Projectivization of twisted bundle
nodes.statement: Moreover, it identifies $F_d({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ with the projectivization of the (twisted) vector bundle $p_{d*}{\mathscr{E}}_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d}$, where~${\mathscr{E}}_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d}$ is the (twisted) universal sheaf on the product ${\mathscr{X}} \times_S {\mathscr{Z}}_d$ and~$p_{d} \colon {\mathscr{X}} \times_S {\mathscr{Z}}_d \to {\mathscr{Z}}_d$ is the projection. This is equivalent to the statement of the proposition.
nodes.statement_short: Projectivization of twisted bundle

nodes.name: Case d = 1
nodes.statement: For $d = 1$ also a relative version of the argument of Proposition~\ref{proposition:fd-zd} works.
nodes.statement_short: Case d = 1

nodes.name: Relative Hilbert scheme $F_4(\mathscr{X}/S)$
nodes.statement: Taking into account Remark~\ref{remark:f4} and Proposition~\ref{proposition:md-zd} one can prove with the same argument that the relative Hilbert scheme $F_4({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ is an \'etale locally trivial ${\mathbb{P}}^3$-bundle over ${\mathscr{Z}}_2$ with the same Brauer class~$\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2}$ as~$F_2({\mathscr{X}}/S)$.
nodes.statement_short: $F_4(\mathscr{X}/S)$ is a $\mathbb{P}^3$-bundle over $\mathscr{Z}_2$ with Brauer class $\beta_{\mathscr{Z}_2}$.
nodes.label: remark:f4-family

nodes.name: Regularity via Hilbert schemes
nodes.statement: The total space of ${\mathscr{X}}$ is regular if and only if $S$, $F_2({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ and $F_3({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ are regular.
nodes.statement_short: The total space is regular iff S, F_2 and F_3 are regular.
conclusions: The total space of ${\mathscr{X}}$ is regular if and only if $S$, $F_2({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ and $F_3({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ are regular.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 5.18
nodes.statement: By Proposition~\ref{proposition:fd-md} if $d \in \{2,3\}$, the morphism $F_d({\mathscr{X}}/S) \to {\mathscr{Z}}_d$ is smooth, hence the Hilbert scheme~$F_d({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ is regular if and only if ${\mathscr{Z}}_d$ is regular. So, Proposition~\ref{proposition:smoothness} applies.
nodes.statement_short: F_d -> Z_d is smooth by Proposition 5.16, so regularity transfers; apply Proposition 5.13.

nodes.name: Birational Hilbert schemes give isomorphic $\mathscr{Z}_d$
nodes.statement: Let ${\mathscr{X}} \to S$ and ${\mathscr{X}}' \to S$ be two du Val families of sextic del Pezzo surfaces with regular total spaces ${\mathscr{X}}$ and ${\mathscr{X}}'$. Assume for $d \in \{2,3\}$ there is a birational $S$-isomorphism $\psi \colon \xymatrix@1{F_d({\mathscr{X}}/S) \ar@{-->}[r]^-{\sim} & F_d({\mathscr{X}}'/S)}$. Then it induces a biregular isomorphism $\varphi \colon {\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}/S) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } {\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}'/S)$ over~$S$ and we have $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}/S)} = \varphi^*\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}'/S)}$.
nodes.statement_short: For regular total spaces, a birational S-isomorphism of F_d induces an isomorphism of Z_d preserving Brauer classes.
assumptions: Let ${\mathscr{X}} \to S$ and ${\mathscr{X}}' \to S$ be two du Val families of sextic del Pezzo surfaces with regular total spaces ${\mathscr{X}}$ and ${\mathscr{X}}'$.
Assume for $d \in \{2,3\}$ there is a birational $S$-isomorphism $\psi \colon \xymatrix@1{F_d({\mathscr{X}}/S) \ar@{-->}[r]^-{\sim} & F_d({\mathscr{X}}'/S)}$.
conclusions: Then it induces a biregular isomorphism $\varphi \colon {\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}/S) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } {\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}'/S)$ over~$S$ and we have $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}/S)} = \varphi^*\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}'/S)}$.
nodes.label: corollary:birational-isomorphism-fd

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 5.19
nodes.statement: Recall that ${\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ is the base of the maximal rationally connected fibration for the morphism~$F_d({\mathscr{X}}/S) \to S$. Therefore, the birational isomorphism $\psi$ of Hilbert schemes induces a birational isomorphism $\varphi_0$ over~$S$ of ${\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ and ${\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}'/S)$. Using Corollary~\ref{corollary:birational-isomorphism-zd} we deduce that it extends to an isomorphism $\varphi \colon {\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}/S) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } {\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}'/S)$. Furthermore, since $F_d({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ is a Severi--Brauer variety associated with the Brauer class $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}/S)}$ of order~$2$ or~$3$, the birational isomorphism of Hilbert schemes implies that either $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}/S)} = \varphi^*\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}'/S)}$ or~$d = 3$ and~$\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}/S)} = \varphi^*\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}'/S)}^{-1}$. In the latter case we replace~$\varphi$ by its composition with the involution $\sigma_{3,3}$ defined in Proposition~\ref{proposition:md-zd}.
nodes.statement_short: Z_d is the base of the MRC fibration of F_d, so the birational map descends; extend by Corollary 5.15 and fix the Brauer class with the involution sigma_{3,3} if needed.

nodes.name: Z_d is the base of the MRC fibration
nodes.statement: Recall that ${\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ is the base of the maximal rationally connected fibration for the morphism~$F_d({\mathscr{X}}/S) \to S$.
nodes.statement_short: Z_d is the base of the MRC fibration

nodes.name: Induced birational map phi_0
nodes.statement: Therefore, the birational isomorphism $\psi$ of Hilbert schemes induces a birational isomorphism $\varphi_0$ over~$S$ of ${\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ and ${\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}'/S)$.
nodes.statement_short: Induced birational map phi_0

nodes.name: Extend phi_0 to an isomorphism
nodes.statement: Using Corollary~\ref{corollary:birational-isomorphism-zd} we deduce that it extends to an isomorphism $\varphi \colon {\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}/S) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } {\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}'/S)$.
nodes.statement_short: Extend phi_0 to an isomorphism

nodes.name: Brauer classes agree after possibly composing with sigma_{3,3}
nodes.statement: Furthermore, since $F_d({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ is a Severi--Brauer variety associated with the Brauer class $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}/S)}$ of order~$2$ or~$3$, the birational isomorphism of Hilbert schemes implies that either $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}/S)} = \varphi^*\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}'/S)}$ or~$d = 3$ and~$\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}/S)} = \varphi^*\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}'/S)}^{-1}$. In the latter case we replace~$\varphi$ by its composition with the involution $\sigma_{3,3}$ defined in Proposition~\ref{proposition:md-zd}.
nodes.statement_short: Brauer classes agree after possibly composing with sigma_{3,3}

nodes.name: Vanishing of Brauer classes and rational multisections
nodes.statement: Let ${\mathscr{X}} \to S$ be a generically smooth du Val family of sextic del Pezzo surfaces with regular total space~${\mathscr{X}}$. \noindent$(1)$ The Brauer class $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2}$ vanishes if and only if the family ${\mathscr{X}} \to S$ has a rational $3$-multisection. \noindent$(2)$ The Brauer class $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_3}$ vanishes if and only if the family ${\mathscr{X}} \to S$ has a rational $2$-multisection.
nodes.statement_short: For a generically smooth family with regular total space, $\beta_{\mathscr{Z}_2}=0$ iff there is a rational 3-multisection, and $\beta_{\mathscr{Z}_3}=0$ iff there is a rational 2-multisection.
assumptions: Let ${\mathscr{X}} \to S$ be a generically smooth du Val family of sextic del Pezzo surfaces with regular total space~${\mathscr{X}}$.
conclusions: The Brauer class $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2}$ vanishes if and only if the family ${\mathscr{X}} \to S$ has a rational $3$-multisection.
The Brauer class $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_3}$ vanishes if and only if the family ${\mathscr{X}} \to S$ has a rational $2$-multisection.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5.20
nodes.statement: Note that the assumption implies that $S$, ${\mathscr{Z}}_2$, and ${\mathscr{Z}}_3$ are all regular (Proposition~\ref{proposition:smoothness}). Furthermore, by base change to an open subscheme in $S$ we may assume that ${\mathscr{X}} \to S$ is smooth (hence ${\mathscr{Z}}_d \to S$ are smooth as well by Remark~\ref{remark:smoothness}). If $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2}$ vanishes then the map $F_2({\mathscr{X}}) \to {\mathscr{Z}}_2$ has a rational section. Moreover, one can assume that such a rational section is not contained in the rational $2$-multisection of $F_2({\mathscr{X}}) \to {\mathscr{Z}}_2$ that parameterizes singular conics on fibers of ${\mathscr{X}}$. This means that there is a birational morphism ${\mathscr{Z}}'_2 \to {\mathscr{Z}}_2$ and a subscheme~${\mathscr{C}} \subset {\mathscr{X}} \times_S {\mathscr{Z}}'_2$ which is a family of conics on fibers of ${\mathscr{X}}$ with the general fiber over~${\mathscr{Z}}'_2$ a union of three smooth conics from distinct linear systems on a smooth sextic del Pezzo surface. Note that smooth conics from different linear systems intersect at a point, hence the projection ${\mathscr{C}} \to {\mathscr{X}}$ fails to be an isomorphism onto its image over a subscheme of ${\mathscr{X}}$ which is a rational 3-multisection of ${\mathscr{X}} \to S$. Similarly, if $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_3}$ vanishes then the map $F_3({\mathscr{X}}) \to {\mathscr{Z}}_3$ has a nice rational section, hence there is a birational morphism ${\mathscr{Z}}'_3 \to {\mathscr{Z}}_3$ and a subscheme~${\mathscr{C}} \subset {\mathscr{X}} \times_S {\mathscr{Z}}'_3$ which is a family of rational cubics on fibers of ${\mathscr{X}}$ with the general fiber over~${\mathscr{Z}}'_3$ a union of two smooth cubics from distinct linear systems on a smooth sextic del Pezzo surface. Smooth cubics from different linear systems intersect at two points, hence the projection ${\mathscr{C}} \to {\mathscr{X}}$ fails to be an isomorphism onto its image over a subscheme of ${\mathscr{X}}$ which is a rational 2-multisection of ${\mathscr{X}} \to S$. Conversely, assume a 2-multisection of ${\mathscr{X}} \to S$ exists, i.e., there is a proper subscheme $T \subset {\mathscr{X}}$ such that the map $T \to S$ is generically finite of degree~2. In the Hilbert scheme $F_3({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ consider the subscheme $F_3^T({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ that parameterizes cubic curves containing the fibers of~$T$ over~$S$. Since on a smooth del Pezzo surface in each linear system of cubic curves there is either a unique curve containing a given pair of points (if the points do not lie on a line), or a pencil of such cubic curves (otherwise), we conclude that $F_3^T({\mathscr{X}}/S) \subset F_3({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ is either a rational section of $F_3({\mathscr{X}}/S) \to {\mathscr{Z}}_3$ or is generically a sub-${\mathbb{P}}^1$-bundle. In both cases it follows that the Brauer class $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_3}$ vanishes generically over~${\mathscr{Z}}_3$, and since~${\mathscr{Z}}_3$ is regular, $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_3} = 0$. Similarly, if a 3-multisection $T$ of ${\mathscr{X}} \to S$ exists, we consider the subscheme $F_4^T({\mathscr{X}}/S) \subset F_4({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ that parameterizes quartic curves containing the fibers of~$T$ over~$S$. Since on a smooth del Pezzo surface in each linear system of quartic curves there is either a unique curve containing a given triple of points (if the points do not lie on a conic), or a pencil of such curves (if the points lie on a conic, but not on a line), or a 2-dimensional linear system (otherwise), we conclude that $F_4^T({\mathscr{X}}/S) \subset F_4({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ is either a rational section of $F_4({\mathscr{X}}/S) \to {\mathscr{Z}}_4 = {\mathscr{Z}}_2$ (in the first case), or is generically a sub-${\mathbb{P}}^2$-bundle (in the third case), while in the second case the subscheme~$F_2^T({\mathscr{X}}/S) \subset F_2({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ provides a rational section of $F_2({\mathscr{X}}/S) \to {\mathscr{Z}}_2$. In all cases it follows that the Brauer class $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2}$ vanishes generically over~${\mathscr{Z}}_2$, and since~${\mathscr{Z}}_2$ is regular, $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2} = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Rational sections of the Severi-Brauer varieties give families of conics or cubics whose mutual intersections form multisections; conversely, curves through a multisection give rational sections or sub-bundles, killing the Brauer class on the regular base.

nodes.name: Base field in Section 6
nodes.statement: Throughout this section the base field ${\mathsf{k}}$ is an arbitrary field of characteristic coprime to 2 and 3.

nodes.name: Segre embedding of $\mathbb{P}(W_1)\times\mathbb{P}(W_2)$
nodes.statement: We denote by $W_1$ and $W_2$ a pair of vector spaces of dimension 3 and let \begin{equation*} {\mathbb{P}}(W_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2) \hookrightarrow {\mathbb{P}}(W_1 \otimes W_2) \end{equation*} be the Segre embedding.

nodes.name: Linear section $X_K$
nodes.statement: We denote by $K^\perp \subset W_1 \otimes W_2$ its codimension 2 annihilator, and set \begin{equation} X_K := ({\mathbb{P}}(W_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2)) \cap {\mathbb{P}}(K^\perp) \subset {\mathbb{P}}(W_1 \otimes W_2), \end{equation} to be the corresponding linear section.

nodes.name: Definition of $X_K$
nodes.statement: X_K := ({\mathbb{P}}(W_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2)) \cap {\mathbb{P}}(K^\perp) \subset {\mathbb{P}}(W_1 \otimes W_2),
nodes.label: eq:xk

nodes.name: When $X_K$ is a sextic du Val del Pezzo surface
nodes.statement: Assume the base field ${\mathsf{k}}$ is algebraically closed. The intersection $X_K$ defined by~\textup{\eqref{eq:xk}} is a sextic du Val del Pezzo surface if and only if \begin{itemize} \item the line ${\mathbb{P}}(K)$ does not intersect the dual Segre variety ${\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee) \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2^\vee) \subset {\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee)$, and \item the line ${\mathbb{P}}(K)$ is not contained in the discriminant cubic hypersurface ${\mathscr{D}}_{W_1,W_2} \subset {\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee)$. \end{itemize} Furthermore, $X_K$ is smooth if and only if the line ${\mathbb{P}}(K)$ is transversal to ${\mathscr{D}}_{W_1,W_2}$.
nodes.statement_short: $X_K$ is a sextic du Val del Pezzo surface iff the line P(K) misses the dual Segre variety and is not inside the discriminant cubic; smooth iff transversal to it.
assumptions: Assume the base field ${\mathsf{k}}$ is algebraically closed.

Furthermore, $X_K$ is smooth if and only if the line ${\mathbb{P}}(K)$ is transversal to ${\mathscr{D}}_{W_1,W_2}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6.1
nodes.statement: First, let us show that the condition is necessary. If ${\mathbb{P}}(K)$ intersects ${\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee) \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2^\vee)$ then $K$ contains a bilinear form $b \in W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee$ of rank 1, i.e., $b = \varphi_1 \otimes \varphi_2$, where $\varphi_i \in W_i^\vee$. The zero locus of~$b$ on ${\mathbb{P}}(W_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2)$ is equal to $({\mathbb{P}}(\varphi_1^\perp) \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2)) \cup ({\mathbb{P}}(W_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(\varphi_2^\perp))$. Consequently, $X_K$ is its hyperplane section, hence is a union of two cubic scrolls, hence is not an integral surface. Next, assume that ${\mathbb{P}}(K)$ is contained in ${\mathscr{D}}_{W_1,W_2}$. Then there are three possibilities: either \begin{itemize} \item $K \subset w_1^\perp \otimes W_2^\vee$ for some $w_1 \in W_1$, or \item $K \subset W_1^\vee \otimes w_2^\perp$ for some $w_2 \in W_2$, or \item $K \subset \mathrm{Ker}(W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee \to U_1^\vee \otimes U_2^\vee)$ for some 2-dimensional subspaces $U_1 \subset W_1$ and $U_2 \subset W_2$. \end{itemize} In the first case we have $\{w_1\} \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2) \subset X_K$, in the second case ${\mathbb{P}}(W_1) \times \{w_2\} \subset X_K$, and in the third case ${\mathbb{P}}(U_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(U_2) \subset X_K$, so in all these cases the surface $X_K$ is not integral. Now, let us show that the conditions are sufficient. So, assume $K \subset W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee$ is such that the line~${\mathbb{P}}(K)$ is not contained in ${\mathscr{D}}_{W_1,W_2}$ and does not intersect ${\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee) \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2^\vee)$. Let $b_0 \in K$ be a bilinear form of rank 3 (it exists since ${\mathbb{P}}(K)$ is not contained in ${\mathscr{D}}_{W_1,W_2}$). Then $b_0$ identifies $W_2$ with $W_1^\vee$ and under this identification $b_0$ corresponds to the identity in ${\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee \otimes W_1) \cong {\mathbb{P}}(\mathrm{End}(W_1))$, so its zero locus is isomorphic to the flag variety $\mathrm{Fl}(1,2;W_1) \subset {\mathbb{P}}(W_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee)$. The subspace $K$ is then determined by an operator $b \in \mathrm{End}(W_1)$ defined up to a scalar multiple of the identity, and the condition that ${\mathbb{P}}(K)$ does not intersect ${\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee) \otimes {\mathbb{P}}(W_2^\vee)$ can be rephrased by saying that the pencil $\{b + t\mathrm{id}\}$ does not contain operators of rank~1. From the Jordan Theorem it is clear that there are only three types of such $b$: \begin{itemize} \item[$(0)$] $b$ is diagonal with three distinct eigenvalues; \item[$(1)$] $b$ has two Jordan blocks of sizes 2 and 1 with distinct eigenvalues; \item[$(2)$] $b$ has one Jordan block of size 3. \end{itemize} It is easy to see that in case (0) the surface $X_b$ is smooth (hence of type 0), in case (1) it has one $A_1$ singularity (and is of type 2), and in case (3) it has one $A_2$ singularity (and is of type 4). It remains to note that case (0) happens precisely when the line ${\mathbb{P}}(K)$ is transversal to ${\mathscr{D}}_{W_1,W_2}$.
nodes.statement_short: Necessity: a rank-1 form or a pencil in the discriminant makes X_K reducible. Sufficiency: a rank-3 form identifies X_K with a section of Fl(1,2;3) by an operator b, and Jordan forms of b give types 0, 2, 4.

nodes.name: Base S of the universal family of codimension 2 linear sections
nodes.statement: Consider the Grassmannian~$\mathrm{Gr}(2,W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee)$ parameterizing all two-dimensional subspaces $K \subset W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee$, and its open subset parameterizing subspaces satisfying the conditions of Lemma~\ref{lemma:xk-duval}: \begin{equation*} S := \{ K \in \mathrm{Gr}(2,W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee) \quad \mid \quad {\mathbb{P}}(K) \not\subset {\mathscr{D}}_{W_1,W_2} \quad\text{and}\quad {\mathbb{P}}(K) \cap ({\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee) \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2^\vee)) = \varnothing \}. \end{equation*}

nodes.statement: Let ${\mathscr{K}} \subset W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_S$ be the tautological rank 2 bundle, let ${\mathscr{K}}^\perp \subset W_1 \otimes W_2 \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_S$ be its rank~7 annihilator, and let \begin{equation} {\mathscr{X}} := ({\mathbb{P}}(W_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2)) \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1 \otimes W_2)} {\mathbb{P}}_S({\mathscr{K}}^\perp) \end{equation} be the corresponding du Val family of sextic del Pezzo surfaces.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 6.2
nodes.statement: Using homological projective duality for ${\mathbb{P}}(W_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2)$, see Theorem~\ref{theorem:hpd-p2p2}, we obtain from~\cite[Theorem~6.27]{kuznetsov2007hpd} a semiorthogonal decomposition \begin{equation*} {\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{X}}) = \langle \Phi_{{\mathscr{E}}_2}({\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}_S({\mathscr{K}}) \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_2)), {\mathbf{D}}(S) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathscr{X}}(1,0), {\mathbf{D}}(S) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathscr{X}}(0,1), {\mathbf{D}}(S) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathscr{X}}(1,1) \rangle, \end{equation*} where ${\mathbb{Y}}_2 \to {\mathscr{D}}_{W_1,W_2}$ is the resolution of singularities defined in~\eqref{eq:def-yy2}, and ${\mathscr{E}}_2$ is the derived pullback of the sheaf ${\mathbb{E}}_2$ defined by~\eqref{eq:hpd-kernel-xx3} with respect to the natural map \begin{equation} {\mathscr{X}} \times_S ({\mathbb{P}}_S({\mathscr{K}}) \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_2) \to {\mathscr{X}}_2 \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_2 \end{equation} (we will discuss this map below), where ${\mathscr{X}}_2$ is the universal hyperplane section of ${\mathbb{P}}(W_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2)$. Mutating the last component to the far left (note that $K_{\mathscr{X}} = {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathscr{X}}(-1,-1)$ in the relative Picard group~$\mathrm{Pic}({\mathscr{X}}/S)$), we get \begin{equation} {\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{X}}) = \langle {\mathbf{D}}(S) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathscr{X}}, \Phi_{{\mathscr{E}}_2}({\mathbf{D}}({\mathbb{P}}_S({\mathscr{K}}) \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_2)), {\mathbf{D}}(S) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathscr{X}}(1,0), {\mathbf{D}}(S) \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathscr{X}}(0,1) \rangle. \end{equation} We claim that this decomposition agrees with the general decomposition~\eqref{eq:dbcx-again} of a du Val family of sextic del Pezzo surfaces. Indeed, the last two components of~\eqref{eq:sod-cx-p2p2} can be considered as the derived category of~$S \sqcup S$ (the trivial double covering of $S$) embedded via the Fourier--Mukai functor with kernel \begin{equation*} {\mathscr{E}}_3 := {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathscr{X}}(1,0) \sqcup {\mathscr{O}}_{\mathscr{X}}(0,1) \in {\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{X}} \sqcup {\mathscr{X}}) = {\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{X}} \times_S (S \sqcup S)), \end{equation*} and the second component is the derived category of \begin{equation*} {\mathbb{P}}_S({\mathscr{K}}) \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_2 = {\mathbb{P}}_S({\mathscr{K}}) \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee)} {\mathscr{D}}_{W_1,W_2} \end{equation*} (recall that ${\mathbb{Y}}_2$ maps birationally onto ${\mathscr{D}}_{W_1,W_2}$ and ${\mathbb{P}}_S({\mathscr{K}})$ by definition of $S$ does not touch the indeterminacy locus ${\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee) \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2^\vee)$ of that birational isomorphism), which is a flat degree~3 covering of~$S$ (since ${\mathscr{D}}_{W_1,W_2}$ is a hypersurface of degree~3), and it is embedded into~${\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{X}})$ via the Fourier--Mukai functor with kernel~${\mathscr{E}}_2$. Let us check that both ${\mathscr{E}}_2$ and ${\mathscr{E}}_3$ are flat families of torsion-free rank 1 sheaves on fibers of~${\mathscr{X}}$ over~$S$ with Hilbert polynomials $h_2(t)$ and $h_3(t)$ respectively, parameterized by the schemes \begin{equation*} {\mathscr{Z}}'_2 := {\mathbb{P}}_S({\mathscr{K}}) \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_2 \qquad\text{and}\qquad {\mathscr{Z}}'_3 := S \sqcup S. \end{equation*} For the second family flatness is clear and Hilbert polynomial computation is straightforward, so we skip it. For the first family we note that the map~\eqref{eq:map-cx2} is flat. Indeed, by~\eqref{eq:cx-p2p2} we have \begin{equation*} {\mathscr{X}} \times_S ({\mathbb{P}}_S({\mathscr{K}}) \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_2) = \Big(({\mathbb{P}}(W_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2)) \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1 \otimes W_2)} {\mathbb{P}}_S({\mathscr{K}}^\perp)\Big) \times_S \Big({\mathbb{P}}_S({\mathscr{K}}) \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_2\Big), \end{equation*} while \begin{equation*} {\mathscr{X}}_2 \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_2 = ({\mathbb{P}}(W_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2)) \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1 \otimes W_2)} Q \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_2, \end{equation*} where $Q \subset {\mathbb{P}}(W_1 \otimes W_2) \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee)$ is the incidence quadric, so the map~\eqref{eq:map-cx2} is induced by the natural map ${\mathbb{P}}_S({\mathscr{K}}^\perp) \times_S {\mathbb{P}}_S({\mathscr{K}}) \to Q = \mathrm{Fl}(1,8;W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee)$. This map factors as \begin{equation*} {\mathbb{P}}_S({\mathscr{K}}^\perp) \times_S {\mathbb{P}}_S({\mathscr{K}}) \hookrightarrow {\mathbb{P}}_{\mathrm{Gr}(2,W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee)}({\mathscr{K}}^\perp) \times_{\mathrm{Gr}(2,W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee)} {\mathbb{P}}_{\mathrm{Gr}(2,W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee)}({\mathscr{K}}) = \mathrm{Fl}(1,2,8;W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee) \to Q. \end{equation*} The first map is an open embedding, while the last map is a ${\mathbb{P}}^6$-bundle, so the composition is flat (and even smooth). Recall the embedding of the Weil divisor ${\mathbb{Y}}_2 \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2) \hookrightarrow {\mathscr{X}}_2 \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_2$ defined by~\eqref{diagram:yy-cx3}. Its preimage under the map~\eqref{eq:map-cx2} is a Weil divisor in ${\mathscr{X}} \times_S ({\mathbb{P}}_S({\mathscr{K}}) \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_2)$ such that for any geometric point~$(K,b,w_1)$ of ${\mathscr{Z}}'_2 := {\mathbb{P}}_S({\mathscr{K}}) \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_2$ its fiber is the Weil divisor \begin{equation*} L := X_K \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1)} \{w_1\} \subset X_K, \end{equation*} i.e., a line on the sextic del Pezzo surface $X_K$ contracted by the projection $X_K \to {\mathbb{P}}(W_1)$ to the point~$\{w_1\} \in {\mathbb{P}}(W_1)$. Thus, by~\eqref{eq:hpd-kernel-xx3}, the sheaf we are interested in is the twisted ideal ${\mathscr{I}}_L \otimes {\mathscr{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1)}(1)$. In particular, it is torsion-free, and its Hilbert polynomial equals~$h_2(t)$. Therefore, the families of sheaves ${\mathscr{E}}_2$ and ${\mathscr{E}}_3$ induce maps \begin{equation*} \mu_2 \colon {\mathscr{Z}}'_2 \to {\mathscr{Z}}_2({\mathscr{X}}/S) \qquad\text{and}\qquad \mu_3 \colon {\mathscr{Z}}'_3 \to {\mathscr{Z}}_3({\mathscr{X}}/S) \end{equation*} such that the Brauer classes $\mu_2^*(\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2})$ and $\mu_3^*(\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_3})$ are trivial and ${\mathscr{E}}_2$ and ${\mathscr{E}}_3$ are isomorphic (up to twists by line bundles on~${\mathscr{Z}}'_2$ and ${\mathscr{Z}}'_3$) to the pullbacks of the universal bundles ${\mathscr{E}}_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2}$ and ${\mathscr{E}}_{{\mathscr{Z}}_3}$, respectively. This means that for $d \in \{2,3\}$ we have isomorphisms of Fourier--Mukai functors \begin{equation*} \Phi_{{\mathscr{E}}_{d}} \cong \Phi_{{\mathscr{E}}_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d}} \circ \mu_{d*} \circ T_d \colon {\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{Z}}'_d) \to {\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{X}}), \end{equation*} where $T_d$ is a line bundle twist in ${\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{Z}}'_d)$. Since both $\Phi_{{\mathscr{E}}_{{\mathscr{Z}}_d}}$ and $\Phi_{{\mathscr{E}}_d}$ are fully faithful, so is the composition $\mu_{d*} \circ T_d \colon {\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{Z}}'_d) \to {\mathbf{D}}({\mathscr{Z}}_d)$. Moreover, comparing semiorthogonal decompositions given by~\eqref{eq:dbcx-again} and~\eqref{eq:sod-cx-p2p2}, we conclude that $\mu_{d*} \circ T_d$ is essentially surjective, i.e., an equivalence of categories. Since $T_d$ is also an equivalence, we conclude that $\mu_{d*}$ is an equivalence, hence $\mu_d$ is an isomorphism. Thus ${\mathscr{Z}}'_d \cong {\mathscr{Z}}_d({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ and the Brauer classes $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_2}$ and $\beta_{{\mathscr{Z}}_3}$ on~${\mathscr{Z}}_2({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ and~${\mathscr{Z}}_3({\mathscr{X}}/S)$ vanish.
nodes.statement_short: Apply HPD for P^2 x P^2 (Theorem C.1) to get a decomposition, match its components with (eq:dbcx-again) by checking that the HPD kernels are flat families of rank-1 sheaves with Hilbert polynomials h_2, h_3. The induced maps to Z_d are then isomorphisms since they induce equivalences.

nodes.name: Extended family of all codimension 2 linear sections
nodes.statement: Considering the family $\bar{\mathscr{X}} \subset {\mathbb{P}}(W_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2) \times \bar{S}$ of \emph{all} codimension 2 linear sections of~${\mathbb{P}}(W_1) \times {\mathbb{P}}(W_2)$ over $\bar{S} := \mathrm{Gr}(2,W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee)$ and applying the semiorthogonal decomposition of Theorem~\ref{theorem:hpd-p2p2}, we obtain \begin{equation*} {\mathbf{D}}(\bar{\mathscr{X}}) = \langle {\mathbf{D}}(\bar{S}), {\mathbf{D}}(\bar{{\mathscr{Z}}}_2), {\mathbf{D}}(\bar{{\mathscr{Z}}}_3) \rangle, \end{equation*} where $\bar{{\mathscr{Z}}_2} = {\mathbb{P}}_S({\mathscr{K}}) \times_{{\mathbb{P}}(W_1^\vee \otimes W_2^\vee)} {\mathbb{Y}}_2$ and $\bar{{\mathscr{Z}}_3} = \bar{S} \sqcup \bar{S}$. nodes.name: Reconstructing a family from $\mathscr{Z}_3 = S\sqcup S$
nodes.statement: Let ${\mathscr{X}} \to S$ be a du Val family of sextic del Pezzo surfaces.
